Uniform Title: Sādhanamālā, Volume 1 Author: Benoytosh Bhattacharya

Description: This text is a compendium of *sādhanas*, that is, ritual procedures for the worship of Buddhist Tantric deities, particularly those of the *Anuttarayoga Tantra*. Each *sādhana* provides a description of the deity—including its form, color, vehicle (*vāhana*), and so forth—along with the corresponding visualization (*bhāvanā*), as well as the deity’s mantra and its applications in ritual worship and yogic practice. These were composed by a wide range of eminent Buddhist masters. The earliest author is the Siddha Saraha, who is dated to approximately 630 CE. Alongside him are numerous other great Buddhist Siddhas, such as Nāgārjuna, Kukkurīpa, Indrabhūti, Kṛṣṇapāda, Śabara, and others, who flourished during the seventh and eighth centuries. The latest contributors belong to the twelfth century, which establishes the terminus ad quem for the compilation of this collection.

Sādhanamālā | Oṃ, homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
I pay homage to the glorious *Trisamaya*, the source of all prosperity and happiness,
which is like a wondrous wish-fulfilling gem for those exhausted by the miseries of existence.
The correct means of proof has indeed been set forth here by the former teachers;
however, fearing prolixity, it is taught here in brief.

In this *Śrītrisamayarāja*, the great king of tantras, a mantra-practitioner who has duly obtained authorization within the great tantra— the maṇḍala of mantras or the maṇḍala of colored powders— and who abides by the commitments (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*) prescribed therein, desires to perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*).

Dwelling in mountains, forests, and the like, or in solitary and secluded places such as caves, houses, gardens, and mountain retreats that are delightful, one should first, in front of an image of the Buddha, prepare a mandala strewn with flowers for this root vidyā, prostrate, and generate the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).

Having surrendered oneself to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should practice the recitation (*japa*) based on that prostration and recite it one thousand times. Thereby, the hundred-thousand-fold recitation for all mantras becomes accomplished. Furthermore, all protective and other such mantras become perfected for him. In this regard, the following is the *vidyā*:
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! May the infinite Victors, together with their Sons— stainless, removers of stains,
and reaching beyond all limits— grant the boon of the *vara-dāma*.
Grant the most exalted, supreme, equal, and eternal boon! In this regard, these are the vajra-words:
*arara asama sama* [k, ḍh: *asamasamantā*] *samantānanta dharma te khaṇa khaṇa mahāvīrācale sama sama asahamahābale kaṇa kaṇa mahāvarāgrike haha haha* [k].
Ḍha: huhu huhu vajra-vajrāhvaye dhara dhara huṃ huṃ maṇḍalaṃ samabalāgravikrame kuru kuru turu turu sarvathā sarvaṃ hi jvala jvala agre agriṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā.

Then, for the sake of exhausting all karmic obscurations, one should recite the hundred-syllable heart-mantra of all the Tathāgatas eight thousand times according to that very same procedure. Karmic obscurations such as those resulting from defiling the True Dharma or the immediate (ānantarya) offenses will be abandoned.
And this is it:

Homage to the Tathāgatas of the three times, who have entered into the nature of phenomena characterized by the attainment of universal unimpededness. Oṃ! O you whose teaching is the attainment of the infinite and the peerless and equal everywhere! Remove, remove! Remember, remember! O you whose awakening-dharma is free from passion! Move, move! O you of equal power! Laugh, laugh! Triple, triple! Oṃ! K! Ḍha! Aṃ! (Note: The syllables *k*, *ḍh*, and *aṃ* are provided as variants in manuscripts *k* and *ḍh*).
A: *trayaṃ trayaṃ gaganamahāvaralakṣaṇe jvalajvalanasāgare svāhā*.
Then, as a limb of the means for achieving one's own and others' exaltation, one should perform the ritual of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) in this manner. Therein, at the outset—
Having risen early in the morning, one should direct one's aspirations toward all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as lords. One should prostrate in this manner:
"As many Victors as there are, together with their sons, residing in the infinite world-systems..."
With body, mind, and speech, I bow down to them all.
Then one should generate the thought of awakening:
"I generate the mind directed toward perfect awakening for the sake of the awakening of all embodied beings."
I shall practice the conduct of auspiciousness, which brings about the welfare of all sentient beings.

Then, for the purpose of destroying all obstacles, one should bind the Vajra-mudrā and recite [the mantra] three times while focusing the heart on Amoghacaṇḍa, who is as immovable as a mountain. In this regard, this is the Vajra-mudrā:
having extended the right hand upward, one should press the tip of the index finger with the thumb.

[Ḍh: with the distracted hand] | The remaining [fingers] have the characteristics of a vajra. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ cāṭ amoghacaṇḍa mahāroṣaṇa sphāṭaya huṃ bhramaya bhramaya huṃ traṭ hāṃ māṃ*.
One should also form the svastika mudrā: having made a fist with the fingers joined together inwardly, the two middle fingers are like needles.
One should hold the two index fingers slightly touching the tips of the thumbs. The mantra is: *oṃ hara hara mahānimitta hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Then, having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, seated comfortably upon a pleasant seat,
and having visualized the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in the ten directions before any one of a cloth painting, a manuscript, or a statue,
he should prepare a mandalaka strewn with loose flowers.

As before, having prostrated with all one's limbs while reciting the verse and having generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should offer oneself to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: "I, who am named so-and-so, offer myself to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; may you accept me in every way and at all times."

"May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas empower me; may the Great Compassionate Protectors become the bestowers of the boon of accomplishment (siddhi) upon me. Then, one should confess all misdeeds. All misdeeds...
Possessing passion, hatred, and delusion,
I confess all [faults] at all times without exception, so that the Blessed Ones, having understood them, may [pardon me].

"Knowing this," one should then rejoice in merit. One should rejoice with the supreme rejoicing in all the accumulations of merit and wisdom— both mundane and supramundane, belonging to the three times— of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Thinking, "Just as the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know," one should then, while remaining in the paryanka posture, bind this Samaya-mudrā. With the hands joined in an añjali at the head, this is the Samaya-mudrā. The mantra is: *namaḥ susiṅge sādhani agre*.
O Compassionate One, O Bestower of Boons, O You of supreme power, homage be to You!
Svāhā! To those who grant excellent accomplishments, the Greatly Merciful Ones! By this, the commitment (*samaya*) of all mudrās and mantras is revealed.

Then, having bound the vajra-mudrā as before, one should recollect the heart-mantra of Acala: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇām acala kālacaṇḍa sādhaya hūṃ phaṭ*. Then, one should place the vajroṣṇīṣa-mudrā upon the head; in the right fist, one should position the thumb upright.
Mantra: Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
O you who possess the three crests at the peak [of the trident], homage be to you! O you who are the supreme Dharma, immovable and endowed with the three qualities on all sides, shake it off!
"Swiftly destroy the thicket of the lotuses of afflictions and suffering for the world, and bestow all happiness;

perform this at the three times, svāhā! By means of this, the practitioner does not fall away from the Mahāyāna, and accomplishment becomes free from obstacles. Furthermore, there is great protection in the five [directions].

One should place [the hands] upon the various locations; great protection will ensue. Having formed the *añjali* with palms facing upward, one should place the little fingers and ring fingers in the middle of the hand.

The little finger is slightly bent outward; one should place the thumb upon it. The middle fingers are like needles, and having bent the two index fingers at their sides, one should place them on the third joint. This is the great mudrā named Asahā. The mantra is:
Homage to all Vajras! Oṃ haṃ [k, ḍh aḥ huṃ huṃ] sphāṭayāmahe huṃ phaṭ!
Then, one should perform the armor-rite with the Mahākavaca-mudrā, the Invincible Vajra; [the fingers] are the little finger and the thumb.

Others are in the shape of a wedge (*śaṅkulā*), with their roots, middles, and tips joined together; these are the Ajitavajrās. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ oṃ haṃ huṃ vajramaye varakavace ho vajra vajra huṃ phaṭ*.
Thus, he becomes utterly invincible to Māra and others.

Having thus performed self-protection, one should perform protection of the place. Therein, with the Vajrāsana-mudrā, one should consecrate the seat as being made of vajra. Having assumed the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka), one should place the right hand upon the upturned left hand.
One should place the Vajrāsana mudrā upon the lap (or, according to k and ḍha: upon the head). The mantra is:

*namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ oṃ haṃ huṃ vajrāsane vaṃ huṃ phaṭ*. Then, with the Vajramaṇḍapa mudrā, one should consecrate one’s own place as consisting of vajra, using the gesture of salutation and joined palms.

Inserting the two index fingers and the two middle joints of the ring fingers inside so that they are broken at the middle joint, and arranging the remaining fingers in the shape of four pillars while the others are in the form of beams, this is the Vajramaṇḍapa mudrā.
The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantavajrāṇām oṃ haṃ huṃ vajrāgrabhuvane*.
*Gramu-vanama* maṃ huṃ phaṭ. Then, one should place the vajra-fence (*vajraprākāra*) with its corresponding mudrā.

Having formed the *añjali* gesture with palms facing upward, one places the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*) between the middle fingers; the middle fingers act as needles, and the pair of index fingers (*tarjanī*) are positioned at the third joint in the shape of a vajra.
One should place the two thumbs on the sides;
this is the *prākāra-mudrā*. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ oṃ haṃ huṃ vajramaṇḍale bandha*.

*Bandha huṃ phaṭ!* Then, one should place a vajra-pañjara (diamond cage) above that with its mudrā: the two ring fingers and the two index fingers of the hands joined in *praṇāma-añjali* are bent back at their backs in opposite directions. Upon the ring fingers and index fingers, there is a wheel; those very [fingers]... [k:]

The two middle fingers should be extended, while the two index fingers and the two little fingers are bent at the back in a reversed manner; this is the *pañjara-mudrā*. The mantra is: *namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ oṃ haṃ huṃ vajrāgrabhuvane muḥ huṃ phaṭ*.
Then, one should place it with that mudrā, held by the Vajrajvālā [mudrā].
One should rotate the left hand, with fingers joined, over the right hand which is in the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayakarā*). This is the Vajrajvālā. The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇām oṃ haṃ huṃ vajrajvāle*.
*Huṃ* *huṃ* phaṭ!
Then one should bind the boundary. Forming a fist with the right hand and raising the index finger, one should rotate it to the right. This is called the "Boundary-Binding" seal (*asīmā*). Of this—
The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ oṃ haṃ huṃ mahāsīmābandhe bandha bandha vajre vajriṇi huṃ phaṭ*.
Then, having thus completed the circle of protection, [the practitioner], while remaining in his own place, [proceeds]...

One should offer the *arghya* to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with the Tathāgata-sambhava-mudrā; then they will attend to one and become bestowers of the boon of accomplishment (*siddhi*). With the hands formed into a fist, the two little fingers are extended and opened.

The Tathāgata-sambhava-mudrā. The mantra is: *namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānām āḥ amalavikrāntatejini araje svāhā*. Then, in the event that external offerings such as perfumes and the like are unavailable— [ṅ:
gandhyāhya, k, ḍh a: gandhāda; k, ḍh a: sambhava]—

Having purified [the offerings] with the Acalavajra-mudrā, one should perform the worship after consecrating the incense and other items eight times each with their respective mantras. Therein, the mantra for the incense is as follows:

Homage to all the Tathāgatas of the three times! O Blessed One, supreme among all incomparable fragrances, radiate throughout the expanse of space, O accomplisher of all goals for the great prosperity!
Svāhā! This is the mantra of flowers. Homage to all the Tathāgatas of the three times!
*Āvartāvarta-mahāpuṣpavati svāhā*. This is the incense mantra.
*Namastraiyadhvikānāṃ sarvatathāgatānām agre agraśikhe dhūmaśikhe svāhā*. This is the lamp mantra. *Namastraiyadhvikānāṃ...* [of all the Tathāgatas of the three times...]

*O you who shine and blaze as the crest of the lamp-light of all the Tathāgatas, svāhā!* This is the mantra for the food offering (*naivedya*). *Homage to all the Tathāgatas of the three times! Arara parara karara, O Bali-deity, bestow the offering! Great Bali, svāhā!* Then...

One should thus offer the various articles of worship situated in the world-systems of the ten directions. Having joined the palms in salutation, one should offer those special articles of worship in the world-systems of the ten directions which are peerless and unappropriated: those born on land, such as jewel-mountains and wish-fulfilling trees; and those born in water, such as oceanic jewels.

One should utter these words: "I offer to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas all things such as golden lotuses and others that exist in all world-systems, including all divine and human forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects. In this same way, one should offer clouds of mental offerings.
One should cause it to proceed. Having formed the *pūrṇamudrā*, characterized by the hands being slightly contracted at the tips in the gesture of salutation (*praṇāmāñjali*), one should speak thus:
"By the power of the empowerment of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and by the power of merit from equal vows..."
And by the power of the spells of knowledge (*vidyā-mantra*), they have manifested throughout the circles of assemblies of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as excellent and sublime [deeds],
brought forth through the conduct of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

Having reflected, "May great clouds of offerings spread forth," one should recite eight times this Great Queen of Vidyās, the performer of the empowerment of offerings: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānāṃ sarvathodgate sphura himaṃ gaganakaṃ samantataḥ svāhā*.

Then, having reflected: "May oceans of clouds of melodic hymns praising the diverse qualities of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and oceans of clouds of melodic recitations of the Dharma, proceed everywhere to purify all world-systems," [one should recite] these eight Vidyārājñīs that bring forth the production of these clouds of melodic hymns of praise.

One should recite the mantra: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānāṃ sarvatra saṃkusumitābhinnārājñi namo 'stu te svāhā*. Then, from all focal points, clouds of emanations of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—equal in extent to the bodies of all sentient beings everywhere throughout the oceans of all world-systems—[proceed forth].
Having emanated [the light] and reflected, "May all the sufferings of all sentient beings be pacified; may they attain all mundane and supramundane prosperity,
up to the purity of the body and so forth of Samantabhadra," [one should recite] this...
One should recite the Mahāvidyārāja eight times: "Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
Homage be to you, O Great Vajra, who brings benefit to all beings! Abide everywhere, having empowered all phenomena (sarvadharmāṇām), svāhā! And all this [should be done] everywhere.

In this regard, one should have faith that worship and so forth can occur unfailingly through the power of mantras and the like. Furthermore, one should dedicate this root of merit toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, just as the Buddha Bhagavāns authorize such a dedication being made.
(9) "By this merit, having fully awakened to the enlightenment of the conduct of Samantabhadra through this root of goodness, may I also [lead] all sentient beings..."
"I establish [all beings] in the purity of the conduct of Samantabhadra.

Then, for the sake of obtaining the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should bind that mudrā and recollect the previously mentioned hundred-syllable mantra or the five-syllable mantra. The two hands are rubbed against each other.
Having joined the fingers with their tips touching and palms facing upward, and having formed the two index fingers and the two little fingers in the shape of a wedge,
one should hold the two thumbs level and facing upward between the needle-like middle and ring fingers; this is the Śatākṣara mudrā.

As for the five-syllable mudrā: having formed the *sampuṭa-añjali*, one should press the tips of the two thumbs with the two index fingers; the remaining fingers remain likewise in the shape of a needle. The mantra is: *namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānām*.
Āḥ vīra huṃ khaṃ!
Then, one should bind the Samantāvabhāsoṣṇīṣa or the Dharmacakra mudrā, which comprises all mudrās.
With both hands extended and palms turned upward, one should place the nails against each other with the middle fingers,
and then press them down with the tips of the thumbs. The two little fingers should be joined at their tips like needles, and likewise the two middle fingers should be joined at their nail-tips.
The middle and middle-fingers are joined in the shape of a needle; this is the Samantāvabhāsa-uṣṇīṣa. Having thus moved the two index fingers, one should touch nail with nail.
In the form of a circle is the *dharmacakra-mudrā*. The mantras for these two, respectively, are: *āḥ maṃ haṃ* and *oṃ dhuna yātaya cchinda cakreṇa vajriṇi hūṃ*. Having bound one of these two, (p.

Having recited the mantra once, whether standing or seated, one should perform the recitation (*japa*). One will not be overcome by Māra and others, and accomplishment (*siddhi*) will become manifest to him. Then, for the sake of swift accomplishment, one should first form the *dharmodaya* mudrā and recollect that mantra. Having formed a fist with the left hand, [one extends] the index finger, the little finger, and the thumb.

And one should extend it upward; this is the Dharmodayā mudrā. The mantra is: *namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānām āḥ sarvathā sarvatrāṇake svāhā*. Having recited the mantra once with one’s own mudrā, one should display the *samaya*. One’s own mudrā, however, should be understood according to the appropriate application.
[It should be said:
Then, practicing the recitation based on prostration to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should recite the mantra as desired— neither too fast nor too slow— and free from improper thoughts.
One should recite with the mind focused on the syllables of the mantra until weariness arises.

Then, having risen, one should recite the noble *Gaṇḍavyūha* and other sūtras, as well as the *Tathāgatahr̥daya*, after recollecting them even once; or, having made offerings, at the very least, having prostrated.

One should eat. While eating, one should consecrate the food eight times with this mantra and, having offered the first morsel to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should eat a moderate portion. In this regard, the mantra is as follows: *namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānām oṃ*.

*Balandade tejomālini svāhā*. From the remains of what has been eaten, a morsel should be offered after consecrating it once with the *Amogha-caṇḍa-hṛdaya* mantra for the goddess Acalā. That becomes a continuous bond there which bestows the attainment of success (*sukhasiddhi*). And when he has rested after eating...
Having performed the confession of misdeeds and so forth, one should remain solely in the delight of the true Dharma.

If one is capable and not distracted, one should perform all these preliminaries—such as the protective rites and the offerings—and recite the mantra even in the afternoon; otherwise, one should rely only on the protection and other rites already performed in the forenoon.
Having firmly resolved that it remains unrelaxed and steadfast, one should dispel the obstacles with the Noble Immovable Vajra Mudrā together with its mantra.

Having performed protection with any one of the five-syllable mantras and so forth together with its mudrā, and having carried out the worship, praise, and other rites, one should perform the recitation (*jāpa*) as before. At the end of the day, having dismissed the enclosure, the cage, and so forth, one should perform the armor (*kavaca*) with the *raśmimālinī* [mantra]. Having formed fists with the fingers interlocked and the middle fingers in the shape of needles—

One should extend the pair of index fingers and place the two thumbs at their third joints; this is the Raśmimālinī mudrā. The mantra is: *namastraiyadhvikānāṃ tathāgatānāṃ mahāsamayagatiṃ gate samate sama sarvathā sattvatrāṇake*.

A: *Trāṇaka*! To that which is integrated within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), *svāhā*. During the first and last watches of the night, one should remain awake through the recitation of the sublime Dharma (*saddharma*) and other such practices. During the middle watch, on a bed free from any elevated headboard, one should sleep while prostrating with all one’s limbs toward all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. [K, Ḍh: one should prostrate, not sleep.]
And one should express this intention: "May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas grant me their empowerment;
may they bestow the boon of supreme accomplishment, and may they pacify all calamities. This very same ritual procedure is to be performed every day.
This continues until one hundred thousand recitations are completed on the full moon day, or until the signs of accomplishment appear. Then,
on the full moon and other such lunar days, having observed the fast by abstaining from food and being bound by the *poṣadha* vows,
one should sit upon young shoots or sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass.
In front of any one of these— a reliquary, a cloth painting, a manuscript, or an image—
one should prepare a mandala strewn with flowers,
having performed the preliminary rites of protection, worship, and so forth, as previously described.
Having formed the *dharmodaya-mudrā*, one should recollect its mantra; then,
having formed the mudrā of one’s own deity, one should recite its mantra seven or eight times.
One should display the *samaya*.
Then, having prostrated to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and taken up the wheel-worship and other offerings,
one should desire the purification of the body and so forth of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra.
Fixing one’s heart upon the accomplishment of one’s own desired goal, and practicing the recitation (japa) while taking as one’s object of focus the prostration to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
one should do so with a mental state that practices the rejoicing in the accumulations of merit and wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
One should recite from the time of the twilight glow until midnight or sunrise;

then that wheel and so forth will certainly blaze. When it blazes, great signs appear from the sky—like the appearance of a Buddha—including rains of flowers, the sound of drums, divine voices, and the words of "Well done! from the Tathāgatas.

There occur most marvelous events, such as the shaking of the Buddha-fields, and all the families of vidyādharas assemble; by them he is consecrated. He becomes one who propitiates the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in all world-systems, possesses the five superknowledges, and is highly rejoiced in by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, he becomes a king of the vidyādharas, accompanied by an infinite retinue of vidyādhara women; following after happiness, he is not separated from that very body. And with that same body, through the gradual accumulation of the provisions, he traverses all the stages of a bodhisattva.
...up until one attains perfect awakening. Furthermore,

other mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*), such as the vision of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), and the auspicious jar (*bhadraghaṭa*), are achieved by this very procedure, or by the procedure seen in the chapter on common objects, after having consulted the tantra.
They are to be accomplished by those free from doubt; they will certainly succeed—this is the method of accomplishment for those possessing the means (*upāya*).
However, those lacking the means should perform the practice according to their ability, thinking, "I am not capable [of practicing] as it has been described."
One must not despair. At the very least,

having performed a single protection for oneself, having contemplated the binding of the boundary (*sīmābandhana*), the worship, and so forth, and having recited their mantras, one should recite or accomplish [the rite] as much as desired, in accordance with one's vigor.

Having obtained permission, the rite will certainly succeed in accordance with the action; even a single person is capable of protecting the three worlds according to the words of the Tantra. This Amoghasiddhi is the King of the Three Samayas, and his accomplishment is free from obstacles.

Regarding the "procedure for desired aims," this means that even without the procedures for prior service (*pūrvasevā*) and so forth, one simply takes as one's object of focus all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The practice of mantras is performed with a mind intent on the welfare of the world.

And in this regard, mantras being accomplished succeed by whatever method or even by whatever desired procedure one chooses. As it is said in this very [text]: "In a secluded and solitary place, free from social contact and crowds..."

For beings who feel remorse, even without worship, even without a painting, even without the practice of ritual bathing and so forth, and even if they have fallen into a lower state, that which is to be accomplished will necessarily be achieved. Furthermore, it is stated twice as something most wonderful: in whatever manner the mantras are practiced, in that very manner they become corresponding; and by which...
They are joined by the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) and through that very means they are accomplished.
Furthermore, it has been said:
"He whose *bodhicitta* is firm and who is free from doubt..."
One should have such a conviction; no doubt should be entertained, for this will certainly succeed for him.
Thus, having generated diligence and abandoned doubt, one must practice; it will certainly succeed. And herein, for the sake of success, the seeker of accomplishment must guard the samaya.

One must cultivate oneself with even firmer effort, for that is the root of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). And that is the *samaya*: the true Dharma must not be rejected; one must not show contempt toward the gurus;
one must not drink intoxicants; one must not sleep on high beds; and one must not break the forms of the *vajra*.

"Those who are to be bypassed," and so forth, must necessarily be understood from the Tantra; however, for fear of prolixity, they are not written here. And by one desiring to bathe, who is a reciter of the Three Samayas, with the Heart-mantra of Noble Acala and Amogha-caṇḍa itself, accompanied by the Vajra-mudrā—

One should perform the consecration of all substances for bathing, such as clay and so forth, as well as the expulsion of the wicked and the binding of the boundary (*sīmābandha*), by means of that very mantra. By that alone, all obstacles are pacified.
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of the *Trisamayarāja*.
This work is by the venerable Paṇḍita Kumudākaramati.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
You who are immovable and equal, whose nature is the essence of equanimity, whose very self is compassion, and who remove suffering from the world.
Bestowing the accomplishment of all qualities without exception, they are stainless and immovable, possessing the supreme dharma of equanimity.
There is no comparison to the sky even for a mere atom or speck of dust among their qualities, which are boundless;
they bestow the supreme accomplishment upon the realms of sentient beings— both existent and non-existent— and are beyond all analogy, possessing universal success.
The accomplishment of their vows, which is eternally stainless, arisen from the impulse of compassion, and characterized by a nature free from contradiction,
shines forth constantly for those whose very essence is great mercy; it is intent upon accomplishing the welfare of the world and is never obstructed.
The one who is filled with the practice of compassion does not go toward cessation; she bestows the supreme accomplishment in the three worlds.
Having reached perfect completion within the immeasurable and the infinite, oh, she has attained the state even among those who have attained their states!
The nature of the sublime Dharma.
May those who have attained the supreme state of the bestowers of boons grant me the supreme accomplishment at the three times, always being intent upon the highest gift.
The Lords, who are the foremost practitioners granting boons to all three worlds, have unobstructed access to the three paths.
Thus ends the praise proclaimed in the *Viśvāmararāja-kalpa* and sung by Vajradhara.
This is the expansion of the marvelous qualities of all the Buddhas;
indeed, all mantras are accomplished even when recited but once.
Truly, those Tathāgatas, being satisfied by this king of hymns,
bestow vast accomplishment that endures for an eon and is impelled by the eon.
And they reveal themselves in forms so enchanting that one can never look enough:
the great lord Vairocana, Akṣobhya, and Ratnasambhava.
They proclaim the Victorious One Amitābha, the pure Amogharāja, and from every perspective, the essence, the elixir, the reality, and the supreme [teachings].
All delightful and vast accomplishments without exception,
as well as the fulfillment of every hope and desired objects of the mind, bestow supreme auspiciousness— knowledge, longevity, strength, and speed.
Thus it is said. This very hymn, along with its benefits, is also recited in the *Vajramaṇḍalalaṅkāra-mahāyoga-tantra*.
Homage to the Buddha!
Having bowed with devotion to the Buddhas of the three times and to the sons of the Buddhas, I shall explain a portion of the *samaya* as proclaimed in the *Śrī-Trailokyavijaya-samaya-tantra*.
The True Dharma must never be rejected nor ever abandoned;
one must not show disregard for the Perfect Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas.
One should be obedient toward the guru, neither showing him contempt nor killing any living beings.
One should not perform mantra and mudrā oneself, nor should they ever be destroyed.
Avarice and the drinking of intoxicants must never be practiced;
the vajra-pledges are not to be transgressed, nor are they ever to be broken.
One should not lie upon a bed, nor show disrespect toward seals and so forth, nor toward the directions;
one should not behave like a child toward the guru or toward the deities.

One should not perform malevolent magic, nor should one offend those of virtuous conduct; one should neither commit an improper act, nor perform what ought not to be done, nor approve of any sinful deed.
In brief, whatever is disagreeable to oneself or another should not be done;
this is the rule remembered in the Great Kalpa in the glorious *Trisamaya*.
Regret, the stain of livelihood, delight in socializing,
excessive doubt, and the grasping for requisites.
Laziness, a dejected mind, self-exaltation, and the like—
these obstructive factors are proclaimed here in this *Kalparāja*.
Freed from these defects, abiding in the previously mentioned time,
free from all attachment, faithful, and possessing a mind fixed on perfect enlightenment;
Dedicated to the welfare of the three worlds, through the activities of speech, mind, and body,
one should accomplish the desired siddhi according to the ritual prescribed for the three samayas.
The Sādhana of Trisamayarāja. This is the work of the scholar Ratnākaraguptapāda.
Homage to Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata! [Ḍh: Homage to the Buddha; k: Homage to Vajrāsana!]
Having bowed to all the Tathāgatas, who are the support of a multitude of virtues, for the sake of others,

I shall explain according to reality that true sādhana which brings about the pacification of the excellent state of Buddhahood— unaffected by the planetary afflictions of the faults of saṃsāra— and which belongs to the Guru whose body is adorned with the name Śrīvajrāsana.
Likewise, the body composed of various colored Tathāgatas and so forth is depicted.
Then, having visualized before him the Blessed One— the Buddha endowed with the colors, arms, and so forth as will be described,
accompanied by all the Tathāgatas and the rest—
one should offer flowers and other gifts, reciting: *oṃ namo akṣobhyāya hūṃ | oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā*.
One should offer each three times: Oṃ namo vairocanāya oṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ namo ratnasambhavāya trāṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ namo'mitābhāya hrīḥ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ...
Homage to Amoghasiddhi! Khaṃ! Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Locanā! Loṃ! Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Māmakī! Māṃ!
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Pāṇḍarā! Pāṃ! Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā! Oṃ...

Again, one should offer a vast, even more abundant quantity of flowers to the one whose form is Akṣobhya and who sits upon the vajra-throne, following this very sequence: OṂ VAJRADHŪPE HŪṂ SVĀHĀ; OṂ VAJRAGANDHE...

Having performed the ritual of worship with "huṃ svāhā oṃ vajranaivedye huṃ svāhā oṃ vajradīpe huṃ svāhā" and so forth, one should then proceed preceded by the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables].
One should visualize a moon disc transformed from the syllable *A* within one’s own heart (*svahṛdaya*), and upon it, the syllable *HŪṂ* of golden color.
Having seen the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas emerging from its rays, one should then [offer worship] with spreading clouds of bathing and offerings.
After bathing, worship with flowers and other offerings;
then perform the confession of sins, the rejoicing in merit, the dedication of merit,
the going for refuge to the Three Jewels, and taking recourse in the path of the Jinas.
Having descended, one should generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) by reciting "The Three Jewels are my refuge," and so forth.

Then, one should meditate upon emptiness. Having meditated on all phenomena as being devoid of intrinsic nature, one should contemplate the syllable-form, which is the very nature of the thought of awakening.

One should perceive oneself as luminous. For the sake of stabilization, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho 'ham*. That very [luminosity] transforms into the form of light, which is a moon-maṇḍala; above that is the syllable *huṃ*.

One should visualize a white-colored moon mandala, completely transformed from all things, surrounded by the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, and further surrounded by the consonants beginning with *ka*. Above that is the seed-syllable *huṃ*.

From that, a yellow-colored vajra is produced; and upon the hub (*varaṭaka*) of that vajra, there is the syllable *huṃ*. Having transformed all of this together, it takes the form of the vajra-throne.
His seat consists of the four Māras, and it is golden in color; these are the Māras of the aggregates (skandha), afflictions (kleśa), death (mṛtyu), and the son of a god (devaputra).
The Māras are white, red, black, and dark green in color. Having visualized their forms in this sequence, one should imagine a lion throne constructed by these Māras;
upon that, a universal lotus and a vajra; and thereon, the Blessed One, two-armed, seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture.
The yogi should visualize himself as peaceful, seated in the paryaṅka posture, with his right hand forming the earth-touching mudrā and his left resting on his lap, his body draped in red garments.
Then he should generate the ego-identity (*ahaṅkāra*)—[the syllable] *huṃ*. Oṃ.
"I am of the nature of the essence of the *dharmadhātu*. Then, to the right of the Blessed One, [one should visualize] the Bodhisattva Maitreya, fair-complexioned, with two arms,

afterwards, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Upon both eyes of the Blessed One is a moon-maṇḍala, and above that is the syllable *kṣīṃ*, white in color.

Upon the lunar mandala at the two ears is the syllable JAṂ, blue in color; upon the lunar mandala at the two nostrils is the syllable KHAṂ, yellow in color; upon the lunar mandala on the tongue is the syllable GAṂ, red in color;
and upon the lunar mandala on the forehead is the syllable SKAṂ, dark green in color; [at the two breasts...]

Then, having visualized in one's own heart a vajra transformed from the syllable *hūṃ* within a moon mandala, and upon that vajra’s central hub (*varaṭaka*) a syllable *hūṃ* atop a moon mandala— one transforms all of that into the Jñānasattva, just like the Samayasattva.
One should contemplate as follows:

then, on the head, there is a moon disc; above that, a white wheel transformed from the syllable *uṃ*; and in its center, the syllable *uṃ* situated upon the moon—this is the purification of the Blessed One’s body. On the throat...
Above that moon mandala is an eight-petaled lotus transformed from the syllable ĀḤ, which is red in color; in its center,
situated upon the moon mandala, is the syllable ĀḤ.
The meditation on the purity of the Blessed One’s speech consists of a moon mandala above the navel;
upon it is a black vajra transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*, and in its center is a *hūṃ* situated upon a moon mandala— this is the meditation on the purity of the Blessed One’s mind.

"Buddha-siddhi" is that which bestows the fruit of Buddhahood. Then, having summoned the Blessed One situated in space by means of the light rays from the seed-syllable in the heart—using the four syllables *jaḥ*, *huṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *hoḥ*—one should establish him in front. To him...
One should offer the *arghya*, *pādya*, *ācamana*, seat (*āsana*), and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Afterwards, one should provide food consisting of milk and other items;
thus is the tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*) prescribed. Then, with this [verse]: "I pay homage to all the Buddhas."

One should perform the praise with a hymn of praise. Then, having unified the *samayasattva* with the *jñānasattva*, one should recite: "You are the pledge (*samaya*), you are the pledge; I am the pledge. Oṃ āḥ hūṃ."
One should make [the deity] non-dual with the mantra. Afterwards, when weary from meditation (bhāvanā), one should perform recitation (japa): *oṃ āḥ vajra hūṃ svāhā*.

This is the mantra for recitation. Afterwards, having dedicated the merit toward perfect enlightenment and having performed the dismissal (*visarjya*), one should dwell as one pleases. By this merit, may all sentient beings quickly attain the gnosis of the Tathāgatas.
[They] come to be.
The ritual procedure for the instruction on the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) of the venerable Vajrāsana is completed.
Following the previously described procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness,
there appears upon a moon disc a blue syllable *HŪṂ* surrounded by the sixteen white vowels beginning with *A*,
and further surrounded by the thirty-four white consonants beginning with *Ka*.

Having transformed all this into a moon disc, one should again place that same seed-syllable upon it; through its transformation, a yellow vajra arises, and within its hub (varaṭaka) is that same seed-syllable.
Having transformed all of this, one should instantly manifest oneself as the venerable Buddha Bhaṭṭāraka on the Glorious Vajra-Throne.

[Viṣpā]: Two-armed and one-faced, yellow in color, seated upon an excellent great lion throne pressed down by the four Māras; above that, on a double lotus and vajra, he is established in the vajraparyaṅka posture, with his left hand resting on his left lap and his right hand in the earth-touching mudrā (bhūsparśamudrā).

Having visualized [the deity] whose body is veiled by garments as red as the hue of the *bandhūka* flower, with a form so enchanting that every limb and member is exquisite, one should cultivate the non-dual ego-identification: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.

One should perform [the rite]. Thereafter, to the right of the Blessed One, one should visualize the Bodhisattva Maitreya, golden-yellow in color, with two arms, wearing a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*), holding a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) in his right hand and a *nāgakeśara* flower bud in his left hand. Likewise...

To the left, one should visualize the Bodhisattva Lokeśvara, white in color, wearing a crown of matted hair (jaṭāmukuṭin), holding a fly-whisk with his right hand and a lotus in his left hand; these two should be seen gazing toward the face of the Blessed One. Then, one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).

One should perform [the visualization]: at the two eyes of the Blessed One, a white syllable *kṣi* situated on a moon; at the two ears, a blue syllable *jaṃ* situated on a moon; then, in the nostrils, a yellow syllable *khaṃ* situated on a moon; on the tongue, a red syllable *gaṃ* situated on a moon; and on the forehead—

A green syllable *skaṃ* situated upon a moon between the breasts; a white syllable *saṃ* situated upon a moon at the center of the chest; then, from a syllable *huṃ* situated upon a moon in the heart, a vajra arises; in its central hub is a syllable *huṃ* together with a moon; on a moon-maṇḍala at the throat, within a lotus born from the syllable *āḥ*, is a syllable *āḥ* situated upon a moon.

[Candra Āḥ]: This is the meditation on the purity of speech. On the moon at the head, within an eight-spoked wheel born from the white syllable OṂ, is the syllable OṂ situated upon the moon; this is the meditation on the purity of body. Above the navel, within a moon, is the syllable HŪṂ together with a vajra; this is the meditation on the purity of mind. Then—

Having drawn forth the Jñānasattva by means of the seed-syllable in the heart, and having unified it with the various offerings such as *arghya* and *pādya*, one should generate the non-dual ego-consciousness (*advayāhaṅkāra*) with the mantra: *oṃ samayas tvaṃ samayas tvaṃ samayo ’ham oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. Then, when weary from meditation, [one should recite] the mantra.
One should recite: Oṃ āḥ vajra huṃ svāhā.
Thus ends the Vajrāsana-sādhana.
Homage to Vajrāsana!
Having first performed the purification of the mouth and other parts, one should visualize a yellow syllable *huṃ* upon a moon disc transformed from the syllable *aḥ* in one's own heart.

Having drawn forth the Guru, the Buddhas, and others with those rays, one should worship them. Then, having performed the confession of misdeeds and so forth, and having brought emptiness to manifestation, one should consecrate it with that mantra. Thereafter, through the arousal of former vows, one should emanate a form-body for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
One should visualize a yellow syllable *huṃ* in the center of a moon disc, encircled by the sixteen white vowels beginning with *a*;
furthermore, it is surrounded on the outside by clusters of letters beginning with the white *ka*.
Having observed that entire [visualization] transformed into a stainless moon disc, one should perform the earth-touching mudrā (*bhūsparśamudrā*) with the right hand.
[He is] seated on the lap, with his left hand [holding the consort], draped in saffron-colored robes,
resting upon four lions of blue, white, red, and black, standing upon a double-lotus and vajra, peaceful, with limbs endowed with the primary and secondary marks. Of that Blessed One...

To the right is the Bodhisattva Maitreya, fair-complexioned, with two arms, wearing a crown of matted locks; his right hand holds a jeweled fly-whisk (*cāmara*), and his left holds a cluster of *nāgakeśara* flowers. Likewise, to the left is Lokeśvara, white in color, holding a fly-whisk in his right hand.
With the left hand, one should visualize him holding a lotus;
both hands should be depicted as gazing at the face of the Blessed One. Then, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*):
at the eyes of the Blessed One, the syllable *kṣiṃ*, white and situated upon a moon; at the two ears...
A blue syllable *jaṃ* situated upon a moon disc in the nostril;
a yellow syllable *khaṃ* on a moon in the tongue; and a red syllable *gaṃ* on a moon in the [tongue]. (p. 25)

One should visualize a dark syllable *kaṃ* situated on a moon at the forehead, and a white syllable *saṃ* situated on a moon between the breasts. Thereafter, having performed the meditation on the Jñānasattva, one should visualize an eight-spoked wheel, white and born from the syllable *oṃ*, atop a moon-maṇḍala upon the head, and the syllable *oṃ* situated on a moon above that, at the throat.

Upon the moon is an eight-petaled lotus born from the syllable *āḥ*; in its center is the syllable *āḥ* situated upon a moon; and in the heart is a vajra born from the syllable *huṃ* situated upon a moon, containing its own seed-syllable. Through the purification of body, speech, and mind, one should meditate on these three in this manner. Thus.
Having meditated upon the Blessed One until weariness arises, one should recite the mantra. In this regard, the mantra is: Oṃ āḥ vajra [vajrasattva] hūṃ svāhā.
Thus ends the *Vajrāsana-sādhana*.
Homage to the Noble Great Vidyā of the Six Syllables.
First, the mantra practitioner, seated on a comfortable seat and having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, should visualize the Guru,
Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas in front of him, emerging from rays of light radiating from the white syllable *hrīḥ* situated upon a moon disc in his own heart.
Having seen [the Buddhas and others] and having worshipped them,
one should perform the going for refuge and so forth with the words, "The Three Jewels are my refuge," and so on. As many sentient beings as are included within the category of sentient beings—

Whether born from eggs, born from a womb, born from moisture, or of spontaneous birth; whether possessing form or formless; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—whatever extent the realm of sentient beings is conceived and designated, it is so designated.

"Having cast them down, I must establish all beings in the realm of nirvana without remainder. Then, one should recite three times: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. Following that, [one should contemplate] emptiness.
One should meditate for a moment [or, according to k and b: having meditated for just a moment]. Immediately thereafter [or, according to k and b:
following that], upon a white lotus in one's own heart [or, according to k, kh, ḍh, and g: in the heart], there is a moon mandala; above that, the white syllable Hrīḥ. From that...
Having meditated on it as emitting hundreds of thousands of manifold rays, by means of those rays,
the entire mass of afflictions such as passion, accumulated since beginningless time by all sentient beings without exception, is purified for those beings.
Then,
one should cause that very thing to enter back into that same place; [one should visualize] oneself as transformed into that lotus.

One should meditate on the form of Lokeśvara, adorned with all ornaments, white in color, and four-armed; holding a lotus in the left hand and a rosary in the right hand, while the other two hands are joined in the *saṃpuṭāñjali* gesture at the heart. To the right...

Likewise, one should visualize Maṇidhara, endowed with his respective colors and arms, seated upon another lotus; and likewise on the left, the Mahāvidyā Ṣaḍakṣarī seated upon another lotus. Then: Oṃ mahāsukha vajrasattva jaḥ huṃ vaṃ hoḥ.
One should recite the sovereign king of empowerment mantras: *suratattvam alalalalahoḥ aḥ aḥ aḥ aḥ*.
Having meditated thus, [one should visualize] from the moon disc at the heart of oneself as Lokeśvara, [the mantra] in the form of a rosary string.

One should visualize this king of mantras— which is like a wish-fulfilling jewel for the hearts of all Buddhas— as white in color, emerging from the mouth and entering the navel by means of the rotation of a wheel, through the yoga of signlessness. Then, one should perform the recitation.
Having attained wandering, entering [into the state], and so forth, through a very short period of time, the faithful, compassionate, and guru-devoted yogi achieves perfection.

*Oṃ maṇipadme hūṃ*—this is the mantra for recitation (*jāpamantra*). Then, at the time of rising, one should rise while uttering this king of mantras: *Oṃ vajrasattva samayamanupālaya vajrasattvatvenopatiṣṭha*.
Be firm for me; be easily satisfied for me;
be easy to nourish for me; be devoted to me; grant me all accomplishments, and [make] my mind [successful] in all activities.

"Bring about the highest good! Huṃ ha ha ha ha ha hoḥ [ho], O Blessed One, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me; become vajra-like, O Great Samaya Being! Āḥ. Having spoken thus, one should dwell according to the face [of the deity]. The *Ārya-Ṣaḍakṣarī-mahāvidyā-sādhana* is completed.
Having prostrated before the Lord born of the Lotus family, who has the Omniscient One as his crown ornament, I shall explain the sādhana that destroys all diseases.
First, there is the accomplishment that follows from the teacher;
therefore, one should worship the guru with all one's being and with great effort.
When the Guru is fully satisfied, the accomplishment of the ritual action arises.
For one who has entered the mandala, accomplishment is authorized in every way;
by guarding his own samaya and vows, he will certainly attain success.

Having first performed the purification of the face and other preliminary rites, one should bring down the Blessed Lord (Bhaṭṭāraka) depicted on a cloth or similar medium into a temple. Then, within one's own heart, by means of the first syllable, one should visualize a moon-maṇḍala; upon that, the fourth letter of the eighth group as the seed-syllable (bīja), with its seat provided by the second letter of the seventh group, adorned by the fourth letter of the first group.
Then, having emitted from that white-colored, delightful [syllable] joined with the sixteenth [vowel], rays of light in all directions,

and having seen the Gurus— manifested by those rays— in the form of the Buddhas, one should worship and pay homage to them with this mantra: *oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajradīpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajragandhe hūṃ*.
Oṃ vajranaivedye hūṃ. Then:
"The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds."
I rejoice in the merit of the world and fix my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly;
I generate the mind of awakening for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others.
I generate the supreme, excellent thought of awakening;
I invite all sentient beings in great numbers.
I shall practice the desired course of conduct for supreme enlightenment; may I become a Buddha for the benefit of the world.
Thus, preceded by a formal resolve (*praṇidhi*), one should meditate upon the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*) with this mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.
One should contemplate the seed-syllable as having an appearance like an illusion (*māyopamākāra*).
The entire triple world is seen and indeed touched in every way, just like an illusion;
yet the stability of the whole world is not apprehended at all.
Having thus resolved, one should then remove the seed of unreal conceptualization belonging to beginningless time and resolve upon the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
*Oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho 'ham*. Then, from the aforementioned seed-syllable, a lotus is produced; above that is the syllable *hrīḥ*, and all of that—
When it is perfected, one should visualize the illustrious Lokanātha seated upon a moon within a lotus and vajra,
in the vajra-paryaṅka posture; he has the luster of the moon, the brilliant color of a jasmine flower or the moon, wears a crown of matted locks, is peaceful,
bears Amitābha as his crest-jewel, and is clothed in a tiger skin.

One should visualize [the deity] with four arms, adorned with various ornaments; the right hand holds a lotus embellished with jewels; the two [other] hands joined together in the *sarvarājendra-mudrā* situated at the heart.
Then, one should generate the sense of identity, thinking, "I am indeed Lokeśvara. Thereafter, having summoned the Jñānasattva...

One should offer the *arghya*, *pādya*, and so forth with one’s own mantra according to the instruction. According to the instruction...

Having performed the consecration, the binding of the armor and the turban, the visualization, the rhythmic clapping, the offerings, and the praises, one should perform the recitation preceded by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). One should visualize the six-syllable mantra upon a moon disc at one's own heart—like a garland of lamps illuminating the interior of a house. The mantra is: [k: mantraḥ]

[Having been dropped in: *oṃ maṇipadme hūṃ maṇipadme hūṃ*. One should recite this one hundred thousand times (*akṣaralakṣam*). Then, by the second and third [recitations], one becomes free from defilement; even for one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), success is achieved through ten million recitations (*koṭijāpena*).
Then, desiring to rise, one should offer the water for honor (*arghya*) and so forth, and conduct oneself with a distinguished sense of self (*viśiṣṭāhaṅkāreṇa*).
Having recited [the mantra] during the four junctions of the day, having dedicated the roots of merit for the attainment of one's desired goal,
at midnight, having dismissed the gnosis-being (jñānasattva),
having uttered the hundred-syllable mantra, and having performed the protection of body, speech, and mind—
"One should dwell at ease. If one wishes to destroy diseases and the like, then, according to the instruction,
one should prepare a square mandala before the Blessed Lord using cow dung fallen during the Puṣya constellation, interspersed with the intended six-syllable mantra, one hundred and eight times.
One should recite the eight-syllable mantra. It is accomplished in six months; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the sādhana composed according to the tradition of the *Kāraṇḍavyūha*.

According to the previous injunction, [one should visualize] the lunar disc, the seed-syllable with three and a third [parts], surmounted by the thirteenth [vowel], adorned with the moon-drop; from that very [syllable] is manifested the illustrious Lokanātha, wearing a crown of matted hair, peaceful.

One should visualize [the deity] as stainless like a moonbeam, adorned with all ornaments, holding a lotus in the left hand and displaying the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) with the right, seated upon a lotus and moon throne. Having formed fists with both hands, one should seal [the deity] with this mudrā, which resembles the closing of the middle petals of a lotus. Then, perform the recitation (*jāpa*).

One should recite: *Oṃ maṇipadme hūṃ*. By one hundred thousand recitations, one becomes free from defilement; in the second or third [hundred thousand], one sees dreams. Even for one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, success is achieved through ten million recitations.
The *Śrīmallokanāthasādhana* is complete.
Perfectly arisen from the gnosis of the syllable Hrīḥ, Hālāhala possesses a great body;
he has three eyes and three faces, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
The god who bears the crescent moon, whose crest is formed by a skull-cup,
within whose matted locks resides the image of the Jina, and who is adorned with all ornaments.
Resplendent like a white lotus, imbued with the erotic and other aesthetic sentiments,
possessing six arms and a smiling face, and beautifully clad in a tiger skin.
In the right hands, he displays the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), a rosary (*akṣamālā*) in the second,
and the dance of Śarabha in the third; in the left hands, he is adorned with a lotus.
In the second [hand] she holds a breast, and in the third a bow;
in the right [hands] there is a trident encircled by a serpent.
In her left hand is a full skull-cup filled with various fragrant flowers,
resting upon a red lotus and held in a graceful, playful pose.
The practitioner of yoga should meditate upon [the deity] situated within a cave of a jewel mountain,
manifesting through various miraculous displays consisting of radiant images composed of Buddhas.

While consuming all kinds of food, one should recite mantras as internal speech through non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) and cultivate them according to the sequential yoga; thus,
enlightenment that brings supreme bliss is swiftly attained.
The samādhi named Vajra that Accomplishes All Desires and Satisfies Hālāhala.

Having placed the syllable *hrīḥ* upon the moon in the heart— [according to manuscript *k*: the syllable *jīḥ*]— and having performed the meditation on the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*),
one should emanate red rays from it.
Equal to the sky.
And having transformed the world of moving and stationary beings into the form of Lokeśvara for the sake of the bodhisattvas, he caused them to enter his heart.
Having instantaneously transformed that syllable Hrīḥ through the yoga of gnosis,
it becomes white and red in color, with a luster like that of a ruby.
Wearing a crown of five Buddhas, his eyes wide with joy; and on the left, holding a sixteen-petaled lotus stalk in emulation.
He causes a lotus to blossom with his right hand at his heart;
he is seated upon a peacock in the center of a lunar disc.
Seated upon the sattva-paryaṅka, amidst the festival of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa),
performing the great rite within the caitya, he dwells in the gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra).
One should constantly meditate upon the supreme Vajradharma; thus one shall attain awakening.
Tired of meditative cultivation, one should recite with an undistracted mind, having placed [the mantra] like a garland upon the moon of the heart. In this regard, the mantra to be recited is:
Oṃ Vajradharma Hrīḥ. This is the concise *sādhanopāyikā* of Vajradharma.
Homage to the Six-Syllable Lokeśvara!
Having taken hold of embodied beings with a mind rightly intent upon the welfare of others, [k, g: saṃrahi]...
It is the complete pacification of all suffering and is established in true happiness.
With the mind fixed upon that, having reflected in the heart, one should meditate on the one of pure radiance;
with its shimmering rays, one should illuminate one's own body.
Having rested according to the rule and having withdrawn [the visualization] with right reflection,
the practitioner should clearly recite the mantra, radiant as white light.
Having thus caused [the breath] to enter by means of the circle of one's own navel, one should withdraw it into the heart;
performing this, one should meditate threefold for the purification of body, speech, and mind.

In that regard, one should contemplate the purification of one's own body and so forth by means of the mantra residing within one's own body, while one should contemplate the purification of living beings by means of the mantra gone outside.
One should perform the ritual for each of the three deities appearing before one, who have arisen from the mantra recited as seen [in the scripture],
according to the sequence of the mantra's utterance and withdrawal.
The manifestation of various offerings and their actual production, as well as their dedication;
then, from that, fulfillment, purification, and the dedication for the sake of the desired goal.
Then one should perform the recitation of the mantra according to the prescribed rule;
at the conclusion of the recitation, having performed the worship and other rites as before, one should dissolve the deity into one's own heart.

Having attained meditative concentration and so forth, the mantra-practitioner, performing this rite at the four junctions of the day, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times in solitary places such as houses.
Without concern for the breath, the recitation should be performed, refined by the radiance [of the deity].
For the destruction of evil and in all such cases, the mandala should be square.
Having had [an image] such as a cloth-painting made, or having meditated upon the All-pervading Lord before it,
or having performed the worship of the mandala or the ritual adoration,
one should carry out these prescribed rites.

In this regard, the instruction on the form of the deity is as follows: [one should visualize him] seated in the paryanka posture, white in color, holding a rosary and a lotus, with his hands joined in the *sampuṭa-añjali* gesture.
Having seen the Lord and his image, the Goddess, seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana).
One should contemplate the Noble Lady as yellow, holding a jewel-tassel in her left hand and an empty right hand,
wearing a jeweled crown, and seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana).
[The one who is] all-pervading and eternal.
Thus, in the *Āryaṣaḍakṣarīmahāvidyālokeśvarabhaṭṭārakopadeśa* (p.
in a certain section on the practice of the *Ṣaḍakṣarī*, the Blessed One is described as holding a lotus marked with a jewel and a book.

Maṇidhara, however, holds a jewel and a lotus, but without a book; Ṣaḍakṣarī holds a book and a lotus, but without a jewel. The worship mantra is: Oṃ Lokeśvara, accept this flower, svāhā!
