The phrase beginning with “naivedyādi” (food offerings, etc. is to be understood. For another deity, the invocation should be performed accordingly.
This is the mantra for summoning the circle of gnosis (*jñānamaṇḍala*): *oṃ mahāsukha vajrasattva jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ suratastvaṃ alalalalahoḥ aḥ*.
Aḥ aḥ aḥ.
The Sadhana of the Six Syllables.
Homage to Khasarpaṇa!
First of all, the practitioner, having sat upon a comfortable seat and performed the purification of the mouth and other preliminary rites—
In a clean, open space, having visualized a moon disc within one's own heart by means of the syllable *A*, and above that the white syllable *Hrīḥ*,
one draws in the Gurus, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others from the sky in front by means of its rays.
Having performed worship with clouds of offerings arising from the rays of light of the seed-syllable in the heart, and having performed the confession of misdeeds and so forth,
as well as the meditation on the four divine abodes, one should then meditate on emptiness: *oṃ*.

One should consecrate oneself with the thought: "I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Thereafter, as before, having visualized the syllable *hrīḥ* and having expanded it throughout the expanse of space, one should withdraw it and [visualize] that which arises from it.

One should visualize oneself as Lokeśvara, possessing the radiance of ten million moons, wearing a crown of matted hair with Amitābha as his crest-jewel, adorned with all ornaments, with a smiling face,
seated in the half-lotus posture upon a lotus and moon seat, and displaying the gesture of granting boons with the right hand.

Holding a lotus in the left hand; on the right side are Noble Tārā and Sudhanakumāra, and on the left side are Bhṛkuṭī and Hayagrīva. Then, having visualized the syllable Oṃ at the head, the syllable Āḥ at the throat, and the syllable Hūṃ at the heart, one should remain until exhaustion. Upon exhaustion, however—
One should recite the mantra. In this regard, the mantra is: Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā.
Thus concludes the *Ārya-khasarpaṇa-lokeśvara-sādhana*.
Homage to Khasarpaṇa!
You possess the glory of a wish-fulfilling tree, resplendent in bestowing desired fruits.
The caravan leader who ensures safety on the great path of the Sugata’s method; the son of the Sugata,
whose nature is equal to existence and equal to peace, and who is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
May this very one, whose hand holds a lotus, pacify the sins of the world.
Having performed the purification of the face and other parts in the morning in a secluded place,
one should sit upon a soft seat, with rays from the seed-syllable on the moon at the heart.
Having meditated on one's own seed-syllable in the heart, as radiant as the full moon,
and having stimulated it, one should bring it forth from its rays into the courtyard of the sky.
One should worship the glorious protector Khasarpaṇa, along with the lineage of gurus, buddhas, and their noble sons,
with various clouds of offerings arising from their respective seed-syllables.
Then, having paid homage, one should perform the confession of sins and so forth.

Whatever unwholesome deed I have committed, caused others to commit, or rejoiced in while it was being committed by another, as I wandered through beginningless saṃsāra— all that I confess before the Blessed Ones.
Having rejoiced in all the merit performed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the sons of the Buddhas, the noble ones, and others, I fully dedicate it without exception toward perfect awakening.
I go for refuge to the Buddha, the supreme one composed of compassion;
and to the Dharma, which, by means of all phenomena, has the nature of the essential flavor.
And it is with form, yet stainless.

And likewise, I entreat the Buddhas— who have entered the stages beginning with *muditā* (the Joyous), who possess the lineage of Bodhisattvas, and who desire to bring about the cessation [of suffering]— to remain for a long time for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others.

I generate the mind set upon awakening (*bodhicitta*), which is the cause for uprooting all obscurations; and with pure intention, I take refuge in the single path of the Sugata and his sons. Then, having reflected that this entire world—both moving and unmoving—is empty because it is devoid of being one or many: *oṃ*.

One should consecrate emptiness with the thought: "I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Having consecrated it and observed that "all these phenomena are pure by nature, and so am I," one should recite: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho 'ham*. Then...

The meditator, whose nature consists of consciousness alone and who is impelled by previous vows, [perceives] upon a stainless full moon disc— arisen from the syllable *A* (or *Hūṃ*)— upon a lotus of his own color transformed from the syllable *Paṃ*.
Having visualized the syllable *hrīḥ* as exceedingly luminous, pervading the expanse of the sky with its mass of radiating rays,
one should behold a fully blossomed lotus transformed from that [syllable], adorned with a stalk and containing its own seed-syllable within its pericarp.

Then, one should meditate upon the Blessed One as the self who has fully matured into this form: his body white as the rays of ten million moons, with matted locks bound upward in a crown and Amitābha as his crest-jewel.
[Amṛtābhakṛta]: Seated upon a moon disc atop a multicolored lotus in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka), his body adorned with all ornaments,
possessing a smiling face, appearing about sixteen years of age, and [wearing a webbed hand]— [k, ḍh, g].
His body has a hand in the boon-granting gesture on the right,
while the left hand holds a lotus with its stalk; he delights in consuming the streams of nectar flowing from his hands, and beneath that [lotus] is placed a face looking upward.
Having a large belly, an extremely emaciated body, and a very white complexion, with a needle-like mouth, he satisfies [beings],
dwells within the interior of the glorious Mount Potalaka, and gazes with a compassionate and affectionate look.
[She has] a gentle gaze, is attended by the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*), is exceedingly peaceful, and is adorned with various marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
In front of her is Tārā, and on her right side is Sudhanakumāra. There, Tārā is dark-complexioned...
She is dark-complexioned, with her left hand holding a lotus with its stalk and her right hand opening it;
she is adorned with various ornaments,
her breasts swelling with fresh youth, and the young Sudhana stands before her with his palms joined in reverence.
He has a radiance shining like gold, assumes the form of a youth, carries a book tucked under his left arm, and is adorned with all ornaments.
To the west is Bhṛkuṭī Hayagrīva, and to the north is Bhṛkuṭī; there, Bhṛkuṭī is four-armed, golden-hued, and wears matted hair and a skull-tiara.

[Jakalapiṇī]: In her left hand she holds a triple staff (*tridaṇḍī*) and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*); in her right hand she displays the gesture of salutation (*vandanābhinaya*) and holds a rosary (*akṣasūtra*). She has three eyes. (p. 41) [Ḍhandhanā]

Hayagrīva is red in color, dwarfish, and pot-bellied; his tawny hair blazes upward, and he wears a snake as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). His round face is adorned with a row of tawny beard and mustache, and his three eyes are red and circular; his eyebrows are arched and furrowed in a frown.

b, g: [Bhṛkuṭī], wearing a tiger-skin garment, holding a staff as a weapon, and making the gesture of salutation (*vandanābhinaya*) with her right hand. All of these should be visualized as standing in whatever posture is most beautiful, their gazes directed toward the faces of their respective lords. Then, upon a moon disc in one's own heart, the syllable *hrīḥ*.
Having visualized this, one should emanate various forms of rays from it,
filling the triple world; having established all sentient beings in the state of Lokeśvara,
one should cause those rays to re-enter that very same seed-syllable.
Then, having drawn forth the *jñānasattva* by those very rays and made it one in form with the *samayasattva*, like milk and water; thereafter, through the purification of body, speech, and mind,
one should place a white syllable *oṃ* on the head and [the syllable *āḥ*] on the throat in due order.
One should visualize a red syllable *māḥ* at the heart and a black syllable *huṃ*;
these [syllables] incessantly emit infinite webs of light rays that destroy the entire mass of defilements of the multitude of sentient beings.
One should make the meditation clear according to one's capacity.
Through the yoga of meditation, the energetic practitioner attains proficiency, retention, wisdom, good fortune, health, prosperity, and direct realization.
But one who is weary from meditation should recite the mantra with a one-pointed mind. Herein is the mantra: Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā.
And these syllables are like a garland of stars, stainless as autumn.
Radiant like a garland of jasmine stars, with many shimmering rays of light,
one should dedicate the merit from the fatigue of recitation, rise up,
and wander at ease while maintaining the divine identity (*devatāhaṅkāra*).
By whatever merit I have acquired through composing this heart-pleasing manual for the practice of the glorious Lokeśvara, may the entire world attain that very state.
Thus ends the *Khasarpaṇa-sādhana*.
This is the work of the venerable Padmākaragupta.
Homage to the illustrious Khasarpaṇa!
Here, a lay follower (upāsaka) named Śubhaṅkara, who performs auspicious deeds and is filled with compassion, was indeed preparing to go to Potalaka; while traveling through the district of Khāḍī—
There is a village named Khasarpaṇa where he resided; however, the Blessed One Āryāvalokiteśvara gave him this injunction:
"Do not go there; rather, establish us here according to the sequence of the Vairocanābhisambodhi Tantra-king. By that, [great benefit] was achieved.

(43) "The welfare of sentient beings will be accomplished. Regarding this, there is the traditional teaching that he caused the Blessed One to act with great speed. In that context, the perfection of the vision for the sake of accomplishing the Blessed One's purpose is performed.
For it is said: "O monk, it is better for a monk to have a failure in ethical discipline than a failure in view.

Therefore, having first observed all phenomena as momentary and selfless, and being free from all conceptual constructions, one should cultivate a compassionate intention, thinking: "Alas! These sentient beings are afflicted by afflictions, karma, and so forth. Then...
Being excessively tormented by the sufferings of birth, old age, and death, they experience manifold forms of misery.
Therefore, having become the Lord of the World (*lokeśvara*), I shall remove their suffering and establish them in the knowledge of the Omniscient One.
Having thus formed this resolute vow, [he visualizes himself] in the center of the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus born from the syllable *paṃ* within his own heart.

Having placed the five seed-syllables— *a*, *āḥ*, *trāṃ*, *suṃ*, *bhṛṃ*, and *haṃ*— upon a moon disc arising from the syllable *a*, and having summoned and brought those Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas by means of their garlands of light rays, one should place them in the expanse of the sky directly in front.

Having performed the sevenfold worship—consisting of prostration, offering, confession of misdeeds, taking refuge in the Three Jewels, and so forth—or the elevenfold worship, one should cultivate the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras), such as loving-kindness and compassion. Then: Oṃ.
Having recited, "I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness," and having realized the awakening of emptiness,

the Blessed One Avalokiteśvara becomes the self of yoga. He is white as an autumn reed, wears a crown of matted hair upon his head bearing Amitābha, is adorned with all ornaments, and stands upon a thousand-petaled lotus atop a jeweled lion throne.
Lalitākṣepa has two arms and one face; with his left hand he holds a lotus, and with his right he displays the gesture of granting boons while pouring forth a stream of nectar.
Seated upon a sattva-paryaṅka, in front of him is Tārā, with a complexion like dark gold,
her breasts high and full, adorned with all ornaments, her two hands placed near her eyes like the buds of blue lotuses,
and possessing three eyes. Following her is Sudhana-kumāra, radiant as gold and adorned with jewel ornaments.

Adorned with extensive ornaments and a jeweled crown, with a lotus tucked under his left arm, he has his palms joined in reverence. Following him is [the goddess] Bhṛkuṭī, wearing a crown of matted hair, adorned with a *caitya* upon her head, radiant as gold, clad in red garments, and performing a salutation with her right hand.

Another holds a rosary, with his two left hands occupied by a triple staff and a water-pot. Following that is Hayagrīva, blazing and radiant, with tawny hair standing erect, adorned with snakes, red in color, pot-bellied, clothed in a tiger skin, and holding a staff in his hand. Thus is the Blessed One fivefold in nature.

One who is to be meditated upon along with his retinue, and likewise one who is to be worshipped, should be treated in this manner. Then, having first prepared a mandala within the constructed mandala, one should perform the protection rite: *Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi rakṣa rakṣa māṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. *Oṃ vajrarekhe hūṃ* is the mandala mantra. *Oṃ āgaccha bhagavan*.

Upon the lion throne in the mandala, when the request has been made with the mantra "Oṃ Āḥ," one should worship the fivefold deity seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus atop the lion throne in the center of the constructed mandala.
In that regard, the offering mantras are: Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ; Oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ; Oṃ vajragandhe hūṃ.

Oṃ vajrāloke hūṃ | Oṃ vajrāhāre hūṃ | Having thus performed the worship and offered praise, one should perform the recitation of the mantra: Oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāmeghaprasarasamūhe hūṃ | This is the mantra for the consecration of the offering.
Oṃ [k: oṃ ā& trā& tṛ& hu& phaṭ svāhā] āḥ tā& su& bhṛ& ha& phaṭ phaṭ svāhā | Oṃ, with the beautiful, graceful bows of all the Tathāgatas, I bow to the Blessed One: jaḥ huṃ vaṃ hoḥ.
"Accept this handful of flowers, O Lord! Hoḥ! is the mantra for salutation.
"Oṃ muḥ svāhā" is the mantra for dismissal. "Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi gṛhṇa gṛhṇa gṛhṇantu sārvabhautikā imaṃ baliṃ svāhā" is the mantra for the bali offering. Now...
At the time of beginning the worship, having uttered this, one should purify the mind by thinking: "I shall desist from all misdeeds;
I shall train in the training of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas until I have completed the ritual of worship."

If this were not done, then there would be roots of virtue born of passion, hatred, and delusion. For here all sentient beings possess intentions characterized by passion, hatred, and delusion. Thus, by means of a root of virtue born of passion, the two naga kings Nanda and Upananda [were established]; by one born of hatred, Rāvaṇa; [by one born of delusion, ...]
Vaiśravaṇa became a yakṣa through that which is born of delusion (*moha*). Therefore, having abandoned passion, hatred, delusion, and the like,
one should perform all roots of merit, such as giving and so forth, with a mind purified by compassion.
Thus ends the *Khasarpaṇasādhana*.
Homage to Khasarpaṇa!
First of all, the practitioner, seated on a comfortable seat, [visualizes] a moon disc in his own heart by means of the syllable *A*. Then...

One should visualize the syllable *hrīḥ* as white in color, and by means of the white rays of light emanating from it, see the Guru, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas in the sky before one. Having honored them with rays from the seed-syllable at one’s own heart, one should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth. One should then consecrate [oneself] with the thought: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness. [One should dissolve] oneself into emptiness.
Having visualized [the field], one should meditate on oneself in the form of Lokeśvara through the sequence of radiating and reabsorbing by means of the previously mentioned syllable *hrīḥ*—
white in color in all limbs, adorned with a crown of matted hair,

with Amitābha as his crest-jewel, decorated with all ornaments, seated in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), with the right hand in the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) and the left holding a lotus.

[The deity] is seated upon a lotus and moon throne. On the right side are Ārya Vasudhārā and Sudhana; on the left side are Bhṛkuṭī and Hayagrīva. One should visualize the syllable Oṃ at the Lord’s head upon a moon, Āḥ at his throat, and Huṃ at his heart. When weary from meditation, the yogi should recite the mantra. There, this is the mantra: Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā.
The *Āryāvalokiteśvarakhasarpaṇasādhana* is completed.
Homage to Siṃhanāda!
He has two arms, one face, is white in color, possesses three eyes, and has a lion as his vehicle.
I pay homage to the Lion’s Roar, the Guru who removes all diseases.

First, the practitioner, having performed the purification of the mouth and other preliminary rites, sits upon a comfortable seat in a place conducive to the mind. He should visualize a white moon disc transformed from the syllable *A*, and upon it, the white syllable *Hrīḥ* (or *Hrī*) in his heart. With its rays illuminating the three realms, he [visualizes] the one residing in the Akaniṣṭha heaven...
Having summoned all the venerable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with a lion’s roar and established them in the space before one,
and having thereafter performed the worship, confession of misdeeds, and so forth, and having meditated upon the four Brahma-abodes,
[one realizes that] all phenomena have the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness: OṂ.

One should consecrate emptiness with this mantra: "I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Then, recollecting one's aspiration, there is a lotus transformed from a white syllable *paṃ*, upon which—

A moon disc transformed from a white letter *ā*; above that, a white lion transformed from a white letter *ā*; above that, a white lotus transformed from a white letter *aṃ* (or *oṃ*); and upon its pericarp, a white letter *hrīḥ*, emitting a multitude of shimmering rays. These...

Having transformed everything, one should visualize oneself in the form of a lion’s roar— white in all limbs, with two arms, one face, and three eyes; wearing a crown of matted hair, with Amitābha adorning the head,
standing in the posture of royal ease upon a lion throne, and clad in a tiger skin garment.

He is vibrating with the five Tathāgatas, his five locks of hair are disheveled over his shoulders, and he is adorned with a crescent moon [or marked by a moon]. In his left hand, resting upon a white lotus, is a white sword;
nearby, on another white lotus, is a white skull-cup filled with various fragrant flowers.

48) On the right, having meditated upon the Blessed One in such a form—with a white trident-staff encircled by a white serpent atop a white lotus—the practitioner, weary from meditation, should recite the mantra. There, this is the mantra: *oṃ āḥ siṃhanāda hūṃ*.

*phaṭ svāhā*. Herein is the procedure: before an image of the Blessed One, whether fashioned as a statue or depicted on a cloth, one should perform the maṇḍala once with this dhāraṇī. This is the dhāraṇī: *Namo ratnatrayāya, nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya*.

It is as follows: *Oṃ akaṭe vikaṭe nikaṭe kaṭaṃkaṭe karoṭavīrye svāhā*. Having consecrated fallen cow dung with this mantra, one should make eight mandalas. Reciting the dhāraṇī thirteen times for each mandala, one should use the remaining cow dung from each mandala to polish it.
Having consecrated it seven times with the *dhāraṇī*, one should smear the disease with it; on the seventh day, the thirteenth day,
or the twenty-first day, even those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution will achieve success.
If it is not accomplished, then may I become a perpetrator of the five acts of immediate retribution.
The *Siṃhanāda-sādhana* is complete.
Having performed this auspicious practice, whatever merit I have obtained—
by that may the world become free from disease through the Lord Siṃhanāda.
This work is by the venerable scholar-avadhūta, the glorious Advayavajra.
Homage to the Lord of the World.
As before, by means of the sequential yoga, one should visualize the Lord of the World, radiant as the moon,
arisen from the syllable HRĪḤ, and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Seated within the matted locks of Vajradharma, he is the destroyer of all diseases;
likewise, he grants boons with his right hand and holds a lotus in his left.

Tārā, who stands to the right, is situated in a graceful pose, exceedingly gentle and radiant; she is benign, with hands displaying the gesture of granting boons and holding a blue lotus, and is adorned with ornaments.
Then, to the left, Hayagrīva has his hand in the *daṇḍa-hasta* (staff) gesture;
he is red in color, extremely fierce, and fond of garments made of tiger skin.
Upon that lotus with eight petals, one should place Maitreya and the others, in accordance with the mandala.
Maitreya is yellow in color and bestows the excellent nāgapuṣpa flower;
Kṣitigarbha is dark green in color and likewise holds a kāśa flower and the gesture of fearlessness.
And Vajrapāṇi is white in color, holding a vajra in his hand and bestowing boons;
Khagarbha is the dark-blue color of the sky, bestowing the wish-fulfilling jewel as a boon.
Mañjughoṣa is golden-hued and holds a sword and a book;
Gaganagañja is red in color and bestows boons with a blue lotus.
Viṣkambhin is the color of alkaline ash and bestows the boon of the supreme jewel;
Samantabhadra is yellowish in luster and bestows the boon of a jewel-lotus.
The four goddesses beginning with Dhūpā, and those stationed at the gates beginning with Vajrāṅkuśī,
have colors and weapons as previously described, according to the sequence of the maṇḍala.
One should meditate upon the Lord of the World as endowed with such qualities;
having transcended the stains of all afflictions, one’s every aspiration shall be fulfilled.
The mantra for this is: Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā.
Thus ends the Sādhana of Lokanātha.

From the seed-syllable *loṃ* (or *lāṃ*), having performed everything as before up to the point of purification, one then transforms *loṃ* (or *lāṃ*) into Lokanātha Candraprabha, resplendent with all ornaments, wearing a crown of matted hair, seated in the lotus posture upon a lotus and moon, holding a lotus in his left hand and displaying the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*) with his right.
One should contemplate the Samayamudrā: having formed two fists, one should join the two middle fingers in the shape of a closed lotus. One should recite the mantra: *oṃ maṇipadme hūṃ*.
The *Lokeśvarasādhana* is completed.
(51) Homage to Siṃhanāda!
Having first performed the purification of the mouth and other preliminary rites, the yogi, seated in a comfortable posture, [visualizes] within his own heart a solar disc.
Having visualized the syllable *ĀḤ* before him, he should summon the Guru, the Buddhas, and so forth, and perform the confession of misdeeds and other preliminary rites.
Then, having brought emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to manifestation and bestowed his blessing upon it, he should recollect his vow (*praṇidhi*).
Following that, there is a moon disc transformed from the syllable *A*; above that—

A red lotus transformed from the syllable Oṃ; upon that, a white lion transformed from the syllable Āḥ; above that, on a moon disc, the Lord Siṃhanāda, born from the syllable Hrīḥ, who is white, wears a crown of matted hair, has three eyes and two arms, assumes the guise of an ascetic, stands in the posture of royal ease (mahārājalīlā), and [rests] upon a lotus raised up from his left hand.

One should meditate upon him as having a blazing sword raised upward in his right hand, and in his left a white trident entwined by a white serpent and a white skull-cup filled with various fragrant flowers; he is crowned by Amitābha, the five Tathāgatas radiate from him, and he possesses a great emanation-body.
The mantra for recitation is: *oṃ āḥ hrīḥ siṃhanāda hūṃ phaṭ*.
Thus ends the *Sādhanā* of Siṃhanāda.
Homage to the Triple Gem!

First of all, the practitioner of mantra, having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, [sits] upon a soft seat... [k, ḍh, g]

Having sat down on a soft, open seat and being established in a comfortable posture, one should visualize a white syllable *hrīḥ* upon a moon disc in one's own heart. Having meditated on the Guru, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas drawn forth by its rays, one should then perform the worship, confession of misdeeds, and so forth, and [contemplate] emptiness.

Having meditated upon this, one should stabilize the visualization with the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* (instead of the usual *oṃ śūnyatā... svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’ham*). Then, instantaneously, there appears a red lotus transformed from the syllable *paṃ*.
Above that, one should meditate upon oneself in the form of Siṃhanāda Lokeśvara, arisen from the syllable Hrīḥ on a moon disc above a white lion transformed by the syllable Siṃ;
he is white, wears a crown of matted hair adorned with Amitābha, has three eyes and two arms, assumes the attire of an ascetic, and stands in the posture of royal ease (mahārājalīlā).
He stands with a flaming sword upon a lotus rising from his left hand,
while in his right is a white trident entwined by a white serpent; in his left is a white skull-cup filled with various fragrant flowers,
radiating the five Tathāgatas and possessing a great emanated form.
One should meditate on form (*rūpa*) as having the nature of form (*rūpitā*). The mantra for recitation is: *oṃ āḥ hrīḥ siṃhanāda hūṃ phaṭ*.
The *Sādhanā* of Siṃhanāda is complete.
