Immediately following that is the dhāraṇī: Homage to the Three Jewels! Homage to the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Great Compassionate One! It is as follows: Oṃ akaṭe vikaṭe nikaṭe kaṭaṃkaṭe karoṭe.

"Karoṭavīrye svāhā! This is the ritual procedure for the mantra: at dawn, in front of the Blessed One, one should prepare eight mandalas with cow dung that has not fallen to the ground, and recite [the mantra] thirteen times over each mandala. Having empowered the remaining cow dung seven times, one should smear it upon the disease.

One should smear it upon the root of disease; it pacifies all diseases. If, on the seventh day, the thirteenth day, or the twenty-first day, this does not succeed even for one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, then I myself shall become a perpetrator of the five acts of immediate retribution.
The Siṃhanāda Dhāraṇī is completed.
Homage to Khasarpaṇa!
Having bowed to the Lord Khasarpaṇa, who has become the protector of those in suffering,
a certain practice manual for him is written here, abridged from the extensive version.

First of all, the practitioner, having washed his hands, feet, and so forth with water and become supremely pure, should sit upon a soft, beautiful seat in a secluded mountain cave, a clean place, or anywhere else that is agreeable to the mind. Having visualized in his own heart the mandala of the sun, which is free from defects and the source of all defects, as the transformation of the first vowel, he should [place] within its center by means of his mind...
One should visualize the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*, radiant with a mass of rays like the autumn moon. Then, emerging from that very seed-syllable *hrīḥ*...

By means of the rays of light, which are like goads and which destroy the mass of darkness that deludes the world, they illuminate all those infinite world-systems situated in the ten directions; and though remaining there, they are themselves incalculable and immeasurable.

The gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas are drawn into the expanse of space and established there. Subsequently, for those gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas residing in the expanse of space— who are supremely compassionate—
one offers flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, flags, and so forth.

[Omitting the phrase "whatever merit one might rejoice in"]: Whatever evil karma I have committed, caused others to commit, or rejoiced in while committing— whether by body, speech, or mind— as I wandered through this birth or other births in the beginningless and endless cycle of rebirth,
all that [I confess before] the Blessed Ones.

Having confessed according to this procedure— saying, "I confess before the Blessed One, the Great Festival of the Three Worlds, and the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas"— and having taken up the vow of non-repetition, one should perform the rejoicing in merit (*puṇyānumodanā*).

"I rejoice in all that is wholesome belonging to the Perfect Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, the Śrāvaka-buddhas, their sons the Bodhisattvas, and even to the sentient beings dwelling within the belly of the three worlds. Following that is the going for refuge to the Three Jewels: "I go for refuge to the Buddha."

"I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost among the two-footed; I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost among those free from passion; I go for refuge to the foremost of assemblies. Thereafter follows the taking of the path.

And that path which was taught by the Perfectly Awakened One for those who have set out upon the three vehicles—that alone is to be followed by me, and no other. Immediately after that, one should perform the entreaty: "May the Blessed Ones act for the sake of sentient beings as long as cyclic existence endures."
"May the Fully Awakened Ones and their sons, the great bodhisattvas, remain until my final parinirvāṇa. Following that, he made such a request for the unsurpassed teaching of the Dharma.

"May the Blessed Tathāgatas teach that by which sentient beings may swiftly cross the bottomless ocean of saṃsāra. Following that request, one should perform the dedication of merit; whatever root of virtue has arisen through the sevenfold supreme worship, that very thing—
"I dedicate [this] toward perfect enlightenment. Alternatively, one may recite these verses which, in brief, indicate the sevenfold unsurpassed worship:
"Whatever evil has been committed by body, speech, or mind, I confess it before the Victors."
I constantly rejoice with great joy in all the merit of the three worlds.
I always go for refuge here to the Three Jewels and take shelter in the path spoken by the Victor.
May the Buddhas and their sons also constantly act for the benefit of sentient beings within this very existence.
[Of him] ||

"May my ancestors remain for as long as the world endures; may they grant me their blessing, O progenitors of beings! May those of great power indeed fulfill such a command of mine regarding the Dharma."
So that beings may easily and swiftly reach the far shore of the ocean of saṃsāra and attain abundant happiness,
I dedicate all this abundant merit here toward complete enlightenment.
To the Victors and their Sons, and to my gurus,
I offer myself at all times with my whole being for the sake of the worlds.

Having thus performed this sevenfold worship, one should dismiss [the deities] with "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Mur. Immediately thereafter, one should meditate upon the four immeasurables—loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—according to the sequence to be described below. Among these, loving-kindness is as follows:

[Great love] is characterized by a parental affection for all sentient beings that exceeds [all other forms of affection]. But what is compassion like? It is [the wish to rescue] the infinite realms of sentient beings who have fallen into the midst of the fathomless and shoreless ocean of saṃsāra.

The resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is the thought, "I shall deliver them. Furthermore, what is sympathetic joy (*muditā*) like? It is a state of joyful mind toward the good conduct of sentient beings dwelling in the three realms, as well as toward their enjoyments, sovereignty, and so forth.
What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)? It is the practice of supreme benefit toward sentient beings, whether they are beneficial or harmful, having abandoned the bonds of aversion and attachment;
it follows the cultivation of the four immeasurables and consists in the complete purity of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
I too should reflect: "All these phenomena are by their very nature and in their essential form completely pure; I too [am so]."
One should bring to mind the passage beginning with "naturally pure" (*prakṛtipariśuddha*). One should reinforce this very purity of the nature of all phenomena by means of the mantra:

*oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho 'ham* ("Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature"). And in that which is naturally pure, all phenomena... [k, ḍh, b: ...purity] ...[k, ḍh, b: ...in] all phenomena.

[Ḍh, b: The consequence that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) would be immediately liberated is unavoidable. [Dh, c: True, but this consequence is entirely untenable. Why is it untenable? Because all phenomena are variegated by the stains of passion and so forth, which are the causes of *saṃsāra*. Furthermore, how could there be their removal—or rather, their subsiding?

By means of the cultivation of the distinguished path, that [affliction] is ceased. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "Cessation is to be realized directly. Therefore, statements such as "all phenomena are pure by nature" are indeed logical; enough with excessive talk. Having brought to manifestation the natural purity of all phenomena...

One should meditate on the emptiness of all phenomena. In this regard, emptiness is as follows: this world is merely mind alone, appearing in various forms as having the nature of luminosity, just as in a dream there exists nothing external to the mind that can be grasped by the mind.
Because there is no object of apprehension (*grāhya*), the mind as the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) also does not exist. Consequently, all phenomena have the nature of the mind;
their reality is the emptiness of the entire conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) consisting of the duality of subject and object, and so forth.

The meaning is that this is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This point should be contemplated as follows: the entire world, including the moving and the unmoving, is essentially nothing but the manifestation of non-duality (*advaita*). One should consecrate this very emptiness (*śūnyatā*) with the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* ("Oṃ! I am of the nature of the diamond of the wisdom of emptiness"). Thereafter, [one should contemplate it as] free from the marks of blemish—
The seed-syllable *hrīḥ*, exceedingly white, mounted upon the orb of the moon.

To the Blessed One, the glorious Lokanātha Khasarpaṇa, whose body is as exceedingly white as the rising of hundreds of stainless autumnal moon-maṇḍalas, whose form is radiant and beautiful with supreme passion (*śṛṅgāra*), and whose limbs are adorned with various jewels and ornaments; [k: ...]

[He has] a body radiant with splendor, wearing a crown of matted locks, with eyes like blooming white lotuses; the region of his head is adorned with the jewel of the Blessed One, the Victorious Amitābha;
his body is clothed in pure garments washed by water and golden sand.
[He is] washed by showers of sand;
seated upon a most beautiful white lotus the size of a cartwheel,
resting on a seat that is the stainless orb of the moon, he sits in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka) with his right hand...
Having thus produced the Blessed One— who grants boons with his left hand and holds a blossoming, enchanting white lotus—
one should visualize oneself in that same form. To the right side of the Blessed One are Noble Tārā and Sudhana.

On the left side, Bhṛkuṭī and Hayagrīva are to be visualized. Above the stainless lunar disc on the head, one should see the syllable Oṃ; then, above the pure lunar disc at the throat, the syllable Āḥ; and at the heart, above the disc of the stainless moon, the syllable Hūṃ. One should continue in this sequence for as long as desired.

One should meditate thus. Immediately thereafter, one should visualize the syllable HRĪḤ, resembling the autumn moon, the jasmine flower, or the *kunda* blossom, situated upon a lunar disc free from all stains and positioned at the heart of this very Blessed One Lokanātha, who is in the form of the Samayasattva.
—By means of the spreading rays of light emerging from the seed-syllable, which dispel the darkness of ignorance throughout the three worlds, (p. 60) [g:
reads *kamalam* after *hṛdistha*; g: omits *andhakārāpahāribhiḥ*].

Having gone there with those who carry him away, the Blessed One, whose nature is that of the Knowledge Being (jñānasattva) and who has been established from beginningless time, is brought from a very distant island-land; having brought him, that very Blessed One—
Having placed you in the space before him,

with fragrant water and scented flowers contained in vessels of gold and other materials inlaid with various jewels, [he offers them] to that very Blessed One, the Lord of the World, who has assumed the form of a *jñānasattva*.
Having offered water for the feet (*caraṇārgha*), one should thereafter worship the Blessed One,

who is of the nature of the Knowledge Being (*jñānasattva*), with divine flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, and mirrors. Having worshipped and praised him again and again, [one recites] *jaḥ* *huṃ*.

One should display the mudrā with these four syllables: *vaṃ hoḥ*. Having formed a hollowed *añjali* (joined palms) slightly raised, one should make the two middle fingers like needles and slightly contract the remaining fingers.
One should hold the two thumbs face-to-face without touching, placing them near the two index fingers;

this is the *vikasitamakala* mudrā. Having satisfied with this mudrā the Blessed One who has been invited, characterized as the *jñānasattva*, one should cause him to be absorbed into the Blessed One in the form of the *samayasattva*. Oṃ Āḥ... [k]

With the syllables *jhāḥ* and *huṃ*, one should resolve upon the non-duality of these two. Immediately thereafter, from the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*— which is as radiant as the mass of rays from a hundred moons and is nestled within a lunar disc as white as a mass of stainless moonbeams— there emerge innumerable and immeasurable [rays].
Having illuminated numerous world-systems in the ten directions from the Blessed One, the venerable Lord Śrī Khasarpaṇa Lokeśvara, he [illuminated] those situated therein as well.
By raining down jewels such as gold, rubies, pearls, royal cloths, coral, lapis lazuli, and sapphires upon sentient beings, they remove the sufferings of poverty and so forth;
and by means of a continuous stream of nectar from the teaching of the unsurpassed dharmas— such as momentariness and selflessness— they [liberate them].

They satisfy [beings]. Having repeatedly and incessantly performed various kinds of deeds for the sake of others, they bring even the entire world to perfection in the form of the Blessed Lord Lokeśvara; and even therein, she resides within the center of the orb of the cool-rayed moon.

One should meditate through the sequence of emanation and reabsorption—wherein those very Blessed Ones arrive and enter into the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*, which resembles the rays of a crystal gem—until exhaustion arises. Furthermore, when weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra. In this regard, it is as follows:
The mantra is: Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā. This mantra is the heart-essence of the Blessed One, Lokanātha.

This king of mantras possesses extraordinary power; it is honored, revered, and saluted by all the supreme Victors. Having arisen from meditative absorption, he beheld the world as having the form of Lokanātha.

"By means of that ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), one should roam as one pleases. Generally, by this method, one should meditate upon the Blessed One; all the great supernatural powers (*mahāsiddhi*), headed by the sword, collyrium, and so forth, having assembled, fall at one's feet—how much more so the minor powers? Indeed, they do so most certainly. As for those who...

Those who dwell in forest groves, cemeteries, or mountain caves and meditate upon the Blessed One will, before long, certainly behold the Blessed One here; the Blessed One himself will grant them consolation, breath, and so forth. Let it be so.
[Up to: What more need be said? Buddhahood is supremely and exceedingly difficult to attain.
Even when cast [into it], it remains for them like a jujube fruit resting in the palm of the hand.
Thus ends the somewhat detailed *Sādhana* of the glorious Khasarpaṇa Lokeśvara.
By whatever merit has been acquired through performing this supreme sādhana of the venerable Lord Khasarpaṇanātha, may the world go to the city of the Sage.
The work of the Elder Anupamarakṣita.
I pay homage to the Lion’s Roar, the Guru who removes all diseases;
by the mere application of meditative cultivation, one is liberated from all sins.

First, having performed the cleansing of the face and other preliminary rites, clad in clean garments and seated comfortably on a pleasant seat in a pure location, one should visualize the syllable *hrīḥ* upon a moon disk in one’s own heart. Having drawn in all the Tathāgatas by means of its rays and honored them, one should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth. Then, one should cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Having meditated on the fourfold analysis and preceded by the recitation of the mantra of natural purity, one should contemplate emptiness with: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho’ham; oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako’ham*. Immediately after this—
Having visualized one's own body as a mere appearance, transformed into a red syllable *repha* (ripha) upon a red eight-petaled lotus.
Through the transformation of the syllable *hrīḥ*, one should visualize a white lion; upon its back, on a moon disc, is the syllable *hrīḥ* with rays of light.

Having summoned all the Tathāgatas by means of those very rays and caused them to enter, one should meditate on oneself as Siṃhanāda Lokeśvara, white in color, with three eyes, wearing a crown of matted hair, and devoid of ornaments.

One should visualize [the deity] covered with a tiger skin, seated upon a lion throne, possessing the majestic bearing of a great king, seated on a moon, and having the luster of the moon; in his right hand a trident entwined by a white serpent,
and in his left a lotus vessel filled with various fragrant flowers.

One should visualize a flaming sword resting upon a lotus raised from the left hand, radiating the five Tathāgatas within one’s own body. Then, having attracted the Jñānasattva by means of the seed-syllable at the heart and caused him to enter, one should emanate the Tathāgatas and consecrate oneself.
One should visualize the primary seal of Amitābha. Then, one should recite the mantra while assuming the form of the deity. In this regard, the mantra is:

*oṃ āḥ hrīḥ siṃhanāda hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Following that, having prepared a mandala with fragrant substances and the like, and having presented flowers and other offerings for worship, one should perform the ritual adoration.

Furthermore, one should recite the garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*): *Oṃ namo ratnatrayāya nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya | tadyathā oṃ akaṭe vikaṭe nikaṭe kaṭaṅkaṭe karoṭe karoṭavīrye svāhā*. By means of this mantra...
Having taken earth from a mandala and recited [the mantra] twenty-one times, one should apply it as an ointment to the disease; thus one becomes healthy.
This concludes the *Sādhana* of Lokanātha Siṃhanāda.
It is finished.

First of all, the practitioner, seated on a comfortable seat, [visualizes] upon an eight-petaled lotus transformed from the syllable *paṃ* in his own heart, [the syllable] *a*, transformed from the syllable *a*.

Having visualized a moon disc above that with the syllable *hrīḥ* emitting rays of light, and having seen Lokeśvara residing in the Akaniṣṭha heaven drawn by those rays and stationed in the sky before one, one should perform the confession of sins and so forth. Namely: the confession of sins (*pāpadeśanā*), the rejoicing in merit (*puṇyānumodanā*), and the dedication of merit (*puṇyapariṇāmanā*).

Having performed the going for refuge, the offering of one’s own body, the supplication, and the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should cultivate the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*): loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Then, one should meditate on emptiness with the mantra:
*oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. [It is] mere appearance...
Having observed one's own body as a mere appearance by means of that ray,
[one should visualize] in the center of the heart, upon an eight-petaled lotus born from the syllable *paṃ*, a moon mandala produced by the syllable *a*, and above that—
One should visualize oneself in the form of Lokeśvara by means of the entry of all the Tathāgatas, who have been summoned by the red light rays from the syllable Hrīḥ;
he is white in color, wears a crown of matted hair, has his right hand in the gesture of granting boons,
holds a bright white lotus in his other hand, and sits in the half-lotus posture.

One should visualize oneself as adorned with all ornaments, wearing a crown of Amitābha, possessing the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, seated upon a moon-disc, and radiant with moonlight. Then, to the right are Āryatārā and Sudhana; to the left are Bhṛkuṭī and Hayagrīva; in the east is Vairocana; and in the south is Ratnasambhava.
In the west is Amitābha; in the north, Amoghasiddhi; in the southeast, Locanā; in the southwest, Māmakī;
in the northwest, Pāṇḍarā; and in the northeast, Vajradhātvīśvarī. Then...

Having summoned the Jñānasattva with rays of light from the seed-syllable in the heart, one should cause him to enter. Having performed the consecration of the eyes and so forth, as well as the consecration of body, speech, and mind, one should request the empowerment:
"Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon their birth..."
In that way, I shall bathe you with pure, divine water.

Oṃ [k: has āḥ huṃ after oṃ] sarvatathāgatābhiṣekasamayaśriye [k: māśraye] huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having emanated the ten deities beginning with Locanā and having performed worship and praise, one should recite the mantra. In this regard, the mantra is: oṃ hrīḥ svāhā.
The *Khasarpaṇasādhana* is completed.
Homage to Hālāhala!
Having meditated upon the sequence up to emptiness as before,
[one visualizes] the Great Compassionate One Hālāhala, arisen from the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*.
He has three eyes and three faces, and is adorned with a crown of matted locks.
His first face is white, the right blue, and the left red;
he bears the crescent moon upon his head,
with a skull serving as his crest-ornament.
The Jina situated within his matted locks is perfectly adorned with all ornaments,
radiant as a white lotus, and beautiful with the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa).
He has six arms, a smiling face, and is fond of garments of tiger skin.
In his right hands, he holds the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), a rosary (*akṣamālā*) in the second,
and a dancing arrow (*śaranartana*) in the third; likewise, in his left hands, he holds a bow (*cāpa*).
In the second [digit] there is a white lotus, and in the third, a breast.
He holds his own consort, white in color, upon his left knee;
she holds a lotus in her left hand and is intent on embracing the Blessed One with her right arm. Her mass of matted hair is adorned with flowers.
On his right side is a trident entwined by a serpent, and on his left side...

One should visualize the Blessed One standing with a playful, graceful posture upon a red lotus moon disc, holding a skull-cup resting on a lotus and filled with various fragrant flowers; then one should recite the mantra: Oṃ Vajradharma Hrīḥ.
Thus concludes the sādhana of Hālāhala Lokeśvara.
Homage to Hālāhala! Having bowed to the perfected Hālāhala, who destroys the diseases of the world and consists of the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), I shall explain the sequence of his sādhana.

Therein, first of all, the mantra-practitioner, having stationed himself in some location on earth that is agreeable to the mind, should— through the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that "all phenomena are originally unarisen, naturally parinirvāṇized, and like an illusion, a dream, or a city of the Gandharvas"— empower this very internal knowledge of self (*ahaṃjñāna*).

Relying upon the assemblies of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vidyās, and Krodhas established throughout the world-systems extending to the infinite limits of the ten directions: Oṃ sarvavit pūra pūra āvartta āvartta.
Having emanated various kinds of offerings by means of this [mantra] and having worshipped mentally, he should prostrate with the state of non-existence (*abhāva*),

place his knees upon the surface of the earth, and with palms joined at his heart, speak thus: "May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Bodhisattvas, the Great Compassionate Ones, the Vidyā-devis, and the Great Wrathful Ones, attend to me."
Abiding in all world-systems—I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly until enlightenment. I offer myself to them; may the Leaders accept me.

While wandering through beginningless saṃsāra, or in this present life, whatever evil karma I have committed with body, speech, and mind—whether it be the false accusation of faults against the Three Jewels, teachers, preceptors, parents, monks, nuns, or ordinary beings; or that which leads to poverty; or that which leads to disease—[I confess it all].

Alternatively, whatever action has been performed by me personally—whether done, caused to be done, or approved—all of that, whether committed just now before you or at any other time, I confess while not perceiving it through the yoga of signlessness (*animitta-yoga*).
I shall never do such a thing again. And whatever [has been done] from the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathama-cittotpāda*) up until [the attainment of] unsurpassed...
From perfect enlightenment up to the realm of nirvana without remainder,

I rejoice in all the roots of virtue of all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, vidyās, krodhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and other ordinary beings within this interval. May there be love for the Buddhas through this rejoicing.
I generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of enlightenment,
just as the Protectors of the three times have made their firm resolve for perfect awakening.
I dedicate all of this root of virtue toward perfect enlightenment through the dedication practiced by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones; then, having visualized the vajra-añjali gesture— (p.

Oṃ! May all the accomplishments of sentient beings be perfected by those who are committed to all the Tathāgatas, and may all the Tathāgatas empower me! Reciting, "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature," one should release [the mudrā] upon one's own head. For this very reason, all phenomena are pure by nature through liberation.
There is no doubt that the pacification of obstacles occurs through this continuous application of the prescribed meditative visualizations.

Thereafter, having placed upon the moon at one's own heart the heart-mantra arising from the syllable *A*, which flashes with immeasurable rays of light, one should contemplate the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*). From those syllables of one's own heart, clouds of light-rays [emanate].
Having expanded that [light], one should behold all things, both stable and moving. Having manifested the form of Hālāhala, one should contemplate it as follows:
realizing that the entire world is like an illusion, one should perceive oneself in the form of Hālāhala, joined with ten million moons, wearing a crown of matted locks.
Resplendent like a white lotus, blue-throated, and three-eyed.
He stands upon a red lotus uprooted by a great serpent,
situated within a cave on a mountain of jewels, beautifully clothed in a garment of tiger skin.
Seated in the paryaṅka posture, established in meditative absorption, adorned with four arms,
the hero holds a water-pot and a rosary, with Amitābha as his crest-ornament.
One should visualize a trident with its tip pointing upward and a khaṭvāṅga staff bound with a skull-tube, held by his left hand, while a skull-cup is held by his right.
[One should visualize] the Lord, who is filled with flowers, belonging to the Kulika family, and possessing a formed hood, gazing [downward].

Then, one should perform the placement of the five limbs (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) by means of mudrās conjoined with mantras. With the hands held palm-upward, one should, due to the swaying of the topknot, touch the second joint on the side of the binding.
One should place [the hands] on the palms and from the sides of the hands; this is the *mūlamudrā*.
Having encircled [the head] and having pressed down with both palms, it becomes the *parītata* [mudrā].
If one places this very [mantra] upon the head by means of inverted application,
it becomes the crest-lock (śikhā) of that very person who has consumed the hālāhala poison.
Having formed two separate fists with the middle fingers linked together,
with the *tāra* (index fingers) as a needle and the *tāla* (little fingers) at the sides, it becomes the armor (*kavaca*).
Having cast them apart, one should employ those very same *tāla* fingers for the rites of weapons (*astra*) by those skilled in such rituals.

*Tārā* is the index finger (*tarjanī*), *tāla* is the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*), *dhārā* is the ring finger (*anāmikā*), and *madhyā* is a synonym for *śikhī*. Now, the mantras for these mudrās are as follows: *Oṃ saḥ svāhā* is the heart-mantra of Hālāhala; *Oṃ jvalini svāhā* is the head-mantra; *Oṃ prajvālanadīpāya svāhā* is the crest-mantra; and *Oṃ aghryāya svāhā* is the armor-mantra for all limbs.

With *phaṭ*, which contains infinite power, [one places] the weapon (*astra*) in both hands. Possessing the ego-identification, "I myself am that very Ārya Hālāhala," one should meditate on oneself as Hālāhala until fatigue arises. When fatigue occurs, having placed the syllable *huṃ*—blazing with its own flames—upon the moon at one's own heart, and while [the deity] is illuminated by its rays, [one should place it] upon the mantras at the periphery.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra syllables, one should perform the recitation with a concentrated mind;
one may recite the heart-mantra, or even the garland-mantra.
When ten million recitations of the heart-mantra have been performed, or a hundred thousand recitations with a rosary,
all his prosperities and [cures for] diseases are accomplished in every way.
Having performed the recitation as much as desired and also meditation according to one's ability,
one should then ask the Lord for forgiveness and dismiss him with the root-mudrā.

Now, if one wishes to propitiate the Blessed One by means of the procedure for a cloth painting (*paṭavidhāna*), then one should visualize the previously described form upon the cloth; such is this procedure for the cloth painting.
The second [image] is described:
one should depict Halāhala as golden-colored, or else with three eyes, endowed with two arms, possessing a beautiful blue throat,
standing upon a mountain of jewels, well-composed, slender, with tawny matted hair.

One should draw two serpents in front of him, their feet treading upon his tails, their bodies half-way up and raised on high like pillars, colored like precious blue gems, and gazing at the Lord from both sides; and one should draw a skull in front [of them].
This pair of feet and this pair of hands are completely filled on all sides with various flowers;
this measurement has been declared by the Jina. Furthermore, the practitioner should indeed be positioned here below, with his hand holding incense at the level of the knees.

Then, having spread out one of these cloths and having prepared a mandala with cow dung fallen naturally in the morning, one should invoke [the deity] by means of the root-mudrā together with the mantra through a symbolic gesture upon the form of the cloth, and perform the five-limbed placement (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) using the very same mudrās and mantras as previously described. Then, by means of the root-mudrā alone—

Having worshipped the Blessed One with the fivefold offerings and mental worship, one should invoke him and display the mudrā; either the *kanyā-śṛṅkhalā* or the *elā* [mudrās] should be placed upon the back of the joined *tārā*. This is the procedure for the stream of the crest (*śikhā-dhārā-vidhi*). The two index fingers are made into pointers. Oṃ visphuliṅgāṭṭahāsakeśari.

The mantra: Then one should contemplate oneself in the form previously described; or, if devoid of that form, one should recite the previously mentioned garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*) nine times, as before, thirteen times. One should smear the disease with the cow-dung [of the mandala].
Within six months, all diseases [will be cured].
They are pacified. Alternatively, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. There is no need for hesitation here regarding the fulfillment of all hopes.
In that regard, the noble *Ārya-hālāhala-hṛdaya-mantra* is as follows: *Namaḥ sarva-buddha-bodhisattvebhyaḥ*.
Homage to the great bulls among men! Having paid homage to the noble Avalokiteśvara, Maheśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
the noble Maitreya, Samantabhadra, the noble Vajrapāṇi, and the rest of the great bodhisattvas and others—
O Blessed One, noble Avalokiteśvara, [I speak] to you:
I shall cause the Heart-mantra to revolve, which accomplishes all desires,
is unassailable by all beings, and destroys the path of worldly existence.

Namely: *He bodhisattva priyabodhisattva mahābodhisattva he hale āryāvalokiteśvara paramamaitracitta hitacitta mahākāruṇika kuru kuru mahāvidye dhuru dhuru dharādhara acalendrācala namaste'stu hrīḥ sarvasattvābhayaprada harihariharivāhanodbhava bhavābhava*.

O sinless one, do, do, do, do; ghuru, ghuru; suru, suru; muru, muru; curu, curu! O you of most gracious, stainless, and pure form, Noble Avalokiteśvara, Greatly Compassionate One, wearer of the black antelope skin, holder of the rosary, holder of the staff, with matted locks and a crown hanging down low, mala, mala; kala, kala; cala, cala!

*Tala tala nala nala phala phala hulu hulu hulula halāhala! O Bodhisattva, Mahābodhisattva, homage be to you! Hṛ& hṛ& hṛ&! Act! Act! Remember my heart! Remember the pledge! Remember your birth! Accomplish this task for me; fulfill my desire! Svāhā!* And the dispatching:
"May everyone become like Puṇyajana, saying 'Hālāhala!
May I too become Mañjughoṣa, fulfilling the hopes of the world."
This ritual of the Lotus-Bearer has been narrated by one named Prajñāpālita, through the essence of the pollen from the lotus feet of Mañjughoṣa, until the attainment of awakening.
The noble *Hālāhala-sādhana* is completed.
Having bowed with devotion to Āhālāhala, who fulfills all hopes,
the sādhana of that compassionate one is here stated in brief.
First, in a charming place well-smeared with sandalwood paste and other substances,
one should bring down the Blessed One from his representation on cloth or other media and worship him.
The mantra for offering flowers and so forth is: *oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajradīpe hūṃ*, and so on. *Oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāmeghaprasarasamūhe sphara*.
k, b: ghurahimaṃ] himaṃ gaganakaṃ hu& — this is the mantra for the offering of all worship.
Having worshipped before him and seated himself on a comfortable cushion,
the Great Compassionate One cultivated loving-kindness and compassion for the world.
Having placed the mantra, the syllable *hrīḥ*, upon the moon behind his heart,
he should behold the sky filled with perfectly awakened Buddhas who are bowed in reverence.
Clearly, it is connected with their sons.
Having worshipped those [seeds] with offerings of light-rays from the syllable *hrīḥ*— [the semen of the syllable *hrīḥ*]— and being free from delusion,
one should perform the confession of sins and so forth for the increase of merit.
One who has taken refuge in the Three Jewels and so forth, possessing a mind of compassion, should utter this foremost mantra which illuminates the supreme selflessness of all phenomena.
"Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. Thus, bringing the meaning of the mantra to mind, one should perceive every object with a great-souled [mahātman] perspective.
One should cultivate the state of mere cognition, which is free from the grasped and the grasper.
Having perceived that which is to be individually realized, one should meditate on the syllable *hrīḥ* situated upon a moon, and from that,
a white lotus whose pericarp is endowed with the syllable *hrīḥ*.
Then, having emanated a flood of Buddhas and established the world as Buddha,
he should re-enter that very place and himself become Hālāhala.
Three-faced and six-armed, peaceful, he dwells in a cave on a mountain of jewels;
seated upon a white moon resting on a red lotus, he stands in the graceful *lalitākṣepa* posture.
His faces on the left and the other sides are white, yellow, and deep blue;
he wears a tiger-skin garment, possesses three eyes, and is beautiful with all his ornaments.
Holding in his sprout-like hands the boon-granting eye, arrows, and the breast of a beautiful woman in the right [hands], and a white lotus and a bow in the left.
Having placed a skull-cup filled with various flowers on the left,
and likewise a trident entwined by poisonous serpents upon a lotus on the right.
He has a crest-jewel of true Amitābha, with a skull forming his topknot;
he possesses a mass of lofty matted locks adorned with a crescent moon and a crown.
Having shaken off the web of conceptual construction,
with the radiance of a multitude of manifest Buddhas,
one becomes Hālāhala in this manner within one's own heart, throat, and head.
Huṃ Āḥ Oṃ— one should visualize [the syllables] blue, reddish, and white respectively upon the moon;
likewise, in the center between the heart and the throat, the syllable Hrīḥ, situated upon the moon, is to be meditated upon.
Then, meditating on all phenomena— both stable and moving— as having that very form,
one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind, free from all conceptualizations of the unreal.
Oṃ hālāhala hrīḥ! Having performed the recitation comfortably— neither too fast nor too slow, with internal speech that is very clear— one should perform the concluding worship upon the dismissal.
Having praised, having made firm, and having recited the hundred-syllable mantra.

In this regard, here is the hundred-syllable mantra: Oṃ Vajrasattva, maintain the pledge; abide as Vajrasattva; be firm for me, be well-pleased with me, be well-nourished by me, be devoted to me, and bestow upon me all accomplishments.
And in all my activities, O Blessed One, make my mind auspicious! Huṃ hahaha hoḥ! O Lord, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me;
become vajra-like, O Great Samaya Being! Āḥ! Oṃ.
[The dismissal formula *oṃ kṛto vaḥ* etc. is not found in K. What has been done for you?
The accomplishment for the benefit of all sentient beings has been granted according to their needs;
go now to the realm of the Buddhas, and return once more.
Having exhorted him with this, one should recite the mantra: "Oṃ, the syllable *a* is the mouth of all phenomena because they are primordially unarisen.
Having arisen from meditation, the yogi should give gifts according to his capacity.
[To the extent of one's ability] (p.
while enjoying the desires for forms and so forth, with all conceptual constructions entirely cast aside.
The supreme practitioner shall soon attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
Whatever supreme merit I have gained by writing this *sādhana* that has been obtained—
By that, may the entire world soon become like the Hālāhala poison.
The *Hālāhalasādhana* is completed. [In versions ḍh and g, it reads only "the *Hālāhalasādhana*."]

According to the previously described procedure, one should meditate upon oneself as Padmanarteśvara, transformed from a red syllable *Hrīḥ* on a moon disc atop a universal lotus; seated in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, with two arms and one face, red in color,
adorned with all ornaments, bearing Amitābha on his crown, and resting on his left side.

He is embraced by Pāṇḍaravāsinī; his left arm, positioned in the gesture of embracing, holds a red lotus, while his other right hand, in the dancing gesture, opens it with the *sūcīmudrā*. Then, one should recite the mantra: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of body, speech, and mind. Thereafter, in the eight directions...
One should visualize the eight goddesses.
There, on the eastern petal of the eight-petaled red lotus, is Vilokinī, white in color and holding a red lotus; on the southern petal [in the yantra], Tārā is green.

Palāśapadmadharā is on the western petal; Bhūriṇī, holding a wheel and a blue lotus, is on the northern petal; the white Bhṛkuṭī, holding a yellow lotus, is on the eastern corner petal; and Padmavāsinī, yellow in color and holding a madder-red lotus, is on the [southwestern] petal. (p. 76)

On the petal in the southern corner is Vajrapadmeśvarī, sky-colored, holding a white lotus; on the petal in the western corner is Viśvapadmā, white, holding a black lotus; on the petal in the northern corner is Viśvavajrā, multicolored, holding a crossed lotus. All of these are seated in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, two-armed, single-faced, and gentle.
In the pericarp, however, is the Blessed One himself. Then one should recite the mantra. The mantra is: Oṃ hrīḥ padmanarteśvara hūṃ.
[End of] the *Sādhana* of Padmanarteśvaralokanātha.
Homage to Padmanarteśvara!
In this regard, upon a moon disc atop a multicolored lotus, one should visualize Padmanarteśvara, transformed from the red syllable *hrīḥ*.
He is red in color, with one face, a crown of matted hair, three eyes, and eight arms; he is adorned with all ornaments.

Wearing a snake as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), he performs the *tāṇḍava* dance with his first two arms in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*); with his second right arm he displays the gesture of dancing at his heart, and with his left arm he forms the *sūcīmudrā*. With his third pair of arms, he holds a red lotus placed upon his head and a trident topped with a vajra.

One should meditate upon Padmanarteśvara Lokanātha, who holds a rosary and a water-pot with his two fourth arms [and wields a vajra and a staff], surrounded by eight goddesses, and appearing in such a form.
[The Sādhana of Padmanarteśvara]

77) Following the previously described procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one should visualize a white syllable *hrīḥ* upon a moon disk situated on a universal lotus; then, through its transformation—
According to the tradition of Padmanarteśvara, one should visualize oneself as the venerable Āryāvalokiteśvara:
with one face and eighteen arms, seated in the half-lotus posture, with Amitābha at the center of his matted hair-tuft, holding a double lotus in all his hands, and surrounded by a host of yoginīs.
With Tārā, Sudhana, Bhṛkuṭī, and Hayagrīva situated at his right and left sides, adorned with divine ornaments and garments; then one should recite the mantra: *oṃ hrīḥ padmanarteśvara hūṃ*.
This brings great benefit for the pacification of diseases and other afflictions.
Thus concludes the *Sādhana* of Padmanarteśvara.

Following the previously described procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness, one should visualize the Blessed Noble Avalokiteśvara, born from the white syllable *hrīḥ*, originating from Hari-Hari-Harivāhana [or Hari-Hara], with all his limbs white, wearing a crown of matted hair, and possessing a peaceful appearance; with his right hand, he holds the Blessed Tathāgata.
With the second [hand], he makes a witness; with the third, he holds a rosary; with the left [hand], he instructs the world on the wicked deceiver;
with the second [left hand], he holds a staff; and with the third, he holds a black antelope skin.
Having meditated upon oneself as holding a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and seated upon the shoulders of a lion, Garuḍa, and Viṣṇu, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ hrīḥ huṃ*.
This is the *Sādhana* arising from Hari, Hari, and the vehicle of Hari.

78) First of all, the mantra-practitioner, seated on a comfortable seat with the intention of uplifting the world, performs the sevenfold supreme worship beginning with the confession of misdeeds; [he visualizes] that which is produced from the syllable *yaṃ*... [k, ḍh:]...
The wind mandala, marked by a blue banner, is shaped like a bow;
above it is the fire mandala, red in color and triangular, marked by red lines, produced from the syllable *re*; and above that is the water mandala, circular, produced from the syllable *vaṃ*.

It is white in color and marked with a white banner—or, according to versions kh and ḍh, marked with a white vase—above which is the Maheśvara-maṇḍala, produced from the syllable *laṃ*. It is square, yellow in color, and adorned with four corners featuring yellow three-pronged vajras; above that is [the palace] produced from the syllable *suṃ*, consisting of the seven precious gems.

Having visualized Mount Sumeru with its eight peaks, upon which is a universal lotus transformed from the syllable *paṃ*, and upon that, having meditated on oneself, one should sequentially place *oṃ hrīḥ huṃ* at the head, throat, and heart; thus,
one becomes free from the obscurations of karma accumulated since beginningless time.

The practitioner of mantra should visualize the form of Kumāra, who has arisen from Hari, Hari, and Harivāhana, who possesses the body of a Lord of the World, and who is filled with the blazing rays of gold and jewels. Afterwards, through the purification of merit and wisdom, he should visualize a moon-maṇḍala and a sun-maṇḍala within his own heart; there, by means of the rays and flames issuing from the syllable *hrīḥ*, he should summon the Jñānasattva.
Having worshipped him in the form that is about to be described with the previously mentioned offerings, one should— through the unification of the *jñānasattva* and the *samayasattva*—
visualize oneself as the Lord Lokeśvara, who originated from Hari, Hara, and Harivāhana, with a steady mind, possessing six arms, white in color, and wearing a crown of matted hair.
He has a peaceful appearance; with his right hand he makes the Fully Awakened One his witness,
with the second he holds a rosary, and with the third he instructs those dwelling in miserable states toward auspiciousness.

One should meditate upon the Blessed One holding a staff in his left [hand], a black antelope skin in the second, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in the third. Regarding the purification therein: Hari [is purified] by the two mandalas of wind and fire, and by the mandala of Varuṇa.
The Garuḍa is the purity of the Māhendra-maṇḍala and Sumeru; the yogi who constantly meditates upon him as Hari becomes capable of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings,
becomes beloved by all people, becomes possessed of great wisdom, becomes free from disease and free from calamity, and becomes wealthy.
One becomes greatly empowered in the ritual of subjugation through the use of a corpse (*śava-viṣa-karman*). The mantra for recitation is to be learned from the oral instruction of the Guru.
[This concludes] the *Sādhana* of Lokeśvara, who arises from Hari, Hari, and the vehicle of Hari.

First, having displayed the yogi-cloth (*yogipaṭa*) in a place favorable to the mind, one should draw a moon-maṇḍala with saffron in the center of a great maṇḍala (*māhendramaṇḍala*) before it, using the mantra *oṃ vajrarekhe hūṃ*. Thereafter, *jaḥ hūṃ*.

Having performed the invocation with the mantra *vaṃ padmasthahor*, one should worship the Lord Trailokyavaśaṅkara Lokeśvara in the center of the maṇḍala with this mantra: *oṃ trailokyavaśaṅkarāya vajrapuṣpe huṃ pratīccha svāhā*. Then, *oṃ*...
Having uttered "muṇivajre" [or "maṇivajre"] and "mur," one should visualize a red syllable *ĀṂ* in one's own heart;
through its transformation, a sun disk appears, upon which is a red syllable *HRĪḤ*. By the rays of light from that [syllable], the Tathāgata Amitābha is drawn forth.
Having performed worship and the confession of misdeeds and so forth, and having brought the three worlds under control,

one should cause the rays of light to enter one's own seed-syllable; through their transformation, one instantly becomes Lokeśvara, whose entire body is intensely red with great passion, who has one face, two arms, and three eyes, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
Having visualized oneself as adorned with divine ornaments and garments, seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon a red lotus, holding in one's hands a noose and a goad marked with a vajra,
and [surrounded by] Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who assume various emanations and are situated above a vajra-noose located at the center of the three worlds—
Having recited *hrīḥ huṃ yāṃ* [k, ḍh: *yoṃ, ḍh, a; āḥ, g:
*yīṃ*] and meditated upon the three-syllable mantra, one should say: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako’ham*; *oṃ vajrātmakāḥ sarvadharmā vajrātmako’ham*.

Thus one should recite these two mantras consisting of vajra-nature. For one who practices in this manner, qualities such as shaking and trembling arise. Following that, one should recite: *oṃ hrīḥ aḥ hāṃ hārīti yakṣeśvarī svāhā*.

One should offer the *piṇḍa* with the mantra: "Oṃ Āṃ Kroṃ Hrīṃ! To the retinues of all the Gaṇas, Vīras, and Vīreśvarīs: *a a*, descend, descend; may the world-protectors of the ten directions descend! Accept, accept this *bali*! Huṃ Svāhā! Having thus offered the *bali*, one should dwell in the yoga of the deity.
The *Sādhana* of Lokeśvara, the Subjugator of the Three Worlds, composed by Saraha-pāda according to the tradition of Oḍḍiyāna, is completed.
Homage to the Lord of the World!
First of all, the practitioner of mantra, in a place agreeable to the mind—

Having displayed the *yogipaṭa* in the proper place, one should draw a moon-maṇḍala with saffron in the center of a great maṇḍala before it, using this mantra: *oṃ vajrarekhe hūṃ | jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ padmastha hoḥ*. Having performed the invocation with this mantra...

In the center of the maṇḍala, one should worship the venerable Lord Lokeśvara, the Subduer of the Three Worlds, with this mantra: Oṃ trailokyavaśaṅkarāya vajrapuṣpe hūṃ pratīccha svāhā. Oṃ munivajre muḥ—this is the mantra for dismissal. Afterwards, [one should place him] in one's own heart.

One should contemplate the syllable *āṃ*. Through its transformation, a solar disc is produced. Upon that, one should visualize the seed-syllable of Śakti, possessing a radiance equal to the rising sun. Having worshipped Amitābha [and the Tathāgatas, as added in manuscript *k*] with its rays, and having performed the confession of misdeeds and so forth, [one should again [place it] upon the body].
As all this enters, it instantly transforms into [the deity] seated upon a lotus in the vajra-paryaṅka posture,
with three wide-open eyes, wearing a crown of matted locks, red in color,
and holding in his hands a noose and a goad marked with a vajra; he stands upon two lions of the triple world bound by a noose atop a vajra.
The Vajrayoginīs, who assume various emanated forms, bestow empowerment while remaining there; likewise, the Bodhisattvas,
adorned with various ornaments, perform worship.

The hosts of Vidyādharas, Harihara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and various Yoginīs perform dances, instrumental music, and other such acts; likewise, he is surrounded by various groups of spirits and the like, adorned with garlands of human heads and skulls.
One should visualize various parasols, chowries, and so forth. At such a time, one should see the Tathāgata Amitābha upon one's head.

One should contemplate oneself in this manner. Afterwards, having visualized a solar disc composed of rays of light above the navel, one should place the seed-syllable *Śakti* above it on the left and the seed-syllable of Wrath (*krodhabīja*) in the heart.

"Adorned with the vowel ĀḤ" is the mantra to be meditated upon [k, b: reads "this is the heart-mantra of the Lord"]. Having meditated on all this as being of the nature of the Vajra, one should recite the mantra of the Vajra-nature and contemplate that which is of the nature of the Vajra: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the self whose essence is the Vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. This is the mantra of the Vajra-nature.

And by means of the yoga of practice, having performed shaking, trembling, and possession, non-dual knowledge arises. That yogi roars like an elephant and, as if intoxicated by wine, sports with the five colors. If...

When one does not abide in the five colors, then trembling, shaking, possession, and so forth do not remain in one's body. Thus, having understood this very point, one should abide in the five colors; by that, accomplishment will be attained.
Once success has been achieved, having performed shaking, trembling, and possession within the body of another, one suppresses passion, hatred, and the like.

Just as copper pierced by alchemical elixir (*siddharasa*) abandons its blackness, so too the very body, when pierced by the elixir of non-duality (*advaita-rasa*), abandons passion, hatred, and the like. *Hrīḥ*. [k, kh, g: *huṃ huṃ yā*, k,]
kh: *hrīṃ* *huṃ* *aḥ*, ḍh: *hrīṃ* *huṃ* *āḥ* *huṃ* *yāṃ*—this is the mantra to be recited (*japyamantra*). oṃ *hrīḥ* [k, g, ḍh:
oṃ *hrīṃ* *aḥ*, k, b: oṃ *aḥ*, kh: oṃ *hrīḥ* *aḥ*] *aḥ* *hāṃ* Hārītī, Queen of the Yakṣas, *svāhā*—this is the Hārītī mantra. oṃ *āṃ* *kroṃ*.

*Hrīṃ!* With the retinues of all the heroes and heroines of the Gaṇas, descend, descend! May the world-protectors of the ten directions descend! Accept this offering, accept it! *Huṃ svāhā!* This is the mantra for the offering (*balimantra*).
Thus ends the sādhana of Lokeśvara, the Subduer of the Three Worlds, who emerged from Oḍḍiyāna and was brought down by the venerable Saraha.
Homage to Lokeśvara!
Oṃ ciṭi cinaṭi vikloli vikloli amukaṃ sadhanaparivāraṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā! Ten thousand preliminary services (*pūrvasevā*) [are required].

Regarding the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*): having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times as the preliminary service—as indicated by *k*, *b*: "ten thousand of the preliminary service," and *ḍh*: "the preliminary service is ten thousand"—one should thereafter begin the practice (*sādhana*). One should visualize the Lord Āryāvalokiteśvara, red in color, accompanied on his right and left sides by the two goddesses Tārā and Bhṛkuṭī, and adorned with red garlands, garments, and unguents.

One should contemplate oneself at the three junctions of the day as having four arms, holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and an arrow; possessing the singular aesthetic sentiment of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic love), red in color, and situated beneath an *aśoka* tree covered with flowers.

One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of salt; within seven days, this brings a woman or a man under one's control, and within twenty-one days, a great man. This is done with *madana* combined with salt.
Having accomplished the *puttalikā*—
having fashioned an image measuring four finger-breadths— one should recite the mantra at the three junctions of the day over smokeless embers of *khadira* wood.
By heating [it] with the name of someone, that person becomes entirely submissive.
Having consecrated salt with *vajrodaka* (diamond-water) and recited [the mantra] over it one hundred and eight times, whoever is given this [salt] becomes submissive the very moment it is consumed.
It comes to pass.
The *sādhana* of Raktalokeśvara is completed.

According to the previously mentioned procedure, likewise, immediately after emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there appears a red lotus born from a red syllable *hrīḥ*. In its center is the noble Avalokiteśvara, transformed from a red syllable *āḥ*, red in color, and wearing a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*).
Having visualized oneself as wearing a crown of matted hair containing Amitābha within it, holding a red lotus in the left hand and opening it with the right hand,

and adorned with various ornaments and garments— one should contemplate white bees, whose forms are produced from the sixteen vowels, upon the petals of a red lotus arising from the syllable *hrīḥ* at one’s own heart. Then:

Having visualized a lotus in the heart of the object of practice (*sādhya*) as before, one emits bees from the lotus situated in one’s own heart through the path of one’s own vajra— having emanated them— with the mantra *oṃ bhamarāḥ sādhyahṛdi padmāmṛtam ākarṣaya jaḥ*, and having caused them to enter the vajra of the object of practice, [one takes] the nectar residing in that lotus.
The bees, having drawn them in,
once again eject them through their own vajra-path by means of that same vajra into that very place.

One should visualize those [beings] emitting drops of the nectar-honey of that mind as they enter; the mantra is *oṃ hūṃ*. One should contemplate this without interruption for seven days, visualizing the object of practice falling at one's feet.
The ritual procedure for the subjugation of Lokeśvara.
Homage to the Lord of the World!

First of all, the practitioner, having risen at dawn, should sit upon a comfortable seat in the sattvaparyaṅka posture and visualize a yellow syllable Hrīḥ upon a moon disc transformed from the first vowel [A] in his heart.
Having brought forth the Blessed One being visualized by means of masses of light-rays from that very seed-syllable,

one should worship him with emanated flowers, incense, and so forth, perform the confession of misdeeds and other rites before him, and practice the cultivation of the four divine abodes, such as loving-kindness. Thereafter—

Having meditated upon all things, both external and internal, as being empty by nature, one should repeat the mantra: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. Immediately thereafter, in the expanse of space, by means of the first vowel, there appears a moon disc; above that, the yellow syllable Hrīḥ, and from that very [syllable], a red lotus.
Having transformed all that which is presided over by those seeds, [one should visualize] the Blessed One, yellow in color,
with a crown of matted hair marked by a crescent moon, the region of his head distinguished by Amitābha,
seated upon a red lotus on the skin of a black antelope.
Seated in the vajraparyaṅka posture, bearing above the samādhi-mudrā a skull-cup filled with various jewels, and wearing a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) made of deerskin; (p. 86) [kh: ...]
Clad in a tiger-skin garment, devoid of ornaments,

blue-throated with a throat distinguished by a blue goitre, and having two cobras on either side whose tails are joined to one another and whose jewel-adorned hoods are distinguished by their upward-turned faces looking toward the Blessed One—
One should recite the mantra. Therein, this is the mantra: *oṃ sphuliṅgāṭṭahāsa kṣaḥ*.
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of Noble Avalokiteśvara Nīlakaṇṭha, which possesses immeasurable benefits.

Following the previously described procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one should visualize in the sky a vajra-fence and a vajra-canopy, which have arisen from the transformation of a *viśvavajra* produced from the syllable *huṃ* situated upon a sun disk born from the syllable *repha*.
In the center of that is a terrifying cremation ground, and in the middle of that is a red eight-petaled lotus, and in the center of that—

One should visualize the Blessed Noble Avalokiteśvara, born from the syllable *Nīlahrīḥ*, black in color, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a solar disc; he has five faces, three eyes, and twelve arms;
his two right faces are white and red, and likewise his two left faces are yellow and green; with his right hands...

He holds a *ḍamaru* drum, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a goad, a noose, a vajra, an arrow, and a bow in his left hands; he holds a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), a skull-cup, a red lotus, a jewel, a wheel, and a bow in his right hands; his entire face is terrifying with bared fangs, and he is endowed with the six seals (*ṣaṇmudrā*).
Having instantly visualized oneself as naked, with a body adorned by a garland of fresh heads, beautiful in every limb, [one should contemplate] within the moon at the heart.

One should recite the mantra—*oṃ āḥ hūṃ munivaravajre hrīṃ hūṃ jaḥ*—which revolves around the syllable *hrīḥ*, in the form of a rosary. Even one who has committed the five sins of immediate retribution attains accomplishment through one hundred thousand recitations.
This concludes the Sādhana of Noble Avalokiteśvara according to the *Māyājāla* sequence.
Homage to the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Great Compassionate One. It is thus:
Oṃ cala cala cili cili culu culu kulu kulu mulu mulu huṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ, O you who hold a lotus in your hand, svāhā! [Recite this] five times every day.
One should recite this at the three junctions of the day. Even a donkey can memorize three hundred verses. This is the *Padmahastā Dhāraṇī*:
*Nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya tadyathā oṃ dharaṇīdhare dharādhare bhadre subhadre svāhā*.

During a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse, having washed [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and having placed one hundred and eight *māṣa* beans in its mouth, one should recite the mantra until it is liberated. Standing before a cloth painting or an image of Lokanātha, [one should offer] a lamp with clarified butter...
Having lit a lamp and kindled it, and having prepared a mandala with sandalwood or with fallen cow dung,
one should station the superior practitioner, who is pure in conduct, at the door,
while oneself—

Not looking at the moon or the sun, having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times as preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one should accomplish it while observing celibacy (*brahmacarya*). At that very moment, one understands even those treatises (*śāstra*) not previously heard.
The teachings heard do not go to waste because of the power of his dhāraṇī;
they are placed upon his head after having been ground into powder at his feet.
He attains complete mastery over all things as long as the moon and sun endure;
no diseases arise for him, nor do *ḍākinīs*, malevolent spirits, or thieves.
By anointing [with this], there is constant pacification of all diseases,
having visualized the Lord of the World as arisen from the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*.

The wise practitioner should, according to the prescribed rite, meditate upon the Lord as two-armed, white in color, granting boons with his right hand and holding a lotus in his left; with Amitābha situated within his matted locks, seated upon a moon on a universal lotus, and resting in the vajra-paryaṅka posture.
The Dhāraṇī of Māṣamukha, together with its ritual procedure, is completed.

Oṃ. Following the previously described procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness, one should visualize the venerable Lord Lokeśvara, Sugatisandarśana, who arises from a white syllable Hrīḥ, is white in color, and has six arms.

One should meditate on [the deity] holding the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), as well as a rosary (*akṣamālā*) in the right hands, and holding a lotus (*padma*), a water-pot (*kuṇḍī*), and a triple staff (*tridaṇḍī*) in the left hands;

adorned with jewel ornaments, wearing a sacred thread (*vratasūtra*), and a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmukuṭa*); seated upon a moon disc atop a lotus; and possessing a serene form. His mantra for recitation (*jāpamantra*) is: *oṃ hrīḥ*.
Svāhā!
Thus concludes the *Sādhanā* of Lokeśvara, the Revealer of the Happy Rebirths.
p.
89) Thus, immediately following the meditation on emptiness, [one should visualize] the deity arising from the white syllable *hrīḥ*, wearing a crown of matted hair, with six arms;
the first pair of arms in the boon-granting (*varada*) gesture, the second pair holding a jewel and a manuscript, and the third pair of arms—

One should visualize [the deity] as white in color, possessing a gentle form, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a rosary and a triple staff (tridaṇḍika), holding a vow and a rosary, and seated upon a moon disc atop a lotus; the mantra is likewise the same.
The Sadhana of Lokeśvara Satisfying the Hungry Ghosts.

Homage to the one with the steady wheel! Homage to the Buddha, who is radiant, having dispelled the entire expanse of delusion through the majesty of his glorious speech, and who is as pure as the orb of the rising, golden-hued sun.
Having bowed with devotion to the one who possesses the form of a child yet is aged, who bears a sword of exalted luster and wisdom— I, for the sake of recollecting myself,
shall here write down this jewel of a wheel.
Having thoroughly contemplated the infinite oceans of omniscient wisdom in all directions,
Those who are intent upon rescuing the vast multitude of sentient beings who are terrified.
Having performed various kinds of worship for them— known as the wish-fulfilling jewel of the mind—
in order to protect the world, (p. 90) [he set out].
One should bestow one's own body.
Then, for the sake of increasing virtue, the practitioner should perform this:
"Terrified, I confess all my sins; with joy, I rejoice in the virtues of the world;
I go for refuge to the Three Jewels."
I direct my mind toward the enlightenment of the Perfectly Awakened One.

Thereafter, one should again undertake this: "This world, through the abandonment of the grasped and the grasper, is like a dream or a magical illusion; it is pure by virtue of its intrinsic luminosity and rests upon a likeness to space."

Having briefly ascertained that the self is composed of the play of the mind, one should again meditate upon the syllable *mūṃ*, which is dense with a network of rays, as arising from that [syllable].
Then one should contemplate the orb of the moon, which has turned back from its course, its full disc stained tawny with saffron paste,
crowded with a garland of stars shining with their own luster, and illuminating the quarters of the sky with its rays.
Then, one should again visualize the orb of passion-rays arising from the seed-syllable *mūḥ*,
entirely surrounded by the letters beginning with *ka* and *kha*.
Above that, it is reddish like glowing light and saffron.
And in that [space], the mantra-practitioner, beholding the syllable *mūḥ*, [should visualize] a beautiful lotus with radiant petals produced from it.
One should visualize an *indīvara* lotus with a shimmering mass of rays, in the center of which is the seed-syllable *mūḥ*.

Filling the world with rays of light arising from that, which are produced by the emanations of Buddhas, he is seated upon the moon, radiant with rags as brilliant as the darkness-dispelling glow of bees.
He who dispels the dense mass of darkness with nets of red rays,
who is fully skilled in bestowing the excellence of all forms, the glorious Lord of Speech.
Delightful with the grace of the erotic sentiment, it possessed the beauty of a lotus-face expanding in full bloom.
One who desires his state should meditate upon the Hero, who wears the ornaments of a youth.
Having reflected thus, one should meditate upon Vāgīśa as the syllable *mūḥ* within the heart—
blazing, with the luster of red color, and emitting a circle of light.
Therefore, one should fill with rays the eight-spoked wheel that has arisen from that, which destroys the darkness of the heart; one should behold the Lord, who consists of gnosis,
fashioned by the radiance of the sharp rays of the Sun.
It was as if strewn with heaps of the radiance of the flames of molten gold,
and covered with red syllables like clusters of red flowers.
92) In that regard, one should first contemplate the syllables as follows: on the spokes of the wheel—in the east, south, west, and north—respectively, the syllables *ara*, *pa*, *ca*, and *na*.

Having ascertained with unwavering certainty that the letter *na* is at the navel, and that the consonants beginning with *ka* are located in the southeast, southwest, and northwest [respectively], one should then [visualize] the mass of rays from the assembly of letters of the wheel,
which dispels the circle of darkness within the heart.
[The syllable *vaya*], having emerged from the pores of one's own body,

becomes of one flavor with the nectar of gnosis from the hearts of the Tathāgatas situated in the world-systems of the ten directions; then, emerging from those [pores], by means of those very [rays].

One should meditate for a long time on [the deity] entering through the pores of the skin and illuminating one's own body. Then, for one whose mind has become steady, one should subsequently cultivate [this vision] according to the method of radiating and reabsorbing, until it appears as a direct perception.
Together with those who maintain the state of non-duality with Mañjuśrī, they shine brilliantly with their very colors.
As this wheel attained clarity through his constant application to meditation day and night.
Even regarding all the previously unseen collections of arts within the realm of literature,
his intellect proceeds as he desires, illuminated by the light of a jewel-lamp, dispelling the darkness of the heart.
Indeed,

this wheel, when examined for even a single fortnight— whether by those seeking one's own welfare or out of mere curiosity— will soon awaken the true nature of the Sugata within all states of existence.
[To you who are present] ||
If there is any merit here arising from the arrangement of this wheel, may it shine within the minds of those whose hearts are not moved by passion,
dispelling the dense darkness of delusion like the newly risen sun.
May this assembly of people proceed toward the glorious splendor of the speech of the Lord.

The *Sthiracakrasādhana* is completed. [After this colophon, manuscript Kh provides the date in the following words: *saṃ 285 pauṣyamāse*, meaning in the month of Pauṣa in the year 285 (Newari Śaka), which corresponds to A.D. 1165, and not 1167 as Bendall states.]
Having bowed to this glorious wheel of the Protector Mañjuvajra, it is written here in clear words for the sake of the understanding of beginners.
Seated on a comfortable seat, the yogi should visualize the Guru, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas situated in the sky;
having performed various kinds of mental offerings to them, he should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth. Then, he should realize that the entire universe is mind-only (*cittamātra*).

Having ascertained oneself—free from the grasped and the grasper, like a dream or a reflection—as being of the nature of the syllable *mūḥ*, reddish-brown like saffron, [p. 94] born from the syllable *mūḥ*...
