[k, ḍh, g: varjitaṃ]... [k, ḍh, g: varjitaṃ]... [k, ḍh, g: varjitaṃ]... [k, ḍh, g: varjitaṃ]... [k, ḍh, g: varjitaṃ]... [k, ḍh, g: varjitaṃ]... [

One should visualize a wheel, red with rays of light consisting of the vowels beginning with *a*, produced from the syllables *ka*, *kha*, *ḍha*, *ga*, and *ca*. Above that, one should contemplate a lunar disc produced from the syllable *muḥ*, radiant and red with the luster of the consonants beginning with *ka*. Above that, produced from the syllable *muḥ*...
Having visualized a radiant, stainless blue lotus born from the syllable *aḥ*,
its filaments empowered by the syllable *muḥ*, one should contemplate that which is transformed from it as being the color of saffron, adorned with five strips of bark-cloth.

One should meditate upon oneself as Vāgīśvara, the youthful ornament whose sole aesthetic flavor is the erotic (śṛṅgāra), holding a sword and a book, seated upon the moon. In his heart, one should visualize an eight-spoked wheel born from the syllable *muḥ*, stable, consisting of rays of light, blazing, encircled by a garland of the letters beginning with *a*, and externally adorned with a sacred thread consisting of a garland of the letters beginning with *ka* radiating forth.

And having visualized the letter *A* at his navel, the letter *Ra* on the eastern spoke, the letter *Pa* on the southern spoke, the letter *Ca* on the western spoke, the letter *Na* on the northern spoke, and the letters of non-proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) with the luster of saffron in the intermediate directions beginning with the southeast, he illuminates the interior of the body with the mass of light rays from that wheel.

One should contemplate for a long time the mantra-body (*mantra-śarīra*)—[k, g: *mantraḥśarīraṃ*]—issuing forth from the pores of every hair, illuminating the world-systems of the ten directions, and then re-entering through those very same pores to illuminate the interior of the body. The recitation mantra is: *oṃ arapacana muḥ*.
Having performed the sādhana of the Stable Wheel, whatever merit has been acquired—
by that may the entire world possess a splendor equal to Mañjuvajra.
The practice of the stable wheel by one who is liberated.
p.
95) Homage to the illustrious Vādirāḍ Mañjughoṣa!
First of all, having performed the washing of the face and other preliminary rites, one should sit upon a soft and comfortable seat. [k:]
[With a face of bliss], one should visualize a moon disc by means of the syllable *A* upon a lotus born from the syllable *Paṃ* in one’s own heart;

then, having drawn forth from the Akaniṣṭha realm the eternally perfected Mañjuśrī Kumāra by means of rays of light from the syllable *Maṃ*, one should contemplate him before oneself. Thereafter, having performed the external worship with flowers, incense, and so forth, and having paid homage, [one should proceed] afterwards.

Having performed the confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, the dedication of merit, going for refuge to the Three Jewels, the generation of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), the request [to the Buddhas not to pass into nirvāṇa], and the offering of one’s own body, one should cultivate the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra).
Furthermore, one should contemplate emptiness, which is the summary of the essential reality of all phenomena. [Emptiness...]

One should contemplate: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* (I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness). Then, recollecting one’s former vow (*praṇidhāna*), one should observe one’s own body as mere appearance within one’s own heart.
Upon a lotus and moon, through the entry of all the Tathāgatas via the light rays from the seed-syllable *maṃ*,

one should visualize oneself in the form of Mañjuśrī: yellow in color, holding the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyānamudrā*), adorned with jewel ornaments and a jeweled crown, bearing a blue lotus in the left hand, seated upon a lion throne, with Akṣobhya as his crest-jewel, and resting on a moon seat.

[The wheel-throne: One should visualize oneself as having the radiance of the moon. Then, on the right side, one should visualize the youth Sudhana, born from the seed-syllable *suṃ*, blazing with various jewel ornaments, wearing a jeweled crown, with a single volume of all the Dharmas tucked under his arm, and with palms joined in the gesture of reverent salutation.
He should stand. On the left side is Yamāri, born from the black syllable *huṃ*, with a distorted face, a mallet in his hand, and tawny hair standing erect.
Adorned with nāga ornaments, [he is seated]. Then, on the right and left sides are Candraprabha and Sūryaprabha;

in the directions starting from the east are Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi; and in the corners starting from the southeast are Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā. Then, by means of the entry of the gnosis-being (jñānasattva),...

Having performed the consecration of the bases of the eyes and so forth, as well as the consecrations, offerings, and praises of body, speech, and mind, one who possesses meditative concentration should subsequently recite the mantra while sealing Akṣobhya upon the head.
In this regard, the mantra is: *oṃ dharmadhātuvāgīśvara muḥ svāhā*.
The Sadhana of Mañjuśrī.

By the command of the Guru— who is great by nature, who is skilled in causing the lotus-pond of wisdom to blossom, and who, though desiring nothing for himself, desires the supreme happiness of all the world— one’s own happiness, however slight, becomes truly one's own.
I, one of dull and very limited intellect, shall now set forth the sādhana of the Blessed Mañjuśrī.
By one who has fully relied upon faith, the mother of all that is auspicious, and by whom every unwholesome action has been abandoned—
that very same person, with a purified mind, should constantly practice meditation and the other virtues after hearing them from the Guru concerning the Blessed One.
First, in a secluded place that is pleasing to the mind, strewn with various kinds of fragrant flowers and other offerings;
Having avoided the thorns of the road such as thieves and the like, and having completed his other duties, he sat down in comfort.
Having with effort made the flickering mind intensely one-pointed,
and having placed the welfare of others within one's intention, one should thereafter meditate upon that.
[He possesses] friendliness toward sentient beings, characterized by equanimity and the joy of regarding them as one's own kin;
and compassion, which desires to uplift the worlds from suffering and even from the causes of suffering.

The wise one should meditate upon equanimity, which is characterized by a particular joy of mind, is harmonious, and is accompanied by the form of turning away from attachment even to what is non-existent.
Thereafter, having brought to mind as much as desired a white-colored orb of the cool-rayed moon of stainless luster,
one should visualize upon it something delicate and of the color of pure gold.
One should visualize a stainless-petaled lotus with eight petals.
The minister should long meditate upon the supreme, upward-tending cavity of rays, golden in form and natural, which belongs to the moon and the lotus whose beams are flickering as they spread;
this cavity, covered by the former two for the welfare of the worlds.
The supreme among men, desiring the state of the most excellent Mañjuvajra.
Subsequently, it becomes agitated by the sufferings of birth, misfortune, affliction, old age, senility, and so forth,
and is shrouded by rays of light taking the form of a pair of a moon and a lotus.
Having observed and scrutinized the entire universe, one should behold one's own self as complete in mind— equal to the Buddhas and accepted by all as the supreme bliss.
Thereafter, having drawn near all the gurus, as well as the Sugatas and the illustrious Bodhisattvas, by means of those rays stationed in the ten directions;
Having placed them before him and having accomplished the ritual of worship consisting of mental constructs,
one should worship them with various flowers, fragrant incense, and diverse forms.
Then, after they have confessed their sins and so forth,
he should cause them to enter into oneness with those very rays through the openings of the hair-pores.

Having entered by way of the massed form and seen him in the heart, one should then meditate upon that arising— the Lord Śrī Mañjuvajra, who is skilled at splitting asunder the great mountain of delusion.
Translucent, bearing the form of a sixteen-year-old, seated upon the back of a tiger, with a pair of lotus-hands busied in exposition, resting in the half-lotus posture on his left side—
he is neither tall nor short, but possesses an incomparable refuge for a mass of beauty.
It was filled with various kinds of ornaments and garlands made of jewels, gold, and gems.

Having meditated for a long time upon the Hero Kumāra, the Lord of Orators, the protector of all beings— who is neither unreal nor non-unreal, appearing like a clear reflection on the surface of a mirror— [one should proceed].
Afterwards, one should meditate upon oneself as Mañjuvajra, free from all defilement, until the wise practitioner’s body becomes equal in form to that of the Blessed One.

When exhausted by meditation, one should recite the mantra ending in *ta*, *ra*, *na*, or *sa*, arranged according to the sequence of consonants; one should recite the syllable *o* (or *sa*, *se*, or *mai*) with a nasalization.
Furthermore, here the virtuous will grasp this special distinction through the very words of the true guru, whose intellect is stainless and pure.
Having received instructions from my preceptor, the most eminent teacher, regarding the practice of meditation and mantras, I am indeed not capable of fully proclaiming all their specific details.
O Mañjuśrī, if even with a mind of mere curiosity one constantly performs propitiation of the Blessed One,
then that wise person, having pleased the feet of the true guru, will certainly shatter the mass of darkness of dullness.

Having properly composed this *Sādhana* of the glorious Mañjukumāra by the command of my guru, whatever immeasurable merit (*puṇya*) has been acquired by me of dull intellect— by that, may he quickly become like the glorious Mañjuvajra, casting aside all effort.
Let all people remain like the wish-fulfilling gem and the kalpa-tree.
The *Śrīmadvādirāṭsādhana* is completed.
This work is the composition of the scholar, the venerable Cintāmaṇidatta.
Homage to Mañjunātha!
To the one whose youthful form possesses the splendor of a beautiful, saffron-red complexion, and who has destroyed the net of immeasurable delusion with the rays of the Perfectly Awakened One;
Bow to the King of the Forest of Desire, who assumes the graceful posture of a lion and performs the exposition of the Dharma through mantras.
First, having risen in the morning, [one should visualize] within the universal lotus at the heart,
above the lunar disc, the syllable *hrīṃ*, reddish like saffron.
Having looked [at the mandala] and performed the purification of the face and other rites, one should enter the pure meditation-chamber.
Having settled into a comfortable posture, one should recite the mantra which is the source of the Buddha's qualities.
May he possess toward all beings a loving-kindness increased a thousandfold by the affection felt for a virtuous son,
and a compassion that desires to lift them up from suffering, for those whose eyes are the cause of their misery.
Constant desire for the cultivation of good qualities, as well as joy,
indifference toward one's own affairs without consideration, and acting for the sake of others— these are [the marks of a friend].
Having meditated, the practitioner, having summoned those Victors by means of an array of radiating rays,
sees the sky filled with them and performs a mental offering.

Having caused the goddess to manifest throughout the universe, she who performs anointing, massaging, bathing, and various adornments, and who is like a cloud for the surging flood of shimmering offerings.
The deity.
Having prostrated with innumerable emanated bodies, each individually,
[I confess] the threefold physical and mental [misdeeds] arising from passion, hatred, and delusion.
Out of a sense of spiritual urgency, one should confess all evil deeds—those committed by oneself, those caused to be done, and those approved;
and together with all sentient beings, one should repeatedly undertake the vow of restraint for the future.
Having rejoiced in the merit born of generosity and other virtues by the Perfectly Awakened One, Mañjughoṣa, and the others,
he requested and entreated them to teach the True Dharma for a long time.
Having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels and having relied upon the bodhicitta, which is the true path,
[one recites]: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrātmako ’ham*.
Then,
having visualized the syllable *maṃ* situated upon a moon atop a universal lotus,
and having seen that throbbing seed-syllable which has made the world beautiful, [one should proceed].
Having entered and drawn [the deity] forth, the excellent mantra-practitioner should visualize Vādirāja,
whose body is as beautiful as saffron-red, who has conquered the god of love through his illusory power.
Seated upon a lion-throne in the posture of a lion, unwavering and in a graceful pose,
he holds a blue lotus in his left forearm.
He is the mass of qualities of the Perfectly Awakened One, radiant with jewel ornaments,
and garlanded by the light of the multitude of Buddhas shimmering from emerging rays of light.

The lotus of his hand is bound with the great seal (mahāmudrā) of the Wheel of Dharma; likewise, upon the blue lotus, there is a similar [seal] produced by the light-rays of the mantra that accomplishes all things.
Having brought the supreme Lord together with the celestial palaces and so forth,
having established his equality, and having caused him to hear the pledge three times,
one should then draw him in, cause him to enter, and bring the Buddha perfectly under control.

Oṃ vajrasattva samayadṛśya hoḥ! You are the pledge, I am the pledge; you are the pledge, I am [the pledge]. Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! Oṃ, the empowerment of body; Āḥ, the empowerment of speech; Hūṃ, the empowerment of mind.
Having performed the empowerment of gnosis with the lotus mudrā and the seed-syllable piṇḍākṣara.
One should become the Wisdom-Vajra Head, whose water-jar is filled by deities emerging from the bodies of the Perfectly Awakened Ones impelled by rays of light;
he is worshipped by the Buddhas of the ten directions and is devoted to the worship of the Buddhas.
One who is devoted to the worship of the Buddha should,
having gathered together, manifest [the rite] for the sake of the purity of the accomplishment of existence for one who is worthy.
Having further cultivated this and attained pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of both body and mind,
one should then commence the recitation of the mantra according to the sequence of the necklace and the swing.
Having visualized the entire universe as an ocean of all qualities, performing the entry and so forth,
one should invite [the deity] with "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ" and ask for forgiveness.
Having oneself become Mañjuvara and beholding the world as being of that same nature, one should contemplate it as such.
Wherever an action is appropriate, one should likewise apply it for the sake of sentient beings.
This sādhana of Vādirāja has been composed for the recollection of disciples who have faith in the Three Jewels; may it surely lead to the accomplishment of worldly goals.

Having included all the gurus, buddhas, and bodhisattvas within one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), one should begin the maṇḍala dedicated to them. *Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā* is the mantra for washing the hands and sipping water. *Oṃ huṃ* is the mantra for the consecration of the seat (*āsanādhiṣṭhāna*). *Oṃ vajrabhūme*.

*Huṃ*, the mantra for the consecration of the site (*bhūmiparigraha*). *Oṃ sarvavighnānutsāraya huṃ svāhā*, the mantra for the water used for cow-dung and other substances. Then, once the sweeping is completed, *oṃ vajrarekhe huṃ* is the mantra for the empowerment of the lines. Again, having offered a single flower upon the maṇḍala, *oṃ surekhe*.

Having recited, "May all the Tathāgatas grant their blessing, svāhā," one should wash one's hands. Thereafter, taking a single flower and reciting, "Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa rakṣa māṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should perform self-protection by casting the flower toward the region of one's own head. Again, [recite] "Oṃ āḥ hūṃ."

Thus ends the mantra for self-protection and so forth. Having visualized that maṇḍala in the form of a universal lotus, one should perceive a moon above it, and upon that, the Blessed One’s seed-syllable, reddish like saffron. By means of its rays, one should attract the eternally perfected Blessed One—drawing him in according to the analogy of the transfer of light from one lamp to another—and [place him] right there.

Having caused [the deities] to enter, one should manifest the Blessed One: *oṃ mañjughoṣāya vajrapuṣpe hūṃ*, *oṃ akṣobhyāya vajrapuṣpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vairocanāya vajrapuṣpe hūṃ*; [and likewise for] Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.
Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā— consecration should be bestowed as before by means of the preparation of flowers,
incense, lamps, food offerings, fragrant scents, and garments.

Having performed prostration, confession of misdeeds, and rejoicing in merit, one should recite the mantra. Then one should dismiss [the deities] with: *oṃ vajra muḥ*. *Oṃ*, the syllable *a* is the gateway to all phenomena because they are primordially unarisen. *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* is the mantra for the bali offering to all spirits (*sārvabhautika*). *Oṃ hārītyai mahāyakṣiṇyai hara hara*.

"May all my sins be exhausted! O you who enter into all yakṣiṇīs, svāhā!"—this is the mantra of Hārītī. Oṃ, svāhā to those seated upon the foremost rice-balls!—this is the mantra for the foremost rice-balls. Oṃ, svāhā to those seated upon the discarded rice-balls!—this is the mantra for the discarded rice-balls. Oṃ āḥ, to the glory of the commitment of the consecration of all Tathāgatas, hūṃ hūṃ!
The bathing mantra for the image and so forth.
The *Sādhana* of Mañjuśrī Vādirāja, spoken by Vajrayoginī, is completed.
(104) Homage to Mañjuśrī!
Following the previously described procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness, [k, g: ...after that]...
Having visualized a red syllable *plīṃ* [or *ka*, or *hrīṃ*] upon a moon mandala atop a universal lotus,
one should cause the wisdom of the Tathāgatas, summoned by its rays, to enter right there; through its transformation, an utpala lotus arises, and within it, that seed-syllable rests upon a moon.

With rays of light emanating from that, the King of Speakers, Mañjuśrī, having produced the world-form, should cause it to enter his own seed-syllable; then, having transformed himself through that, he should instantly manifest as Mañjuśrī— two-armed and one-faced, yellow in color,
seated upon a lion-throne in the *lalitākṣepa* posture, with two hands gracefully forming the gesture of teaching (*vyākhyānamudrā*), and wearing a jewel crown.

Having thus generated the *samayasattva*—whose body is adorned with divine ornaments, whose left hand holds a blue lotus, and who wears Akṣobhya upon his crown—and having seen the *jñānasattva* drawn forth by the seed-syllable in the heart appearing before him, [one should recite: "O *samayasattva*, behold! (*samayasattvaṃ paśya hoḥ*).

Having performed the exhortation of the pledge (*samaya*) by saying, "You are the pledge, I am the pledge; you are the pledge, I am [the pledge]," one should effect the summoning and so forth with the four seed-syllables: *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, *hoḥ*.
This mantra itself is the King of the Multitude of Syllables (*varṇasaṃdoharāja*).
Thus ends the *Vādirāṭ-sādhana*.
p.

105) According to the previously stated procedure, first, within the moon in the heart, one should place the seed-syllable (bīja) of the fifth letter of the sixth group, filled with the fifth vowel, and conjoined with the deity of the two voids.

Having seen the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and gurus who are the masters of the rays from the seeds of those two [syllables], and having made offerings to them and prostrated before them, one should recite this mantra:
*oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajradīpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajragandhe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajranaivedye hūṃ*. Then, one should recite "The Three Jewels are my refuge," and so forth.

Having preceded this with a formal aspiration, one should meditate on the selflessness of all phenomena: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness*. Then, from the seed-syllable [Hūṃ], one should contemplate the three realms in their entirety as having an illusory appearance.
Just as an illusion is seen and touched from every side,
yet is not apprehended at all, so too is the existence of the entire world.

Having thus resolved: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature," one should visualize the glorious Mañjuvajra, arisen from the seed-syllable previously mentioned, a youth with the five heroes as his crest-ornament, adorned with all ornaments, reddish-brown like saffron, holding a blue lotus in his left hand and standing gracefully with his right.
One should visualize oneself seated upon a lion throne in the form of a youth. The mudrā for this is as follows:

having joined the two hands in the *sampuṭāñjali* gesture, one covers the nails of the two ring fingers with the two index fingers, so that they are positioned like a blooming lotus. One should perform one hundred thousand recitations at the heart, the *ūrṇā*, the throat, or the head, [with the mantra] *oṃ vāgīśvara*.
Muḥ.
The Sadhana of Mañjughoṣa.
Homage to the illustrious Vādirāḍ Mañjughoṣa.
Having bowed to the Lord who consists of wisdom and bestows all accomplishments...
I shall state the means for accomplishing that, in accordance with the *Kriyātantra*.
First, the mantra-practitioner, having sat comfortably in a place pleasing to the mind, should behold the realm of sentient beings fallen into the ocean of suffering and make this vow:
"May these suffering beings wander in saṃsāra; may I, becoming Mañjughoṣa, [liberate] all sentient beings."
"all sentient beings [only in k, b] should be established in the unsurpassed state. Then,

having taken as one's focus the Blessed One Mañjughoṣa and the gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas depicted on the cloth or other support, and having honored them with flowers and so forth, one should prostrate.
One should perform the confession of misdeeds, the vow of restraint from future non-virtue, the rejoicing in merit, the offering of one’s own body,
the going for refuge in the Three Jewels, and the generation of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) by means of these two verses:
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds;
I rejoice in the merit of the world; and I set my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha.
I generate the supreme mind of awakening; I invite all sentient beings;
I shall practice the desired conduct of the supreme path to awakening, so that I may become a Buddha for the benefit of the world.

Then follows the taking of the path: having recited three times with the understanding of the meaning, "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature," and having resolved upon natural purity, one should meditate on the selflessness of all phenomena—that the triple world is empty and without characteristics.
Having perceived [the reality] in one's own heart as devoid of the grasped and the grasper,
by means of the syllable *A*, there appears a moon-maṇḍala; above that, the syllable *Muḥ*, with the luster of molten gold.
Having illuminated the expansions of all world-systems with the masses of rays of light produced therefrom, having accomplished the welfare of sentient beings according to their capacity,
and having exhorted all the Tathāgatas and caused them to enter that seed-syllable, one brings all of that to completion.
Through the completion [of the visualization], one should meditate on oneself in the form of Mañjughoṣa, resembling molten gold,
with two arms and one face, seated in the half-lotus posture upon a lotus and moon seat atop a lion, wearing three locks of hair and a jewel crown.
A lunar disc in the form of a youth, adorned with all ornaments,
endowed with the erotic sentiment, slightly smiling, and holding the dharmacakra mudrā with both hands.
His right hand holds a blue lotus together with the *Prajñāpāramitā* scripture, while his left [leg] rests upon the great wrathful deity Yamāntaka,
who is blue in color and terrifying with his gaping fangs.
[He has] tawny, curly hair; eyes with reddish circles; he is terrifying; his head is adorned [with ornaments];
his face is fierce with a frown; his head is decorated with a garland of skulls; and with his right hand [he holds] the Blessed One’s...

Having thus visualized him holding a staff at his left thigh, one should place the three syllables OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ— white, red, and blue in color respectively— upon the moon-maṇḍalas of the body, speech, and mind; then, having contemplated the syllable MUḤ upon the moon-maṇḍala situated between the breasts, from that...
Relying on the non-duality of the object of worship and the worshipper,
and seeing oneself being praised by various deities, one should meditate through the processes of emanation and reabsorption for as long as no weariness arises.
For one who thus constantly meditates for the sake of accomplishing the awakening of a Buddha, [it] is accomplished.
In this very life, one attains the great compassion of Mañjunātha.
Weary from meditation, one should place the mantra upon the moon-maṇḍala in one’s own heart and recite it with an undistracted mind.
Herein is this mantra for recitation: Oṃ dharmadhātuvāgīśvara muḥ.
Having performed the recitation and meditation in this manner without weariness, if one wishes to rise—
Having again performed worship in that same manner and offered praise, one should dedicate the merit for the sake of virtue and ask for forgiveness with this verse:
"Whatever misdeed has been committed by me, who am of dull intellect,
that must be forgiven by you, O Protector, for you are the savior of all embodied beings."
One should make a vow for the welfare of the world. Then:
"By this merit, having attained the state of Buddhahood, may I ferry the entire world across the bottomless ocean of existence."

Then, having focused upon the equality of all phenomena and perceiving everything as consisting of Mañjughoṣa, while maintaining the divine pride of one's own deity, one should dwell at ease. In this manner,
one should practice during the four sessions or the three sessions.
"This was to be done.
Thus, having performed the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), whatever fruit has been obtained by me—
Therefore, this entire world of the three realms of existence has become the vast and supreme Mañjuvara.
The *Ārya-śrīmad-vādirāḍ-mañjuśrī-sādhana* [in version k, b:
it reads "the Ārya-vādirāṭ-sādhana is completed"] is finished.

109) First of all, the mantra-practitioner, having prepared a portion of ground smeared with fragrant substances and strewn with various flowers, should sit comfortably upon a seat in its center and recite the three verses on non-arising (*tri-araṇa-gāthā*). Thereafter, in his own heart...

One should visualize the syllable *A*; through its transformation, one should contemplate a moon disc, and in its center, the syllable *Muḥ*. Then, from the syllable *Muḥ*, one should emit clouds of five-colored light rays from one’s own pores. With those light rays, which take the form of Mañjughoṣa, one should see the sky completely filled. Then, those...

One should worship with flowers and other offerings. Then, one should perform the confession of sins, the rejoicing in merit, the making of aspirations, and so forth. Next, one should cultivate the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). Afterwards, having meditated upon all that as empty, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* ("Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness"). Then, once again—
One should visualize the syllable *A* within one's own heart. That transforms into a moon disc, and in its center, the syllable *Muḥ*.

Through the transformation of that, one should visualize oneself in the form of Mañjughoṣa, seated upon a lion, golden-yellow in color, adorned with all ornaments, and with hands engaged in the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyānamudrā*).

On the left side, one should visualize Akṣobhya holding an utpala lotus and wearing a crown; on the right, Sudhanakumāra; and on the left, Yamāntaka. When weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ vāgīśvara muḥ*.
The Sadhana of Vādirāja is completed.

Having washed [the vessel], one should contemplate the suchness of all phenomena— accompanied by the mantras for worship, confession of sins, the joy of virtue, loving-kindness, and so forth— as being situated within two moons.
He bears a yellow lotus with a shimmering yellow seed-syllable *maṃ*; then, through the transformation of the moon and other elements, he himself instantly becomes Vādirāja.
Then one should recite the mantra of Prajñākara, ending with *ha*, *ra*, *sa*, and *pa*, the highly wise Lord, together with the half-moon (*ardhendu*), the bindu, and the *nāda*.
The *Sādhana* of Prajñāvṛddhinidhi Vādirāja is completed.
This work is the composition of the scholar Śrī Haribhadra.
Homage to you, Mañjuśrī, who acts for the benefit of the world, who assumes the form of a youth, and who teaches the path of suchness.

The sādhana of Vādirāja is now described according to the procedure taught in the *Mañjuśrī-kalpa*. First, one should visualize a pavilion (maṇḍapa) that is square with four doors, adorned with a canopy variegated with various jewels, made of pearls, and decorated with banners, flags, and so forth. In its center, upon a cushioned seat (*masūraka*) covered with silk...
Having sat down there upon a cushion of grass (*paṭamasūraka*),
one should now generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). As many sentient beings as are included within the category of sentient beings— [all those]...
(111) "I must establish all beings in the wisdom of Mañjuśrī," or rather, [one should contemplate that they are] impermanent, momentary, selfless, and produced by the mind.

All phenomena are like dreams and magical illusions; they are mere appearances, primordially quiescent, pure by nature, non-existent, unborn, unarisen, and empty of suchness, the limit of reality, and emptiness—this is a designation for emptiness. Under the power of craving, these sentient beings are blinded by ignorance.

For those who do not perceive the ripening of karma, [the thought] "I shall teach them the Dharma for entering into the profound dependent origination and the activity of karma" is also a synonym for compassion. For this very reason, the Blessed One said at the beginning of the *Samāja* and other tantras:
"Bodhicitta is known as that which is indivisible from emptiness and compassion."

Through the arising of this, the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is produced, and one is called a bodhisattva. Then, having mentally honored all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, one should perceive oneself as the body of gnosis (jñānadeha), observing the syllable *hūṃ* of red color within one's own heart, brilliant and blazing like hundreds of thousands of millions of suns.

Having visualized a sun-maṇḍala with that very [light], and upon it a moon-maṇḍala with the luster of saffron, one should behold there the syllable *maṃ*, the supreme syllable produced from many hundreds of thousands of millions of merits,
endowed with five colors, extending to the limits of the quarters and space; then, having impelled [it] from the peak of gnosis, [one should proceed].
One should visualize the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī, with the luster of molten gold, appearing as a five-year-old youth,

joined with the mudrā of the Wheel of Dharma, holding a blue utpala lotus accompanied by the Prajñāpāramitā, seated upon a lion in the *lalitākṣepa* posture, adorned with all ornaments, and possessing a radiance like the waves of an ocean of amorous grace.

Having brought forth [the deity], who fills the three realms and teaches the Dharma through many voices— both prose and verse— in continuous and abundant refined Sanskrit, preceded by the processes of emanation and reabsorption.

Having caused [the deity] to enter with "Oṃ Mañjuvara Hūṃ," one should stabilize [the visualization] with this and contemplate: "I am of the nature of Mañjuvajra. Then, when weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra: Oṃ Mañjuvara Hūṃ. This is the [mantra] of the Blessed One.
The practitioner, being endowed with pure conduct, should recite [the mantra] seven hundred thousand times.
The *Vādirādasādhana* is completed.
Homage to Arapacana!
To the youth who is as white as the moon, whose hands bear the marks of the sword and the book, who is most beautiful and exceedingly peaceful, and who wears five locks of hair.
Having prostrated before Mañjughoṣa— the one with eyes as broad as lotus petals, who is skilled at burning away evil intellect, and who grants the most excellent liberation— Pṛthu [speaks].
One should provide this very brief instruction on the Wheel-Jewel (*cakraratna*) for the excellent accomplishment of living beings,
by means of which those of superior intellect, meditating with uninterrupted application for half a year, will surely attain awakening that understands all paths.
On a portion of ground strewn with fragrant flowers, sprinkled with scented water, level, clean, and pleasing, the knower of mantras,
having sat upon a seat that is in some places very soft and beautiful, should cultivate the thought of awakening for the sake of blissful delight that is signless.
Having uttered the mantra that is pure by nature (*svabhāvaśuddha*), one should visualize everything as entirely empty on all sides. (pdf 70, p. 113)
Furthermore, one should behold that luminous body of one's own, which is the caravan for the sake of others, all at once.
Then, having visualized a radiant lunar disc in the sky within one's own heart by means of the first vowel,
and then beholding there the syllable *dhīḥ*, one should fashion Mañjughoṣa from it, pure and white.
One should visualize him as possessing the brilliance of ten million moons, resplendent with all ornaments,
solely intent on meditation, seated upon a lotus, slightly smiling with passion, and enchanting.
Having visualized within his own heart the excellent syllable *A*, which flashes forth as an incomparable mass of light-rays in the form of an eight-spoked wheel,
the mantra-practitioner should meditate upon a lunar disc above it, white as the rays of the moon.
That very Mañjughoṣa.
One should visualize Keśinī to his right, smiling with sidelong glances, of beautiful form, and possessing heavy,
full breasts; and to his left, one should meditate on Upakeśī, whose limbs are most lovely and graceful, she who is a treasury of all virtues.
In the navel.

One should indeed place before it the stainless Jālinīprabha, born from a most beautiful *repha*, pure, produced from the syllable *paṃ*, consisting of rays of light, captivating, and possessing the luster of the moon. (pdf 71, p. 114) *paṃ*... *ramaṃ* (variant *raṃ*)... *candraprabhaṃ*.
One should place that behind one's back.
Then one should visualize syllables of vast power, with blazing rays;
they shatter the mountain of ignorance and produce pure, unclouded wisdom.
Visualizing the wheel spinning rapidly below, dispelling all the darkness of delusion,
one should always behold that very same [wheel] as motionless, like the orb of the moon with its vast mass of rays.
Indeed, from the moon, one should see a cloud of broad rays issuing forth and traveling through the ten directions;
having adorned sentient beings and likewise his own body, it returns and finally enters back into the moon.
Reciting the mantra of the six syllables with firm resolve according to the instructions, the preeminent practitioner,
meditating swiftly upon the stages,
shall attain those perfections which are most excellent and delightful, having destroyed the faults of doubt.
Of the Jinas.

The excellent teacher Ajitamitra, who was duly consecrated in the presence of the host of Sugatas by means of the supreme vajras of the Great Teacher and the splendor of the foremost True Dharma, has indeed composed this *Sadarapacanacakra* for the sake of achieving wisdom for all living beings.
Having compiled this supreme and well-arranged cycle, I have acquired vast and universal merit; by means of that, may the entire world be freed from all evil. (PDF 71, p. 115)
May he be Mañjughoṣa, whose sole devotion is to bliss.
The Sadhana of Arapacana.
Homage to Arapacana! First of all, the practitioner, seated on a comfortable seat in a place conducive to the mind,
[should visualize] in his own heart, upon a moon disc arisen from the seed-syllable Ā, the fourth letter of the fourth group, ending in the vowel *ī* and joined with two dots (*bindu*).

Then, having meditated upon that, with the darkness of the afflictions removed from his heart by those rays of light, he should cultivate the four divine abodes—loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—according to the sequence to be described. What is loving-kindness?
It is the state of affection for all sentient beings like that for an only son. What...?

What is compassion (*karuṇā*)? It is the desire to rescue from the ocean of saṃsāra those sentient beings who are afflicted by the three kinds of suffering. What is sympathetic joy (*muditā*)? It is a joyful state of mind toward the roots of virtue produced [by others] and their enjoyments, sovereignty, and so forth. What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
In the state of reality (dharmatā) which is everywhere free from aversion and attachment, there is a spontaneous flow of activity.
Immediately following the cultivation of the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), by means of the rays of light from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart,
all the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas emerge and pervade the entirety of space.
(See *pdf* 72, p.
116) Having beheld those who are solely intent upon compassion for the sake of the world’s purposeful activity through the modes of emanation and reabsorption,
one should, by means of the rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart, cause forth a profusion of divine perfumes, flowers, and so forth, preceded by the [visualization of the] maṇḍala.

With palms joined and the head placed upon the lotus-feet of the Guru, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas, one performs prostration and homage. With flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, flags, and so forth, which have issued from those very rays, one honors them.
And worship consists of honoring [the deity] with outer and inner offerings and so forth. Then one should perform the confession of misdeeds and so on:
"Whatever sin has been accumulated by me through hatred throughout all my births..."

Whatever has caused the delusion of gods born of passion— whether by body, mind, or speech— all that I confess. Whatever evil has been committed, or even caused to be done, whether through passion, or through delusion, or by body, speech, mind, or otherwise— that I all confess before the Victors.
Thus ends the confession of misdeeds.
Whatever merit belongs to all the Tathāgatas,
the Bodhisattvas, the Śrāvakas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the true gurus— I rejoice in all that merit.
And whatever merit belongs to all the Tathāgatas, and to others who rely upon perfect enlightenment, as well as to the Pratyekabuddhas and the true gurus— to all that merit of the Victors,
I rejoice with my own mind.
Thus is the rejoicing in merit.
[One rejoices] in all the Buddhas existing throughout the three times, and in the floods of the qualities of compassion pervading the infinite directions.
Having understood that the noble assembly has abandoned all faults and possesses the true Dharma, I go for refuge with devotion.
Thus is the going for refuge in the Three Jewels.
Having taken recourse in the perfectly pure Jaina path, which is unsurpassed even by Brahmā, Indra, Rudra,
and others, I shall now generate the mind of supreme enlightenment from this mass of merit accumulated by me in this manner.

Thus are the taking of refuge in the path of the Victors and the generation of the bodhicitta. Following these sevenfold unsurpassed offerings, one should contemplate external and internal emptiness according to the words of the Guru; then, in order to further consolidate that realization, [one recites]:
*oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ*.

Having recited the verse "I am pure by nature" (*svabhāvaśuddho'ham*), one should then contemplate one's own mind as mere appearance, transparent and non-obstructive in form, in the shape of a moon disc arising from the primordial vowel;

above that, one should visualize the previously mentioned seed-syllable, and then a sword produced from the transformation of that moon and seed-syllable, shining brilliantly in the center of its hilt.
Upon a moon disc is the previously mentioned seed-syllable; from that, Mañjughoṣa arises, transformed from the seed-syllable of the sword.
He has the luster of an autumnal reed, holds a mass of rays illuminating the ten directions, possesses two arms, and has the form of a youth.
With his right hand, he brandishes a sword of supreme wisdom, solely intent upon cutting through all ignorance.
With his left hand occupied by a single volume of the holy scriptures and arts that constitute all means (*upāya*), adorned with every ornament, wearing red garments, solely intent on meditation,
with a face like a blossomed lotus and eyes like lotus petals.

Having visualized oneself in the form of Mañjuśrī— the embodiment of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas— possessing the marks of a Great Being, with five locks of hair curled like sapphire gems, seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon a white eight-petaled lotus moon, and thus endowed with the pride of the Samayasattva.

The yogi [visualizes] in his own heart the white eight-spoked wheel produced from the syllable *aṃ*, which destroys all ignorance with its mass of shimmering rays, as a weapon arranged in a clockwise direction. (pdf 73, p. 118)

Having seen that revolving [syllable] in the intermediate space above, one should, according to the guru’s instruction, visualize the lunar disc arising from the primordial syllable (A), and upon that, the five-syllable mantra in its proper sequence, resembling blazing fire, radiant with rays, and the destroyer of all ignorance.

The mantra-practitioner, unwearied in accomplishing the form of the deity, should perform the radiation and other rites and then engage in recitation. Alternatively, one should meditate upon [the deity] named Arapacana, white in color, produced from the syllable *Śu* (śubhra) in the center of a moon-disc within the heart; he is adorned with all ornaments, joyful, solely intent on meditation, seated in the vajra-paryanka posture, and with his right and left hands—
Having visualized the Best of Speakers, who holds a sword and a book (or a jewel and a book), wears five garments entirely curved like sapphire, whose face resembles the shimmering moon,
whose heart is joined with his own seed-syllable and the moon, and who possesses a radiance like Jālinī arising from a white *repha* in front of him;
Like Arapacana,

one should visualize [the deity] endowed with two arms and so forth, presided over by its own seed-syllable upon the moon at one’s own heart; thereafter, behind it, one visualizes [the syllable] PA, produced from which arises a moon-light [deity] upon the moon at one’s own heart.

Then, having visualized the seed-syllable joined [with the mantra], one should visualize Keśinī, white in color and produced from a brilliant syllable *ca*, adorned with all ornaments, possessing full breasts,
holding a sword and a book in her right and left hands respectively, within the moon at her own heart.
Having thus meditated upon her as endowed with the seed-syllable,
and having visualized Upakeśinī— produced from the white letter *na*— together with the seed-syllable within the moon at one's own heart,
one should contemplate all [the beings] as being like the Fire of the Dead (Yamāntaka). Thus:
By means of the radiating and reabsorbing of light rays from the seed-syllables in the hearts of the hosts of deities, he cuts through the mass of ignorance in the world;

by means of the entire collection of treatises on the nectar of Dharma and the arts and crafts, he repeatedly satiates all sentient beings; and having meditated upon himself as a form that is transparent and unimpeded according to the instruction of the Guru, he remains concentrated.

(The practitioner) as the mantra-holder should perform the recitation (*japa*). The mantra consists of the five seed-syllables beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ), with the seed-syllable of the *samayasattva* in the middle. When the intention to rise arises, then—

Having recited one's own mantra according to the guru’s instruction, one should thereafter recite the hundred-syllable verse: *Oṃ vajrasattva samayamanupālaya vajrasattvatvenopatiṣṭha dṛḍho me bhava sutoṣyo me bhava supoṣyo me bhava anurakto me bhava sarvasiddhiṃ me prayaccha sarvakarmasu ca me cittaṃ...*
"O Cittaśrī, bring about my welfare! Huṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ!
O Blessed One, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me; become a vajra! O Great Samayasattva, Āḥ!
Immediately after reciting this hundred-syllable mantra, having emitted the radiation and so forth, one should maintain the pride of being the Samayasattva.
Dwelling in all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) with a concentrated mind, the yogi, having become one who has reached the further shore of the ocean of perfect knowledge,
attains unsurpassed awakening (*anuttarabodhi*) in a very short time. Having here composed this pure manual of practice (*sādhana*) in verse, for those who are liberated...
May whatever merit belongs to Padmākara be for the sake of liberation from existence.
The *Muktaka-Ārapacana-sādhana* is completed.
In the center, one should place Mañjuśrī; in the east, Jālinīprabha, red in color; and in the south, [produced from] the syllable *repha*, green in color. (pdf 74, p. 120)

One should draw Keśinī, yellow in color, with the syllable *pa* in the west; [one should draw] Upakeśinī, red in color, with the syllable *na*, as having the luster of the moon and the radiance of the moon. Mañjuśrī should have his left hand holding a lotus and granting a boon, while Jālinīprabha should have his hands holding a lotus and granting a boon, and Upakeśinī should have her hands holding a lotus and granting a boon.

One should meditate on Candraprabhā holding a red lotus and Keśinī with her hand in the gesture of granting boons; at the base of the navel, an eight-spoked wheel revolving with a radiance like fire; above that, a moon mandala; and above that, a four-spoked wheel. One should meditate on the syllables of the mantra within the wheel as the very form of the deity. In their hearts—

These are indeed the syllables; from them arise all phonemes, endowed with all flavors and qualities, extending throughout the ten directions—so it is said. This is the instruction for the meditation on the venerable Āryamañjuśrī.
(The *Sadyo'nubhava-mañjuśrī-sādhana*, p. 121 of PDF 74) is now properly explained for the sake of noble persons who seek wisdom.
For the sake of eliminating the delusion caused by the poison of ignorance.

First of all, the yogi, in some place conducive to his mind, with his intellect fixed upon the moon arisen from the vowel *a* and situated thereon, should contemplate the hook (*aṅkuśa*) emerging from the seed-syllable *dhīḥ*; then,
with his intellect fixed upon the moon transformed into the form of the mind, he should manifest the signless sword produced from the syllable *dhīḥ*.
One should visualize [the letter] *niśita* (sharpened). Above that, upon a lotus transformed from the first vowel (*a*), is the seed-syllable of the sword;

having transformed all of this, one visualizes [the deity] holding a sword and a book, with five locks of hair tied up, clad in a pair of red garments, wearing an elegant and graceful attire, and possessing a smiling, blossoming face.

One should visualize oneself as having a splendor equal to the luster of the moon, seated in the full lotus posture upon a universal lotus, and possessing the form of the Arapacana mantra instantly manifest. Then, from the vowels transformed within one's own heart and so forth, there arises an eight-spoked wheel that does not touch [the body], measuring only a finger’s breadth above it.

One should visualize Mañjughoṣa in that very manner, through the transformation of the sword and other implements, wherein there is a moon disc not touched by the vowels and so forth, and upon it a sword born from the seed-syllable of the Moon, its tip adorned with the Moon, and further embellished by the previously mentioned seed-syllable of the sword. And at its tip—

Having visualized the letter *ra* situated upon the letter *ra* of the sword and other vowels as the Lord of Herbs (*oṣadhīśa*), one should perceive Jālinīkumāra in the form of the Blessed One, transformed from the sword and so forth. Likewise, on the back, in the same manner, by means of the fifth primary syllable, one should visualize Candraprabha; likewise on the right.

With the syllable *ca*, one should meditate on Keśinī, resplendent with the weight of her breasts, in the form of the Lord (*nātha*) on the left; and likewise with the syllable *na*, one should meditate on Upakeśinī.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the white seed-syllable of each of them upon the moon at their respective hearts.

Then, having attained oneness with the Knowledge Being (jñānasattva) who has been summoned by means of the rays emerging from the seed-syllable in the heart of the Leader, one should quickly visualize oneself as being situated within the swiftly revolving wheel, joined by the four deities residing upon the moon,
and manifesting the emanation and reabsorption of the entirety of speech.
One should meditate. When weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra. There, this king of mantras is: *arapacanadhīḥ*.
By whatever merit has been accumulated through this *Sadyo'nubhava-Mañjuśrī-sādhana*, may the world always become equal to Mañjughoṣa.
The Means for the Immediate Digestion of Experience.
Then, one should radiate rays of light from the seed-syllables with the out-breath;
and with the streams of the out-breath, having drawn in the gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*) by means of the rays, one should dissolve it back into the seed-syllables.
Having rested, one of steady intellect should perform the emanation and reabsorption of the seed-syllables of Jñānasattva and the rest during the successive exhalation and inhalation of the breath.
The excellent seed-syllable *asivi* (aḥ), situated upon the lunar disc,
bound by the sequence of its movement, and purified by the melting away of transgressions; thereafter,
that mass of intelligence becomes the form of Mañjughoṣa and others— the wheel of the one of auspicious intellect.
And it bestows liberation at the end of ten million [lifetimes].

In the rite of accomplishment, one should contemplate the five deities as having gone forth and returned after transforming the seed-syllables *bīja*, *asita*, *tuṣṭi*, and the moon-seed (*candrabīja*) into rays of light.

Following the previously described procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness, one should instantaneously manifest oneself as the venerable Lord Vajrānaṅga Mañjuśrī upon a universal lotus and sun disk, arisen from the yellow seed-syllable *vaṃ*, yellow in color and with a single face.
Three-eyed, six-armed, wearing matted locks, sixteen years of age, and possessing a graceful charm;
standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, holding a sword, an arrow, and a mirror in his three right hands, and holding a bow, a blue lotus, and a *kaṅkelli* flower in his three left hands.
Having visualized [the consort] adorned with divine ornaments and garments, wearing a crown of Akṣobhya, one should meditate upon her through the application of passion.
For it is said:
"Piercing her breast with an arrow, one should strike her in the heart with Aśoka flowers."
One should threaten the person to be acted upon with a sword, then show her a mirror;
having bound her feet with a blue lotus, one should draw her in while she is overwhelmed.
"Having loose hair," etc. Oṃ, attract such-and-such a woman, Mañjughoṣa! Hrīḥ Jaḥ!
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of the venerable Vajrānaṅga.

As before, having performed the confession of sins and so forth, and after the meditation on emptiness, one should meditate on a bow joined with an arrow in the center of the hub (varaṭaka) occupied by the syllable *haṃ*, which is produced from the syllable *haṃ*; that [bow] then transforms.

One should visualize the noble Mañjughoṣa, named Vajrānaṅga, yellow in color and possessing six arms; with his two primary hands he holds a flowery bow drawn to the ear with an arrow whose shaft is the calyx of a red utpala lotus; with his second pair of right hands he bears a sword and a mirror; and with his second pair of left hands he holds an indīvara lotus and the sprouts of a red aśoka flower.

One should visualize [the deity] with a crown of matted hair empowered by Akṣobhya, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, sixteen years of age, and possessing a form of great erotic passion (*mahāśṛṅgāra*). Alternatively, one should meditate on him as four-armed, holding a mirror and an *aśoka* sprout, devoid of two arms. Then, having unified him with the Jñānasattva, [one recites]: *Oṃ Mañjughoṣa Hrīḥ Jaḥ*.

One should recite the mantra. By means of one hundred thousand recitations, one brings even the three worlds under one's command as servants. Alternatively, if someone desires to attract a particular woman, then, having performed the visualization described immediately above, with a mind proud of that ego-identification, one should visualize within one’s own heart a red sixteen-petaled lotus together with its stalk hanging down to the navel.

Having grasped the stalk together with its bulb, and having visualized a red syllable *huṃ* at the base of that stalk, one should contemplate the sixteen red vowels arranged clockwise upon its petals.

Upon its filaments, one should visualize the red discs of the sun and moon, appearing respectively by night and by day; in their center, one should see one's own mantra to be described later, interlaced with two red syllables *hrīḥ*. Then, one should visualize those vowels as red bees, exceedingly joyful and robust.
Having visualized [the six-faced one], filling the ten directions with a mass of red rays from his own mantra—[the mantra-arrows]—he goes to the place where the desired woman resides.
Having placed her in the center of the circle of wind, with her neck firmly bound by a lasso consisting of rays of light,
and having brought before him— firmly pierced by the goad— the Dharmodayā,
with her hands joined in *añjali* and all her limbs, eyes, and heart filled with a red syllable *HŪṂ* situated in the center of a whirling circle of firebrands;

One should visualize: then, having perceived within her heart also a sixteen-petaled lotus accompanied by the sixteen red vowels and a stalk with the syllable *haṃ* (or *nāda*), but with a faded color; and in its center, one should meditate on the syllables of the name interspersed with the syllable *hrīḥ*.
Then, originating from the rays of the syllables of one’s own mantra, a very red, sharp, and subtle goad—
followed by swarms of bees impelled by the rays of the syllable *huṃ* situated on a lotus stalk that have risen upward—
emerges from the left nostril of oneself and enters through the right nostril of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*).
Having entered that heart through the opening,
that goad remains intent on drawing out the syllables of his name; and those bees, having violently torn and shattered that lotus, by means of their own mantra—

Sutata, ḍh, g: svatantrata. Thinking "they shall suck the vowels," one should gaze steadily for a very long time. Then, in that same manner, having forcibly seized its name with the goad impelled by that breath, those bees, having drawn forth their own sound (svara), [proceed].

One should observe them as they emerge through the path of the left nostril aperture; then, having drawn them back in with the breath-wind, one should cause those hook-shaped bees to enter through the right aperture of one's own nose, together with the syllable of their name.
Having firmly seized those vowels within one's own heart with the mantra, one should contemplate them as being brought under control by the power of bees moving in every petal;
through this sequence, having unified one's own consciousness with that consciousness, one should behold it. Then, with an arrow consisting of a sharp, red lotus bud, [one strikes] that breast.
(See PDF 77, p.
126) Having observed her pierced and fallen into a swoon from great passion, he bound her pair of feet firmly with his bow as if with a chain, using a stalk of a blue lotus taken from his own breast.

Having bound her by the neck with a noose, having dragged her down and cast her at his own feet, having struck her heart with an *aśoka* branch, having rendered her free from pride, and having terrified her with a sword, he made her take refuge in the Infinite; then, once again, with a mirror... [her own form].

Having displayed her state—her hair disheveled, naked, overwhelmed by intense passion, extremely distressed by separation, and full of devotion—one should cause her to experience one's own love through self-awareness. Then, with a one-pointed mind, one should recite the mantra together with the name: *oṃ amukīm ākarṣaya mañjughoṣa hrīḥ jaḥ*.
Thus, in the sequence just described, one should recite the mantra for as long as it takes from the first day of the bright fortnight until the fourteenth day.

Then, on the full moon day, having performed a grand worship, one should recite throughout the entire night. Thereupon, at dawn, she will certainly arrive. And when she has arrived, for the sake of attaining the great mudrās and other siddhis— [k, kh, ḍh]
For the sake of the supreme goal, one should enjoy [the offerings] at will with the intention of worshipping one’s own deity.
The *Vajrānaṅgamañjuśrīsādhana* is completed.

Likewise, immediately after the meditation on emptiness and so forth, upon a moon disc atop a universal lotus, one should visualize the glorious Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara, born from a white syllable *Āḥ*, entirely white in body, with four faces and eight arms.

He is crowned with the five Buddhas, adorned with divine ornaments and garments, and endowed with the sentiments of the erotic and so forth; his two hands bear the mudrā of the Wheel of Dharma, while his three right hands hold a sword, an arrow, and a vajra.

Having visualized oneself as [the deity] seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, with three left hands holding a Prajñāpāramitā manuscript, a bow, and a vajra-bell, one should contemplate at the moon in one's own heart a blue syllable *Huṃ* from which arises a vajra together with its seed-syllable.

The seed-syllable vajra born from *huṃ*, having the nature of the Mahāmudrā, is at the *ūrṇā* (between the eyebrows) as a yellow *trāṃ*; the seed-syllable jewel having the nature of the Dharmamudrā is at the throat as a red *hīḥ*-born lotus with its seed-syllable; [the seed-syllable wheel having the nature of the Dharmamudrā is at the throat]; and the seed-syllable sword having the nature of the Samayamudrā is at the crown of the head as a green *aḥ*.

Having visualized oneself as endowed with the four mudrās, one should consecrate [oneself] with the mantra: *oṃ huṃ hrīḥ bhagavan jñānamūrti vāgīśvara mahāvāca sarvadharmagaganāmalasupariśuddhadharmadhātujñānagarbha āḥ*. Then, [one should perform] the vajra-bind with the two middle fingers joined together...

The *samayamudrā* is formed by holding the middle joints of the two middle fingers bent in the shape of a sword, while the two index fingers are bent over the raised thumbs. Then, one should meditate on one's own tongue as being presided over by the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*, which is red and situated upon a moon disc.
One should recite the mantra with a wrathful voice. In this regard, the mantra for recitation is: *Oṃ vajratīkṣṇaduḥkhacchedaprajñājñānamūrtaye jñānakāya vāgīśvara arapacanāya te namaḥ*.
And one should recite the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, consisting of eight hundred names, at the appropriate times.
The Sadhana of Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara.
(PDF 78, p.

128) Following the previously mentioned procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), [one visualizes oneself as] the eight-armed, four-faced [deity], transformed from the red syllable *Hoḥ* situated upon a lotus and moon; the primary face—

[The face at the root is found only in manuscript *g*: His right face is red-white, the western is reddish like saffron, the northern is lotus-red, and the [eastern] is yellowish-red; he holds a bow and an arrow with two hands, a noose and a goad with the other two, and again with the remaining two...
Holding a book of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and a sword in his [first] two hands, and likewise holding a bell and a vajra in the other two,
blazing with the sentiment of great passion (*mahārāga-śṛṅgāra-rasa*), seated in the graceful posture (*lalitāsana*) upon a moon on a double lotus (*viśvapadma*),
adorned with divine garments and ornaments, wearing a crown of matted hair topped by Amitābha, and having drawn forth sentient beings by means of rays of light from the seed-syllable in his heart.
Having established [the object] under one's own control, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ mahārāgavajra rāgaya sarvasattvān hoḥ*.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for subjugation (*vaśyavidhi*) in the *Dharmadhātuvāgīśvarasādhana*.
Homage to Mañjunātha!

Preceded by the meditation on emptiness, one visualizes oneself arisen from the syllable *hoḥ* upon a moon disc as the form of Mahārāga, reddish-white and radiant with the sentiment of erotic passion (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).

Seated in the *lalitāsana* posture, four-faced and eight-armed; his first face is red and pale, the right is saffron-red, the western is lotus-red, and the northern is yellowish-red; with two arms he holds a bow and an arrow, with another pair he holds a noose and a goad, and likewise with the remaining pair...

Having visualized [him] holding a volume of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and a sword, and likewise holding a bell and a vajra with the other two hands, one should illuminate the nine [deities] above by means of rays of light emerging from the crown and diadem.

One should visualize them as intensely red, with bodies bowed in prostration. Just as they are situated in the directions— east, south, west, north, and below— they are filled, colored, and drawn in by the rays of the first, second, third, and fourth quarters.

Having filled [the vessel] with water, one should recite [the mantra] three times; then, while mentally visualizing those [beings] as brought under one's own control, one should mutter the mantra repeatedly: *oṃ mahārāgavajra rāgaya sarvasattvān hoḥ*. Thereafter, all sentient beings will certainly become submissive.

Thus concludes the samādhi for the subjugation of all sentient beings by Mañjuvajra, known as the Great Passion, the Form of Forms, the Supreme, which is to be cultivated by those of sharp intelligence.
In the same way, immediately after the meditation on emptiness, within a water mandala, upon the pericarp of a white eight-petaled lotus, one should—

through the conviction that all phenomena are free from death— visualize oneself as white, with two arms and one face, seated in the vajra posture upon a moon disc, arising from the transformation of a white syllable *AṂ*.

Having instantaneously visualized oneself in the form of the venerable Mañjuśrī— possessing hands in the *samādhi-mudrā*, adorned with all the ornaments of a youth, and wearing the five locks of hair— one should [visualize] upon a moon-lotus at one's own heart the syllable *gaṃ* born from the syllable *khaṃ*; within that, the syllable *raṃ*, which is the Vajra-tongue, [to be placed] upon the tongue.

Visualizing a red lotus above the tongue and upon it the Buddha Amitābha, one should meditate on a white syllable *vaṃ* at the region of one's own palate, facing downward and dripping nectar. The mantra for recitation is: *oṃ vākyedaṃ namaḥ*.
This is the practice of Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara, which indicates the samādhi of the Dharma-conch and possesses great merit.

First, having sat upon a soft cushion or similar seat in some secluded, charming, and pure spot of ground, and having beheld the infinite realm of sentient beings suffering from the three types of suffering, [one should think]: "By me, these sentient beings... (pdf 79, p. 130)

Having attained the state of Mañjughoṣa, they were to be established as indistinguishable from that very state; thus, out of compassion, they were positioned upon the floor of a fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī) fashioned from moonstones and jewels, adorned with four non-distinct porticoes and possessed of unsurpassed resolve.

Having worshipped with an offering consisting of the five types of service— including dance, song, and instrumental music— characterized by various jewel-encrusted vessels filled with heaps of flowers scattered by the wings of swarms of bees attracted by the fragrance of incense-bags suspended from wide and variegated canopies, which perfumed the interior space, may there be no more of my poverty.

Thinking that there is something else besides this, and having offered one's body while reciting words such as "I go for refuge to the Buddha," one should approach the refuge of the Three Jewels, confess one's misdeeds, undertake the vow of non-repetition, rejoice in merit, and then instantly perceive everything as empty. Then, seeing this very meaning with certainty, [one should contemplate] slowly.

One should recite the mantra of intrinsic purity three times. Immediately thereafter, one should likewise repeat the mantra expressing emptiness three times. Then, one should instantly visualize the three worlds as consisting of light.

Thereafter, one should visualize a sharp-edged sword produced by the syllable *dhīḥ*, which shines with pure luster, within the orb of the moon— which has been transformed into the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*)— within one’s own heart; and upon its hilt, the white moon produced from the preceding syllable.
One should visualize the seed-syllable of Khaḍga (pdf 79,
together with oneself, transformed into five colors, holding a book in the left hand.
In his other hand he holds the sword of wisdom; his crown is adorned with the five jewels;
his five locks of hair are curled; he wears a pair of garments as lovely as the bandhūka flower;
beautiful ornaments of amorous grace are placed in their appropriate and fitting positions; and the surface of his cheeks quivers with a gentle smile.
One should behold it as if a mass of autumn clouds gathered in one place, or like darkness brought together out of fear. Then,
touching with only the tip of a finger the eight-spoked wheel— which has ripened from the collection of all the phonemes within one's own heart—
one should visualize the lunar disc arising therefrom, and upon that, the sprout of a jewel held by the threatening gesture (tarjanī).
And in his fist, there was likewise a mass of such a nature, as if flooding the quarters of space without interruption with a stream of light; and from that light issuing forth,
upon a thousand-petalled lotus, rested a lotus, a goad, and the orb of the moon.

One should visualize oneself as Mañjuśrī, seated in the firm vajra-paryaṅka posture. Therein, one should behold that very same great vital syllable (*mahāprāṇa*). Then, through the transformation of the sword and other implements, one should meditate upon Mañjughoṣa, endowed with the previously described colors, marks, and so forth.

And at their respective front and back, one should visualize the leaders Sūryaprabha and Candraprabha, whose forms are generated from the moon-discs produced by the joy arising from the swords born from their own respective seed-syllables, as the primary causes; by this very method, they are depicted with variegated lower and upper garments and crowns bearing the Three Jewels.

One should meditate upon Keśinī and Upakeśinī, adorned with ornaments befitting themselves, moving respectively to the left and the right. One should behold the respective seed-syllables of the eight deities of the eight-spoked wheel within the Lord of Life (Prāṇanātha), who is like a moon-lotus in one's own heart—each seed-syllable matted-haired and white as the moon. Then, [one should visualize] the tube of rays from the seed-syllable situated within the mind of the Leader.
Having emerged from the crown of her head with a curved tip, illuminating the entire triple world, she rests upon the petal of the lotus seat.
Having maintained the wisdom-being (jñānasattva), whose essential nature is inseparable from the commitment-being (samayasattva), one should visualize it being brought forth.

Then, with that [wisdom-being] stationed before one, having performed various mental offerings, one should take recourse in their identity while uttering *huṃ vaṃ jaḥ hoḥ*. Immediately thereafter, suddenly—

One should gaze repeatedly at the eight-spoked wheel, which rotates steadily with a clockwise whirling motion, and at the five noble deities situated within the lunar disc, who are in motion; furthermore, one should observe the mass of rays emerging from the pores of the skin, illuminating the entire world,
and then re-entering the seat immediately after the deer-marked moon.

One should contemplate until exhaustion. Becoming weary of meditation, one should gradually recite the six-syllable king of mantras while contemplating the syllables emerging from the mouth, as white as the stalks of ripened autumn reeds. Here too—
Having risen from his seat with averted face, he may dwell as he pleases, having performed the service for the deity.
This is the sādhana of the venerable Mañjuvara, whose speech is excellent, whose hand holds a sword, and whose words are swift.
Whatever benefit has been attained by me here through this composition, may all people quickly reach the abode of the Jina by means of it.
The Sādhana of Arapacana.

Having prostrated before the venerable Vajradharma, who has shaken off the web of faults, whose web of light rays radiates from the mandala of speech, and whose nature is the speech of all the perfectly awakened ones, I shall proclaim this *vāksādhana*.
Having uttered the mantra, which is by nature pure in form, one is caressed by the seed-syllable and the wind.
One should contemplate this entire world as being like an illusion, a mirage, or the moon reflected in water.
Having visualized a universal lotus, which is the source of the seed-syllable *paṃ* and possesses a completely pure form,
[one should visualize] the full moon— born from the syllable *a*, possessing infinite radiance, and complete in all its digits.
Furthermore, there is the supreme secret, the most pure seed-syllable,
which emits a mass of rays of light, resembling the brilliance of the bandhūka flower, and is the sole cause for the expansion of the manifold web of speech.
Born from that seed-syllable, free from faults, with his lotus-hands placed in the mudrā of meditative concentration,
seated upon the vajra-throne, beautiful with compassion, is the glorious Vajrarāga, whose passion is utterly pure.
(From *pdf* 81, p. 134):
With clouds born from the interior of his belly, he brings about the welfare of the world through the pure Buddha.
One should contemplate him performing [this], with an utterly pure intellect, as the very nature of the entire world.
Having beheld the vajra within the lunar disc of the heart, which illuminates all worlds with its flames,
one should visualize it as having assumed a form through the resonance of the syllable *huṃ*, consisting of five essences and emitting clouds of Buddhas.
With his body seated upon the pedestal at the sharp tip of the needle in its center, he is the manifestation of the three worlds,
the Great Imperishable who has destroyed the multitude of beings.
He beheld the mountain-like king, who was shrouded in the darkness of the spreading misery of his lineage.
By means of the beautiful rays radiating from it— pure and lovely in hue like the orb of the rising sun—
the foremost messenger of wisdom [was sent forth].
And having produced a tongue that is the source of auspicious speech and has become like a vajra;

At its tip, one should contemplate the reality of wondrous and fierce passion, possessing noble radiance; by means of its own powers of irresistible vigor, it shall destroy the power of the foremost among opponents.
(As stated in *pdf* 81, p.
135: When this accomplishment in the means of verbal expression has been attained through the power of practice cultivated at every moment;
The yogi speaks incessantly in prose and verse, and he knows various treatises.
He certainly composes various treatises of great significance for the sake of the world;
and he knows the mental states of others,
as well as those various [states] afflicted by the faults of passion and so forth.
When that meditative absorption has attained firmness through an extremely subtle, intense, and clear certainty,
he becomes the bearer of the form that is the abode of all Buddhas; there is no doubt about this.
This is to be investigated.
Through the power of habitual practice, beings that do not exist appear before men;
this is the logic of mental engagement, like beautiful women following those whose minds are agitated by desire.
kh, a: success; g: liberation.
Thus, whatever merit has been acquired by me, may people thereby attain the supreme fortune of the Victors.
I long for that which is free from the thorns of fear, despondency, and sorrow, and as delightful as the rays of the moon.

With minds devoted to uninterrupted virtue, possessing the conduct of precepts and the blissful instructions received from the supreme Guru— may they follow the glory of the livelihood offered by all the families, like bees following the lotus of the ascetic.
Those whose joy is under the control of meditative concentration.
