Following the previously described procedure, after the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one should visualize a white drop upon a moon disc above a lotus.

After performing the radiation and reabsorption (*sphuraṇa*) and so forth, through the transformation of that [drop], one should contemplate Mañjuśrī Arapacana—purely white and born from the syllable *dhīḥ*—within the heart of one’s own seed-syllable, and recite the mantra: *oṃ dhīḥ svāhā*.
Thus ends the Concise Sadhana of Mañjuśrī belonging to the Vidyādhara-piṭaka.
At the beginning, the practitioner of mantra should perform the worship of the Buddhas and others. (pdf 90, p. 152) [In some versions: and the worship of the deities.]
From the transformation of merits, there first arises the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
The practitioner of mantra should contemplate the *bindu* situated in the center of the lunar orb within the heart,
possessing a radiance like a drop of frost released by the rays of the sun.
One should meditate on the entire world being illuminated by the rays of those drops, which have issued forth from every pore,
in a sequence beginning with the span of a cubit (*vitasti*) and so forth.
One should behold the form of the white syllable *dhīḥ*, containing a radiant dot (*bindu*) within it;
having seen it, one should perceive the five fires (*pañcānala*) through the total transformation of that [syllable].
Having visualized the moon-maṇḍala within the heart, with the syllable *dhīḥ* internalized,
one should then cause it to emerge through the nose as a mass of its rays.
One should meditate on sentient beings in the form of Mañjughoṣa by means of the exhalation wind;
subsequently, one should dissolve them into the syllable *dhīḥ* by means of the inhalation wind.
One should recite the seed-syllable of the mantra, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*,
as having the form of the autumnal moon's rays and situated within the lunar disc at the heart.
The Sadhana of Mañjughoṣa Connected with the Vidyādhara Piṭaka.
(From *pdf* 90, p. 153):
"Having the form of a lamp-flame, situated in the center of the moon upon the lotus of emanation, the Hero who melts the syllable *haṃ* was taught by Ravigupta."
Huṃ Āḥ. The Chapter on the Increase of Wisdom.

Having instantly taken recourse to the yoga of Mañjuśrī, one should visualize at the navel, upon a moon disc, a white drop in the form of a lamp flame with rays of light; and at the head, the unstruck (anāhata) white syllable *huṃ*.

One should meditate on the syllable *haṃ* with its head hanging down and accompanied by rays. Then, having been impelled by the rays of that *bindu*, the practitioner, with a steady mind, causes the *bindu* to overflow by means of the *haṃ* syllable which has become liquefied; thus, in no long time, he increases his wisdom (*prajñā*).
Above the region of the navel, within the clearly manifest red *dharmodayā*,
is a five-spoked blue thunderbolt, its brilliance shining with a fierce roar.
One should perceive the *nāda* arising from the *haṃkāra*, born from the head and emerging from the joints, pervading the sky and originating from the smoky-colored *haṃkāra*.
The resonance (nāda) is a line of light rays.
Thus concludes the procedure for the increase of wisdom (prajñā).
Having always bowed at the feet of the Guru and likewise the Vajrācārya, and having first paid homage, I shall write that by which Mañjuśrī is accomplished. (pdf 91, p. 154)
Seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, one should visualize in the heart the seed-syllable adorned upon a moon,
as bright as a conch or jasmine, and pervaded by manifold rays of light.

The fully awakened Buddhas, the Gurus, and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) are produced by them; having seen them, one should worship them with this mantra: *oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajradīpe hūṃ*, *oṃ vajragandhe hūṃ*, *oṃ*.
*Vajra-naivedye hūṃ*. Then:
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds; I rejoice in the merit of the world; I direct my mind toward the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Supreme Assembly;
I generate the mind of awakening for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others.
I generate the supreme mind of enlightenment; I invite all sentient beings.
I shall practice the desired course of conduct for supreme enlightenment; may I become a Buddha for the benefit of the world.

Thus, preceded by a formal resolve (*praṇidhi*), one should meditate upon the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*) with this mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako 'ham* (I am of the nature of the diamond of the wisdom of emptiness).
The seed, having the form of illusion, [is that which] perceives and touches the three realms in their entirety,
just as an illusion is perceived everywhere.
And yet it is not perceived at all, just as an illusion is not perceived in any way;
likewise, the existence of the entire world is not perceived.

Thus one should form a resolve. Then, having removed the seed of unreal conceptualization from beginningless time, one should resolve upon intrinsic purity: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho 'ham* (Oṃ, all phenomena are intrinsically pure; I am intrinsically pure). Then, that which is produced from the previously mentioned seed-syllable...

Within the hilt of the sword is a moon disc; upon that, one should contemplate the previously mentioned seed-syllable. Through the transformation of all those elements, one should visualize oneself in the form of Mañjuśrī, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture upon a lotus and moon seat, thinking: "I alone am the Lord of the entire world."

With the radiance of the moon, he pervades the expanse of the sky with the flashing of many rays; he is clothed in variegated garments, the very embodiment of the world’s bliss, white in color, enchanting, and wearing five locks of hair.
A great hero adorned with all ornaments, his right hand brandishes a sword while his left hand rests upon his heart.
Having taken up the book, one should then form the mudrā. Joining the two hands in the hollowed-añjali gesture, one should cover the nails of the ring fingers with the two index fingers;
positioned like an opened lotus, one should place it at the heart, the ūrṇā, the throat, and the crown of the head.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra *ḍha ga kha a*, one should subsequently visualize a white lunar disc below the navel, shaped like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, by means of the syllable *bruṃ*. Above that is the fourth letter of the eighth group, adorned with the sixteenth letter of the first group.
[Adorned (is found only in k, b)] On the second [line] of the seventh [chapter] (pdf 92,
that which is adorned by the first and the fourth [syllables] is the bud of a lotus (*paṅkajakalikā*) situated above the navel.

One should visualize [the lotus] blossomed by the syllable *haṃ*. Above that is a moon disc; above that, leaving a space of one finger-breadth, is a six-spoked wheel (*ṣaḍara-cakra*) possessing brilliance. Upon its spokes, one should place the pairs of syllables of the twelve mantras.
Having placed each individual syllable of the root mantra above each Pratyekabuddha,

one should meditate on the syllable *dhīḥ* within the central hub of the wheel, radiant with light and motionless; and in the outer hub, the blazing *kāli*-yoga, devoid of the syllables *ka, ga, ṅa, ja, ña, ṇa, na, ma*.

One should visualize as follows: leaving a space of one finger-breadth above that, one sees a moon disc, and upon it the syllables *arapacana*. One should contemplate the wheel spinning with extreme rapidity. For six months, one should recite this mantra:
*oṃ vajratīkṣṇa muḥ*.

[The seed-syllables: *dhvaṃ*, *k*, *b*: *aṃ*. One should recite this ten thousand times every day. Thereupon, even one who is dull-witted becomes a lord of speech, endowed with intelligence; he becomes a sovereign of the earth, grasps a thousand treatises, speaks uninterrupted Sanskrit, becomes a great poet, and reaches the further shore of all scriptures. This occurs when success (*siddhi*) has been attained.
One becomes a sovereign lord of the Vidyādharas and sports with the Vidyādharīs. This excellent wheel is secret; it must be understood through the oral instruction of the teacher.
By whatever fruit arises from drawing this supreme wheel of wisdom,
may this entire world attain the state of Mañjuśrī.

This *Sādhana* of the Lord Mañjuśrī, the Wisdom Wheel (*Prajñācakra*), is completed. [The colophon is read in manuscripts K, Ḍh, G, Kh, A as "obtained through the tradition of the *Nāmasaṅgīti* by the one who has attained the excellent Siddhi of the Wisdom Wheel," and in manuscript Ma as "the *Mañjuśrī-Prajñācakra*."]
[In Kh] it is completed.
Homage to Mañjuśrī! [The practitioner should visualize himself in the form of Mañjuśrī. (PDF 92, p. 157)
In this regard, this is the Dharma-Śaṅkha Samādhi: upon a white, circular, watery maṇḍala,
on the pericarp of an eight-petalled lotus with filaments,
there is a two-armed [deity] produced from the seed-syllable *am*, which illuminates the fact that all phenomena are free from death.

One should meditate on oneself in the form of Mañjuśrī, white in color, seated in the vajraparyaṅka posture with hands in the gesture of meditative concentration (*samādhihasta*), adorned with the ornaments of a youth and five locks of hair, having the nature of clear and stainless primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).
Above the moon at one’s own heart, upon a lotus, from the syllable *khaṃ* (or *vaṃ* according to manuscript *kh*), there arises a conch shell; in its center—

Oṃ vajrajihva raḥ. Thus, upon the tongue is Vajrajihvā on a red lotus; above that is the Buddha Amitābha absorbed in meditative concentration; and above him, at the palate, is the syllable Vaṃ facing downward, dripping drops of nectar—in this sequence.
One should meditate for the duration of a fortnight, a month, or six months. Once success is attained and the signs have been perceived, one should draw the mandala.
On the outside, it is square, with four doors, provided with door-keepers, and adorned with Lāsyā, Mālyā, Gītā, and Nṛtyā.
Inside that is a circle, surrounded by a single white line, with spokes... [k, kh, a]
Having thus drawn a white lotus in the center of that [mandala],
and having offered a bali-oblation preceded by worship, food offerings, and so forth on the full moon day of Kārttika, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, or another such month,
one should sit in the middle of the mandala in the vajraparyaṅka posture with a concentrated mind.

One should meditate on oneself as the form of the Buddha Amitābha, which has transformed from the form of Mañjuśrī, equal to the *dharmadhātu* and luminous. Then, with a steady mind, one should visualize that the body, speech, and mind seals (*mudrā*) of all the Tathāgatas, having arrived from all directions, enter into one’s own body, speech, and mind, becoming firmly established. [One should then contemplate] that which resides upon the moon and lotus at one’s own heart.
One should clearly visualize the conch shell.
Having turned that away, from the filaments and drops whose nature consists of all syllables situated there, the atoms of speech [issue forth] toward the region of the throat.

Having reached the state of the vowels (*svara*), they become the vowels; from the vowels comes the resonance (*nāda*), and from the resonance, having reached the tongue in the form of syllables (*akṣara*) through a succession of vajra-shapes, they illuminate the entirety of space.
They consist of the sixteen sounds that are the veil of the resonance vibrating throughout all space. [k, ḍh, g]

Seeing various [forms] quivering and filling the sky with sound, one should recite the mantra "Oṃ vākya idaṃ namaḥ. While reciting throughout the entire night while seated in the paryaṅka posture, the signs of accomplishment (*siddhi*) arise: rays of light flash from the tongue, and [the thought] "You have attained accomplishment" occurs.

A sound is heard, and various rays of light issue forth from the lips and the teeth. From that time on, intended words, sentences, meters, verses, mantras, vidyās, heart-mantras (*hṛdaya*), and so forth, as well as conch shells and other instruments, issue forth effortlessly. Furthermore, one masters and composes treatises not previously mastered. [One attains] omniscience (*sarvajñatva*).
And it occurs very quickly.
Thus ends the *Dharmaśaṅkhasamādhi-mañjuśrīsādhana*.
159) Homage to Mañjuśrī!
First of all, the practitioner, having risen at dawn and performed the cleansing of the mouth and other such rites, [should enter] the meditation chamber.

Having entered and sat down in the cross-legged posture on a comfortable seat, one should visualize a red-white syllable *mūḥ* upon a moon disc at one's own heart. Then, having drawn forth the Blessed One by means of masses of rays in the form of hooks,
one should visualize him in front, endowed with the colors, faces, arms, hand-symbols, and seat that will be described.

Having worshipped with mentally produced flowers, incense, and so forth, and having performed before them the confession of misdeeds and all other such rites, one should meditate upon the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), beginning with loving-kindness (maitrī). [From the beginning up to *catuṣṭayaṃ vibhāvya*, it is written differently in manuscript *kh* and *a* as follows: "By the previously mentioned procedure, in one's own heart..."]

One should visualize a syllable *mukāra*, red-white in color, upon a lotus and moon disc. Having drawn forth the Blessed One with its rays of light and visualized him before oneself, one should then worship him with flowers and other offerings. Having performed all the rites, such as the confession of misdeeds, in his presence, and having visualized the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), one should bring to manifestation the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*) [and recite] *oṃ*.

One should consecrate [the self] with the mantra: "I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Then, having visualized in space a five-pronged vajra with a seed-syllable by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should, by its rays, appropriately manifest a vajra-fence, a vajra-canopy, vajra-spikes, and a ground made of vajra, reaching down to the subterranean realm (*ārasātala*).
One should visualize that [the syllable] becomes vajra-like rays and remains outside the vajra-fence in the form of fragrance and so forth.

Immediately thereafter, within the vajra-fence, one should see a lotus arising from the syllable *hrīḥ*, and upon the lotus, a moon-maṇḍala arising from the syllable *a*, and above that, [a figure] of reddish-white color.

Having visualized the syllable *Muḥ* in the form of the radiation and reabsorption of numerous Buddhas, one should meditate upon the Lord Mañjuśrī, who has arisen from its transformation; he is reddish-white, seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon a lotus and moon,
with three faces— the first red, the right blue, and the left white— and four hands.
As appropriate, he is endowed with the sword of wisdom, the bow, and the arrows; he wears a jewel crown and is resplendent with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.

Having visualized oneself as the Youth adorned with the ornaments of a youth, upon a moon on a heart-lotus— [having contemplated oneself with Akṣobhya as a crown-ornament]— one sees Satyavatī seated in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, white in color, holding a bell in her left hand as if in competition.

To the right, by means of drawing her from the heart, one should visualize Vajradhāriṇī; likewise situated at the *ūrṇā* (the circle of hair between the eyebrows) is yellow Ratnavajrī, who with both hands binds a flower garland upon the head;
and at the throat is red-white Padmavajrī, holding a lotus stalk with pride in her left hand and [a vajra] in her right.
Having visualized Karmavajrī, green in color, standing as before upon her head with her two hands holding her own head and bearing a three-pronged vajra,
one should recite: *Oṃ vajrāṅkuśa jaḥ*, *Oṃ vajrapāśa hūṃ*, *Oṃ vajrasphoṭa vaṃ*, *Oṃ vajrāveśa hoḥ*.

With these mantras, having respectively attracted, caused to enter, bound, and brought under control the mandala of gnosis upon the lotus and moon, one should form two vajra-fists and create a chain with the index fingers and little fingers, [forming] the mudrā of the arranged vajra-wheel with the palms facing upward.

Having worshipped with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), flowers, incense, and so forth, established by one's own mouth, one should instantly cause [the deity] to enter one’s own body. Thereafter,
one should contemplate oneself as having Akṣobhya upon the crown of the head, preceded by the consecration of all the Tathāgatas.
[Having reflected: The mantra is: Oṃ sarvadhar-mābhāvasvabhāvaviśuddhavajra a ā aṃ aḥ.
All phenomena are pure by nature, namely, because they partake in the purity of Mañjuśrī, the gnosis-body of all Tathāgatas. A ĀḤ.

"O heart of all Tathāgatas, take away, take away! Oṃ hūṃ hrīḥ! O Blessed One, embodiment of gnosis, Lord of Speech, Great Word, you whose womb is the gnosis of the utterly pure Dharma-realm, stainless as the entire sky! Āḥ!"—with this mantra, preceded by the consecration of the beginning, middle, and end.
(From *Nāmasaṅgīti*, p.

161) One should recite the *Nāmasaṅgīti*—or the *Bhaṭṭārikā*, as some read—three times, at each junction of the day, or once a day, while delighting in the cross-legged posture and remaining in meditative absorption. In this manner, one should recite it.
As long as one does not perceive the signs of accomplishment (*siddhi*), one should thereafter practice the means for accomplishment according to the tantra. Thus ends the *Āryanāmasaṅgītisādhana*.
Homage to the glorious Mañjuvajra!
Having become the glorious Mañjuvajra, I shall accomplish the fulfillment of all aims for sentient beings whose vision is wandering; thus one should contemplate at the beginning of [the practice].
Having placed the *mātṛtattva* within the moon of the heart, and having worshipped and paid homage to the mantra-deities,
one should go for refuge to the Guru— the true embodiment of the Perfectly Awakened Ones— and undertake the three refuges and so forth.
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds; I rejoice in the merit of the world; I set my mind upon the awakening of a Buddha.
Because it lacks intrinsic nature, all things are considered empty, signless, causeless,
and devoid of aspiration, due to the departure from the conceptualization of entities.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness.
(pdf 95, p.
162) A triangle, white and high in form.
Having visualized a caitya situated in the center of a universal lotus and vajra, [one should meditate upon] the Perfectly Awakened One, Vajrasattva, together with his consort.
Having entered his very mouth, one's own mind, having emerged from the vajra,
becomes the three syllables within the lotus, colored by two *hoḥ* syllables.
Then, one should contemplate that body as dissolved by those radiations,
gathered within the *kalala* and other stages of embryonic development through the penetration of the essence of the moon and the sun.
The goddesses of all directions, having covered themselves, were intent on chanting exhortations,
reflecting upon how to arise for the sake of establishing the happiness of themselves and the world.

O Vajra-mind, Lord of the World, Savior of the realm of beings, protect me with your delightful passion and great purpose! Love me, O progenitor of beings, supreme Great Bond, if you desire my life, O Mañjunātha!
O Vajra-body, you who look with compassion upon the welfare and the ultimate meaning of enlightenment for the sake of the Buddhas and the beloved circle of many beings—
O Mañjunātha, if you desire my life, please fulfill my passion through the pledge of passion.
O Vajravāca, you who are compassionate toward the welfare of all and always engaged in performing deeds for the sake of the world—
desire me with the practice of supreme bliss, O Samantabhadra, if you wish for my life, O Mañjunātha!
(95, p. 163) You, O Vajra-body, supreme in your commitment, who brings about great benefit and has crossed over the lineage of perfect enlightenment, you who are compassionate and impartial—
desire me, a treasury of virtues, who am like a mine of many jewels, if you wish for my life, O Mañjunātha!
Then, in accordance with that goddess’s song, one should contemplate the Blessed One and visualize the meaning of the mantra, even while bound by illusion.
Having adorned the three worlds with emanations from the surging flood of Buddhas,
one should oneself become Mañjuvajra, arisen from the sign produced by the emergence of one’s own essential nature.
His body is massed together, reddish like saffron, and he has three faces—blue and white;
he holds upon his face his own consort, embraced by her two arms.
Holding a sword and an arrow in his hands, and grasping a bow and a blue lotus;
seated upon the moon on a universal-petal lotus, he is established in the vajra-posture and possesses the luster of the moon.
For saṃsāra arises from attachment to existence; therefore, one who has produced detachment toward all limbs should contemplate all illusion as the glorious Mañjuvajra, the soul of all.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the dharmadhātu.
Then, one should cause entry by means of the seed-syllables with true radiance into the eyes and other sense organs—
namely, *kṣiṃ*, *yaṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *skaṃ*— for the purpose of the subsidiary practice of reanimation (*sañjīva*).
The mandala of the planets is established as the very abodes of Vajra: Kṣitīśa, Kuliśa, Ākāśa, Lokeśa, Skambhi, and Bhadraka.
Upon the moon at one's own head, throat, and heart, with the true radiance of the mantras Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ,
one should perform the meditation on the Lord of Mantras by means of the vajras of body, speech, and mind.
(From PDF 96, p.
164) Oṃ, I am of the nature of the body-vajra of all Tathāgatas; Oṃ, I am of the nature of the speech-vajra of all Tathāgatas; Oṃ, I am of the nature of the mind-vajra of all Tathāgatas.
Having beheld the characteristic of the three vajras from the seed-syllable of the wisdom-being (jñānasattva) in the heart,
he bears the consecration of the family, which consists of the light-rays of the vidyās of all the Buddhas pervading every direction.
[One should visualize her] shining forth from the self-mantra located at the bases of the eyes, body, and so forth,
[and worship her] with the Vajra-bodies and others at the head, heart, navel, secret place, and feet.
One should visualize the true radiance of the five limbs with the syllables OṂ, HŪṂ, SVĀ, Ā, and HĀ;
and by means of Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi as the lords of the body.

The yogi should recite the mantras of the perfectly awakened ones who are well-established from all directions, born from the union of the vajra and the lotus, as well as those of Rūpavajrā and the others, with the thought: "I am the very essence of the nature of the vajra and the lotus."
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the worship of all Tathāgatas; Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra through the passion of all Tathāgatas.
Through all phenomena, by means of divine sounds and resonant echoes directed toward that deity,
one enters into the supreme state of self-identity, wherein one's own mind is the presiding deity.
Homage to you, O supreme Vajradhara, granter of boons; homage be to you, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Homage to you, whose essence is emptiness (*śūnyatāgarbha*); homage be to you, the awakening of the Buddhas.
O passion for the Buddha, homage be to you; O body of the Buddha, homage, homage!
O joy of the Buddha, homage to you; O delight of the Buddha, homage, homage!
O Buddha-smile, homage to you; O Buddha-laughter, homage again and again!
O Buddha-speech, may there be homage to you; O Buddha-nature, homage again and again!
Homage be to you, O source of non-becoming; homage to you, O source of the Buddha!
Homage to you, O source from space; homage to you, O source of primordial wisdom!
Homage to you, O Net of Illusion; homage to you, the Buddha’s drama!
Homage to you who are all things for all; homage be to you, the Body of Gnosis!
The burning away of the entire network of māras and other [obstacles] is called the fivefold [practice];
nectar consumed with the three syllables effects the purification of body, speech, and mind.
For the power of the cause is indeed inconceivable; one who is free from the delusion of passion and the like attains awakening through these very things— so the Sage has proclaimed.
The wise practitioner should recite the mantra consisting of three syllables— which is contained within the vajras of the body and so forth that are radiating light—
pervading space, and then withdraw it at the end of the mantra.

Reciting thus, when weariness arises, one should go toward the nourishment [of the mantra] by means of the *praṇava* moistening the moon at the crown; then, one should recite the *bodhicitta* once more.
Like a dream, an illusion, and so forth, one should constantly meditate upon the Lord as the perfection of Mañjuvajra, for all effects and the entire world are for the benefit of beings.
Having performed worship and other preliminary rites, the mantra-practitioner, having conceived a longing for the virtuous,
should meditate upon the Fully Awakened One as endowed with the three syllables, visualized in terms of body and so forth.
The world is deceived by this reality which consists of wisdom and means;
therefore, one should strengthen the aspiration for the realization of the reality of the world.
From this merit obtained through the meditation on the glorious Mañjuvajra,
may I become the Wisdom Body of Mañjuśrī, bestowing all beings upon the world.

In whatever manner Mañjuśrī conducts himself, may that very same conduct be mine.
For as long as the first limit of cyclic existence, which is without end,
may last, I shall practice the deathless and imperishable state solely for the benefit of sentient beings.
For as many Buddhas as there are who have indeed entered parinirvāṇa, those kinsmen of the world,
for the sake of their teaching, I shall practice in age after age.
I shall wander everywhere in the form of a young child;
in the form of mantras, I shall destroy sentient beings from time to time.
Having arisen from meditative absorption, the practitioner, maintaining composure and bearing pride in Mañjunātha,
should recite the mantra while perceiving all sense objects as having the form of deities.
Through the application of pure faculties, [one should visualize them] with three faces and six arms,
bearing as weapons the wheel, the vajra, the great jewel, the lotus, and the sword.
Those consisting of form, sound, great fragrance, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena,
which arise from the nature of the Body-Vajra, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.
Through the realization of all Buddhas, one should worship the five objects of the senses as well as oneself and others by means of the yoga of one's own presiding deity.
One should arrange everything— eating, sleeping, bathing, sitting, and even standing— in this manner through union with one's own presiding deity.
(From *pdf* 97, p. 167):
May this world become Mañjuvajra, who has composed these well-spoken verses on the fourfold meaning in brief; may he bestow the fruit of happiness.
One who is weary from meditation should recite the mantra: *oṃ vākyedaṃ namaḥ*. Or one should recite the *upahṛdaya*: *oṃ hrīṃ huṃ*.
Thus ends the *Mañjuvajrasādhana*.
Homage to Mañjunātha!

Plīṃ [ḍh, a: thrīṃ]—this single-syllable king of vidyās, named Sarvakāryasamartha (Capable of All Deeds), is the most supreme secret, effective for all rites, and is unassailable and inviolable by all sentient beings.
He is the auspiciousness of all beings, the accomplisher for all beings, the lord of all mantras, the sovereign of all worlds, the friendliness-embodied one among all lords of wealth,
and the compassionate one toward all creatures who harbor enmity.

It is the destroyer of all obstacles [of all sciences]. In brief, however it is employed, it acts accordingly. Even if not yet perfected, it performs all rites. While reciting the mantra, whomever one touches becomes submissive. Having consecrated a garment and put it on, one becomes fortunate. Having consecrated a tooth-stick, one should chew it.
It removes toothache. Having consecrated a twig of white karavīra seven times with mantras, one should chew it; food that was not sought after will be obtained. [In case of] eye pain...
Having powdered rock salt (*saindhava*) and empowered it seven times with mantras, one should fill the eyes; this removes eye pain.

Having taken a *chattrikā* (small vessel) produced from the dung of an elephant while it was trumpeting, having tied a *kiṃśuka* leaf inside it, having cooked it over a gentle fire until it is dried and reduced to the state of rock salt powder, and having empowered it seven times with mantras—[one should apply it].

If one fills the ears with it, it pacifies [the pain] at that very moment. At the time of childbirth, for a woman whose fetus is obstructed and who suffers from labor pains and other ailments, one should grind the root of *āṭaruṣa* (also known as *āḍhavajra*) with water free of living organisms and apply it to the region of the navel; she will give birth easily. Or, [it cures] a man afflicted by a painful splinter.

Having consecrated old ghee one hundred and eight times with mantras, one should have it drunk and smear that area with it; this removes the foreign object (or pain) from that very moment. In cases of indigestion, cholera, diarrhea, and colic, one should consecrate black salt (sauvarcala) seven times with mantras and consume it; thereby, the afflicted person is freed from that disease on that very day.

One becomes healthy. For a woman who is fertile and desiring childbirth, one should grind the root of *aśvagandhā* with cow’s milk, stir it, and at the time of her menses, have her drink it after reciting [the mantra] twenty-five times; then, avoiding the wives of others, she should approach her own husband, and he will procreate a son. This applies in cases of fevers occurring every day, every two days, every three days, every four days, as constant fever, or as chronic fever.
One should eat milk-rice mixed with ghee that has been consecrated one hundred and eight times; one will become healthy.
For those seized by *ḍākinīs* or planetary spirits (*graha*), one should consecrate one’s own face one hundred and eight times and look at them; they will become healthy.
Regarding the Mother of Children (*bālamātṛ*), the worship of *vetālas*, the *kumāra-grahas*, and so forth...

For those seized by all malevolent human beings or by the *dāruṇa* [terrible] spirits of Varuṇa, one should empower one’s own hand eight hundred times with the mantra and touch the head of the afflicted person; he will become healthy. Protection for oneself is achieved with a single recitation; great protection is achieved with two recitations.

With three recitations, there is protection of the house; with four recitations, protection of the village; with five recitations, protection of the city; and likewise, up to six recitations, protection of the army camp and its circles is accomplished. These and other minor rites, even those not explicitly mentioned, [are achieved].

One performs [the rite]. With this very mantra, for women suffering from diseases such as *pradara* (menorrhagia), one should grind the root of *alambuṣa* with milk, empower it by reciting the mantra eight hundred times, stir it with milk, and drink it; thus she becomes healthy.
[The mantra is] adorned with the letter *ha*, the internal and intermediate [consonants], the letter *sa*, and the vowel *ī*.
Having seen the script marked by the half-moon and drop (indvarddhabindu), one should recite [the mantra] while focused on the Guru.
The application of a few rituals for single-syllable mantras is completed.
Homage to the Buddha! May he— whose knees rest upon the earth, who holds a single sword in his left hand and a noose gripped by the index finger in his other clenched fist,
whose body is firm and dense, and who possesses fierce radiance and fierce eyes— pacify the obstacles of cyclic existence.
This is the immovable destroyer of obstacles.
Having mentally performed various kinds of worship with flowers and other offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and leaders dwelling in the ten directions.
Seeing those who are terrified and suffering, the practitioner should offer his own body;
for the sake of increasing auspiciousness, he should perform the confession of evil deeds.

Then, having rejoiced in the entire merit by its very nature belonging to the assembly of perfectly awakened Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as to sentient beings such as those in training and those beyond training;
Having taken refuge in the Three Jewels and being firm in one’s resolve for perfect enlightenment,
one should cultivate the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra) in their proper sequence.

One should contemplate phenomena as empty because they lack the application of defining characteristics, as signless because they are without cause, and as free from aspiration because they are devoid of substantial existence.
One should meditate on the Hero, born from the syllable *HŪṂ*, situated in the center of a universal lotus and sun,
with two red eyes, two arms, and a jeweled crown.
The Lord who instantly removes all sins, who fulfills every wish,
who resembles the flax flower, and who is stainless with the radiance of shimmering Buddhas.
With his fangs and lips pressed together, adorned with all ornaments,
holding a noose with the index finger in his left hand, and with one knee placed upon the ground.
And [he saw] the illustrious Mahācaṇḍaroṣaṇa, his fierce hand occupied with a sword,
squint-eyed, most terrible, and a source of fear even to fear itself.
One should meditate upon the wisdom-being (jñānasattva), intensely radiant, like the commitment-being (samayasattva).
Within the heart of that very being, the practitioner of mantra should visualize the seed-syllable together with its emblem.
When weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra while in union with the form of the deity;
thereby, one will certainly attain the desired accomplishment—of this there is no doubt.

In this regard, the king of mantras is: Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa Hūṃ Phaṭ. This king of mantras, when recited even once, incinerates all sins and brings protection everywhere. By striking with beans and the like, it removes the fear of spirits and other such threats. [It removes fear. In a shallow bowl... [k: āgamaśarāve]
Having written on a raw clay bowl with chalk (*khaṭṭikā*), one should hang it at the door (or, according to other versions, bind it there).

It provides protection for infants who have recently been born. Having fashioned a doll out of *madana* wood measuring four finger-breadths in size, one should write the mantra on birch bark together with the name of the person to be accomplished and insert it into its heart;
then, one should pin its mouth shut with a thorn.
The opponent’s mouth becomes pinned shut. If one pins the feet, movement is paralyzed.
If one pins the heart, anger is paralyzed. By means of a pin made of human shank-bone or an iron pin, if one pins whichever limbs while uttering the name, those [limbs] of his—[the text breaks off].
[They] perish suddenly. One should bury [the empowered object] at the gate of an enemy or cause it to be raised up;

by means of consecrated cremation ashes placed upon the door-panel (*dvārapaṭa*), one causes [the enemy] to be driven away. Having consecrated a sword and entering into battle with it, one attains victory. In which...

When a task has arisen, one should offer an oblation; that will succeed for him. Whatever the practitioner desires—whether it be an auspicious or inauspicious deed—he accomplishes all of it by mere recitation.
Whatever merit I have acquired through writing this, may it accomplish the welfare of sentient beings.
By this, may this entire world become a vessel for perfect enlightenment.
The *Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇasādhana*, together with its ritual procedure (*kalpa*), is completed.
This work is the composition of Prabhākarakīrti.
(PDF 100, p.

172) Following the previously described procedure, after the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one visualizes Śrī Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, transformed from a black syllable *HŪṂ* upon a sun disk atop a white lotus.

[One should visualize] the Blessed One, who resembles an *atasī* flower, whose other name is Acala (or Bala), with one face and two arms, squinting eyes, a most terrible countenance made formidable by bared fangs, wearing a jewel crown, his lower lip pressed between his fangs,
his head adorned with a garland of severed heads, his two eyes bloodshot, and his right [hand]...

One should visualize oneself as Khaḍgadhara, with the left hand holding a sword and a noose at the heart, wearing a white snake as a sacred thread and a garment of tiger skin, adorned with ornaments fashioned from various jewels,
with the left foot touching the ground and the right foot slightly raised, and garlanded with the radiance of the sun.
Having reflected upon the *samayasattva*, preceded by the meditation on the *jñānasattva*, one should meditate [on him] with Akṣobhya as his crown ornament.
Following that is the recitation mantra: OṂ CAṆḌAMAHĀROṢAṆA HŪṂ PHAṬ.
|| The *Sādhana* of Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa.

The yogi, seated in a comfortable posture in a certain place conducive to the mind, should visualize a black syllable *huṃ* above a solar disc within his own heart. He should behold the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas drawn by its rays appearing in the sky.
Then, having worshipped them before him with the fivefold offerings such as flowers, which have emerged from the rays of the *huṃ*, [he should proceed].

One should perform the confession of misdeeds, the rejoicing in merit, the dedication of merit, and so forth. Then, one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward all sentient beings characterized by affection for them as if they were an only son; compassion (*karuṇā*), characterized by the desire to rescue them from suffering and the causes of suffering; and sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which takes the form of gladness.
One should cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*), which has the nature of abandoning improper attachment. Then, having observed the three realms as empty, one should consecrate them with this mantra: *oṃ*.

"I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Then, in the intermediate space, upon a lotus, one should visualize oneself as having been transformed into the form of Caṇḍācala— arisen from a sword produced from the syllable *HŪṂ*, which rests upon a sun-maṇḍala and has its hilt empowered by the syllable *HŪṂ*— with round, blazing, and fiercely red eyes.

With the surface of his forehead marked by a fiercely knitted brow, his teeth and lips pressed together, his left knee planted upon the earth and his right foot treading upon the irresistible Māra; his fierce right hand busy with a sword, and his fist holding a noose with the threatening forefinger that removes the fear of the three worlds; possessing a luster like sapphire, he blazes with a great and most terrible wrath like a flaming fire.
Having drawn in the Jñānasattva by means of rays from the seed-syllable in the heart and caused him to enter the Samayasattva, one should receive the empowerment.
Immediately after the empowerment, one should visualize Akṣobhya upon the head. Then, when weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra.
In this regard, the mantra is: Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa Hūṃ Phaṭ.
The Sadhana of Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa.

Seated on a comfortable seat in a certain place conducive to the mind, one should visualize a black syllable *HŪṂ* upon a solar disc atop an eight-petaled lotus within one's own heart; then, by means of its rays, one should invite the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, as well as Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa who is about to be described, from the expanse of space and worship them.

Having cultivated confession of misdeeds, the vow of non-commission, going for refuge to the Three Jewels, rejoicing in merit, the offering of oneself, the dedication of roots of virtue toward awakening, and [the realization that] this world has suffering as its nature and is of the nature of being without intrinsic existence (niḥsvabhāvasvabhāva), [one should meditate]. (pdf 101, p. 174) [k: lagadiḥkhabhāva]
Having realized that [all things] are free from the grasped and the grasper, like a dream or an illusion, one should contemplate emptiness:

*oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* (I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness). Thereafter, in the courtyard of the stainless sky, upon an eight-petalled lotus and a sun mandala, [one visualizes] a sword hilt produced from a black syllable *huṃ*.
[The syllable] *huṃ*— by means of its rays, having summoned the entire assembly of Buddhas and caused them to enter into the *huṃ*,
there arises from that *huṃ* a form resembling a great dark-blue cloud, filled with garlands of flames from the fire of the non-trivial eon, which destroys the irresistible Māras.

Adorned with various ornaments and jewels, his crown bound with gems and flashing with five youthful heroes; with terrifyingly radiant teeth resembling jasmine, he possesses the splendor of a form both horrific and awe-inspiring due to his clenching of the lips; simultaneously, he gazes with a frown and bared fangs.
His two eyes are directed toward the netherworld (pātāla), his right knee is planted upon the circle of the earth,
and with his left foot resting on a solar seat atop a lotus, he is intent on rising; in his right hand is a flaming blue sword containing the syllable *huṃ*, while in his left fist [is a skull-cup].

One should meditate upon the illustrious Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, who holds a golden noose marked with a vajra for the purpose of binding the hosts of enemies— the afflictions of Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, and others— who are agitated by the threat of his forefinger; and who is solely devoted to bestowing the infinite wealth desired by the world.

One should visualize the sword marked with the syllable *huṃ*, which has arisen from the *huṃ* situated upon a lotus and sun disk in the heart of the Blessed One, the Great Wrathful King Acala; and having transformed that, one should contemplate Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa, born from the *huṃ*, who has the Blessed One within his heart. Of him also...
In the heart, one should visualize a sword marked with a straight black syllable *hūṃ* arising from a *hūṃ* situated upon a lotus and sun;

having seen the Jñānasattva drawn in by its rays as being identical to the Samayasattva, one should summon him with the syllable *jaḥ* and perform the rites of rinsing the mouth, sprinkling, and so forth.

Having offered [the oblation], one should cause [the deity] to enter right there with the syllable *huṃ*, bind him with the syllable *vaṃ*, and satisfy him with the syllable *hoḥ*. One should contemplate the Leader as having become one, like milk poured into milk. [This is] of the Blessed One.

One should place Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Nairātmyā upon the six limbs— namely, the eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, head, and mind— according to their respective positions. Then,
having summoned the host of the five Tathāgatas and goddesses emerging from the syllable *Hūṃ* residing in the heart by means of rays of light, one should [perform the ritual].

Having bathed [the deity] with jars filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should delight Akṣobhya on the crown of the head with goddesses and various offerings such as diverse dances, instrumental music, and so forth. Then the Blessed One, striving for the sake of others, [liberates] all sentient beings from passion, hatred, delusion, and the like.

[He was bound] by Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Kandarpa, and others with great nets of delusion, great nets of hatred, and great nets of fear; then, by the great kings of wrath vibrating from the heart-mantra, he bound the multitudes of Māras in many places— along with their armies, naked, with disheveled hair, wailing, and helpless— with the vajra-noose.

Having bound them, destroyed them, pulverized them, and cut them with a sharp sword, one should— possessing a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*)— re-create them and, in order to discipline them in the Dharma, establish them near one's own station. When weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra, having fixed the mind between the eyebrows.

By the mere recitation of the mantra of the Lord Mahācaṇḍamahāroṣaṇa (also known as Caṇḍaroṣaṇa), whose form is the single essence of the universe, one attains the subduing of the unsubdued, the certain peace of the world, as well as protection,
increase, contentment, nourishment, and likewise the rites of eradication, attraction, killing, and intimidation— all these activities.
One should perform [the rite]. Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ.
Thus ends the *Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇasādhana*.
Homage to Tārā!
Having meditated on [the sequence] up to emptiness as before, there is a blue lotus transformed from the seed-syllable *tāṃ* upon a moon disc.
With that as the seed-syllable within her womb, she is the fully perfected green Amoghasiddhi, crowned by [Amoghasiddhi],
holding the gesture of boon-granting and a blue lotus in her right and left hands respectively,
with Aśokakāntā, Mārīcī, and Ekajaṭā occupying the positions of her right and left sides.
Having meditated upon the divine maiden Alaṅkāravatī and unified her with the gnosis-being (jñānasattva),
one should recite the mantra "Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā" and then wander at will, with that very mind.
Thus ends the *Ārya-khadiravaṇī-tārā-sādhana*.
Homage to Tārā!
First, one should visualize that from the seed-syllable *Tāṃ* situated in the center of a moon disc within one’s own heart, rays of light emerge, from which [the deities] are produced.

One should meditate upon the gurus, buddhas, and bodhisattvas. Having honored them with both external and internal offerings, one should perform the sevenfold supreme offering before them. Then, having contemplated emptiness, one should recite: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho 'ham*. Thereafter, [one should visualize] her arisen from that [syllable] upon a moon disc.

One should visualize Tārā, dark blue in color, arisen from the syllable *Tāṃ* situated upon a white lotus; she has two arms, displays the gesture of granting boons with her right hand, and holds a blue lotus with its stalk in her left;
she is adorned with all ornaments and seated upon a lotus and moon disc. (p. 177)

One should visualize her seated in the paryanka posture. One should bind the samayamudrā: having formed a hollow añjali with both hands, one should cover the two middle fingers with the two index fingers, with the tips of the thumbs joined together.
The mudrā is the blooming lotus. Then, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā*.
The *Mahattarī Tārā Sādhana* is completed.

Homage to Tārā! Having meditated, as before, up to the point of emptiness, one should visualize Tārā— dark blue in color, adorned with all ornaments, holding a blue lotus in her left hand, and arisen from the syllable *tāṃ* within a moon disc arising from the syllable *aṃ*, which is itself situated in the center of a universal lotus arising from the syllable *paṃ*.

To the right is Varadā, seated in the half-lotus posture; on her right side is Aśokakāntā, yellow in color, wearing a crown of various jewels, and holding an aśoka sprout and a vajra in her left and right hands respectively.
Likewise, on the left side is Mahāmāyūrī, yellow in color, holding a peacock-feather whisk and a fly-whisk in her left and other (right) hands respectively.
Ekajaṭā is short, black, wearing a tiger skin, three-eyed, with a face made terrifying by fangs, with blazing orange hair standing erect,
and likewise holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup; likewise, Āryajāṅgulī is dark green.
One should visualize her holding a black serpent and a chowrie in her left and right hands respectively. Thus, when weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā*.
Thus ends the Varadātārāsādhana.

Having meditated on an indīvara lotus born from the syllable *tāṃ* with the syllable *tāṃ* in its center, one should visualize the Noble Tārā arising from its transformation— dark green in color, holding an utpala lotus in her left hand and displaying the gesture of boon-granting (*varada*) with her right.

Having meditated on Amoghasiddhi seated upon a *bhadrāsana* and crowned with [the Buddha] Śyāma, and having unified her with the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*), one should recite the mantra— accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished, either "so-and-so" or "so-and-so woman"— according to the prescribed number mentioned immediately above: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture amukaṃ (or amukīṃ) vaśamānaya svāhā*.
Even in the absence of the arrow and other signs, having bound the throat of the person to be subjugated with a blue lotus,
and having filled that body with the mass of one's own red rays, one should bring them under one's control.
This is the *Tārāsādhana* for the section on subjugation (*vaśya*).
The Noble Tārā, [Kh: Tārā], is completed.
Homage to Vajratārā!
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sādhana of Vajratārā,
which accomplishes all desired aims through the ritual procedure of fire offerings (homa).

In this regard, these mantra syllables are as follows: *Nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya*. Tadyathā: *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture sarvaduṣṭapraduṣṭān mama kṛte jambhaya stambhaya mohaya bandhaya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
[Only] *phaṭ phaṭ sarvaduṣṭastambhani tāre svāhā*. (pdf 103, p.
179) One should visualize the goddess Tārā situated in the center of the circle of Mothers (*mātṛmaṇḍala*).
She has eight arms and four faces, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Resembling the color of gold, auspicious, radiant with the marks of a maiden,
wearing a great crown of the five Buddhas, and born from the consecration of the Vajra-Sun.
Possessing the beauty of fresh youth, with shimmering golden earrings,
seated upon a universal lotus, and adorned with a crimson radiance.
Holding a vajra, noose, goad, conch, and arrow raised in her right hands,
and holding a vajra-hook, lotus, bow, and the tarjanī gesture in her left hands,
one should accomplish the three worlds through the vajraparyaṅka yoga.
To the east is Puṣpatārā, white in color and beautiful,
arisen from the syllable Oṃ, and holding a garland of flowers in her hands.
She has two arms and one face, adorned with all ornaments;
she is the incense Tārā on the right, black in color and beautiful in form.
In the west, one should visualize Dīpatārā, her hand busy with the branch of incense, adorned with all ornaments,
and her hands occupied with a lamp-stand.
In the north is Gandhatārā, yellow in color, adorned with great ornaments, her golden earrings swaying,
and her hands busily holding a vessel of fragrant powder.
One should meditate upon the goddess, who has the appearance of a red color, within the central maṇḍala;
thereafter, one should visualize the female gatekeepers, distinguished as Aṅkuśī and the others.
At the eastern gate is Vajrāṅkuśī, with one face and two arms, holding a vajra-hook and an utpala lotus in her hands;
she has a distorted countenance and is black in color. At the southern gate is Vajrapāśī.
At the western gate is Vajrasphoṭī, yellow in color, with one face and two arms, holding a vajra-noose in her hand;
at the northern gate is Vajraghaṇṭā, white in color, with one face and two arms, having a distorted countenance and holding a vajra-bell in her hand. Both have distorted faces.

These [deities] should be visualized as holding vajras and bells in their hands, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, seated upon sun-discs, possessing solar radiance, garlanded with flames, and adorned with snakes. One should visualize Ūṣṇīṣavijayā above and Sumbhā below.
Having visualized the wheel and the serpent-noose, one should recite the mantra while it vibrates.

Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā. By means of these ten syllables, the ten deities who are the basis of the ten perfections should be meditated upon through practice for the sake of accomplishing all activities.
This supreme and most excellent mantra, honored by all the Buddhas,
which brings swift accomplishment through mere recitation, was spoken by Vajrapañjara.
Having consecrated the hem of a cloth seven times with this mantra and tied a knot,
one will not be overcome by anyone even while traveling through the Vindhya mountains;
tigers, thieves, crocodiles, lions, snakes, elephants, buffaloes, bears, gavayas, and the like [are subdued] by the mere recollection of its name.

They perish and dissolve. One should perform oblations of blue lotuses (*utpala*) up to one hundred and eight times with this mantra: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture amukīṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*. Whomever one desires, that person one brings under control.
With this very same mantra, one should recite it thirty-two times over a crow’s wing-feather and hide it in the house of an enemy.
Within seven days, one causes [the target] to be expelled: Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture, move, move swiftly, O swift-goer! Expel Devadatta!
Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Now, there is also another application: Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture, may the father of the maiden named so-and-so give her to me in marriage, svāhā!
[One should employ] madana, caṇḍabīja, and likewise unmattaka.
One should offer five thousand oblations of Aśoka leaves and flowers.
An oblation of ghee, honey, and molasses is recommended for the attainment of a maiden;
then, within seven days, the yogi shall obtain the maiden of his desire.

Now, there is yet another application: *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture, summon [the one] named so-and-so from her own place to my presence, jaḥ!* With this mantra, one should offer five thousand thorns of the jujube tree (*badarī*) smeared with *svayambhū* flowers. By performing this, [the result follows].
"One may even attract the daughter of kings.

Now, there is another practice: having drawn the Blessed Lady on a cloth stained with menstrual blood—two-armed, one-faced, and holding a goad, a blue lotus, and a noose in her hands—and having performed worship before her, [one should proceed].

With the words "These flowers are auspicious and divine," and so forth, one should subsequently recite the mantra with focused visualization: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture [Name] tell me my desired dream, hūṃ phaṭ*. She arrives after five thousand recitations.
Having bound her by the throat with the noose and pierced her with the hook, one should visualize the subject at the soles of one's feet in the form of a maidservant.
One should eat.

Furthermore, there is another application: having consecrated the Tārādhāraṇī seven times, one should cleanse both one's eyes. One may then enter into the presence of the royal court; then that king will treat one with respect like a disciple and will not act in opposition.
(As stated in *pdf* 105, p. 182:

"He does not speak [harshly], he bestows favor, he engages in pleasant conversation, and he becomes submissive; even when angry, he comes under one's control"—this is a true and established conviction based on observed evidence.
Furthermore, there is another application: having recited the Tārādhāraṇī one hundred times, one should reduce a two-faced venomous serpent to ashes.
Then, having made a wick with the ghee of a red-colored cow or female buffalo and cotton from the Arka plant, one should light it and collect the collyrium.
Having ground that collyrium with Vajrasūrya and Vajradharma, [one should apply it] with *paramānna*.

One should fumigate with *paramāśva*. One should anoint the eyes with ashes. Whomever one sees with the eye-vajra—if she does not protect [one] from Padmanarteśvara at that very moment, then I would not be Tārā, and the Blessed Buddhas would have been slain by me.
"May they become [so].

Now, there is another application as well: having taken a fresh leaf of the *adaśana-śiśu* plant, having consecrated it seven times with the *Tārā-dhāraṇī*, and having combined it with the root of *bhṛṅgarāja* and *gorocanā*, [one should apply it] upon the forehead.
Having applied a *tilaka* mark, whatever woman one looks upon, she brings her under one's control;
she does not take pleasure in another, she does not go to another, and she abandons her own husband.
Furthermore, there is another practice: having consecrated a "belly-worm" (*udarakīṭa*) seven times with the *Tārādhāraṇī*, [one should apply it].

One should give betel leaf together with Vajradharma to the maiden. When she has consumed it, by means of this supreme yoga, she faints; she does not take pleasure in another, she does not go to another, and she abandons her own husband.
Furthermore, there is another practice: having anointed oneself with *mahātaila*, one should recite the Tārādhāraṇī.

One should recite the mantra ten thousand times while engaged in meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*). At the conclusion of the recitation, if a cake made from rice flour and *kuḍmala* flowers is given to a woman, she will not release her hold even in the face of death.
(Source: pdf 105, p. 183)

Furthermore, there is another application: at the time of a lunar eclipse, having performed the service while reciting the *tārādāraṇī*, one should seize the lord of the world of that region and contemplate it as conch-powder. This should be given to a woman;
even when she has passed away, he follows her.

Furthermore, there is another application: having recited the Tārādhāraṇī mantra one hundred and eight times over madana fruit, she whom one anoints with that fruit together with Hayagrīva becomes submissive.

Furthermore, there is another application: *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture, grant the release from bondage for [name], muḥ svāhā*. Having written this mantra, interspersed with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), upon a leaf of the *arka* tree, one should place it in the hole of a crab;
thereby, release from bondage occurs.
The Sādhana of Vajratārā is completed.
Homage to Tārā!
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sādhana of Vajratārā,
which accomplishes all desired aims through the ritual procedure of the fire offering (homa).

In this regard, these mantra-words are as follows: *namas āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya*. Thus: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture sarvaduṣṭapraduṣṭān mama kṛte jambhaya stambhaya mohaya bandhaya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ*.

*phaṭ* only; *sarvaduṣṭastambhanī tāre svāhā*. Therein, first of all, having meditated upon the seed-syllable *tāṃ* within a moon-maṇḍala at one’s own heart (pdf 106, p. 184), [one should visualize] the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas drawn forth by its rays of light.
Having worshipped with various kinds of offerings and the like, and having performed the confession of sins and so forth, one should recite the verse of the three refuges.

Then, having cultivated the four sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*), one should utter the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako’ham*. Thereafter, upon a moon disc above a lotus born from the syllable *paṃ*, there is again the seed-syllable *tāṃ*.
Having meditated on that, through its transformation,
one should visualize the goddess Tārā standing in the center of the circle of mothers,
possessing eight arms and four faces, and adorned with all ornaments.
Resembling the color of gold, auspicious, and radiant with the marks of a maiden,
she is well-seated upon a moon-disc resting on a double lotus.
She has four faces turned to the right, which are yellow, black, white, and red;
each face has three eyes, and she is seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture.
Having a reddish glow, wearing a crown of four Buddhas, with her six right hands shining as they hold a vajra, an arrow, a conch, and the gesture of granting boons,
and her six left hands holding an utpala lotus, a bow, a vajra-hook, a vajra-noose, and making the threatening gesture—
one should accomplish the three worlds through the yoga of the vajra-paryaṅka posture.
In front of that [deity], one should visualize the flower-star (Puṣpatārā), white in color and enchanting.
She is manifested from the syllable Oṃ, her hands are busily occupied with a garland of flowers;
she has two arms and one face, and is adorned with all ornaments.
To the south is Dhūpatārā, black in color and beautiful in form,
her hands busily occupied with an incense burner, and adorned with all ornaments.
In the west is Dīpatārā, yellow in color and captivating;
she holds a lamp-stick, is divine, and wears swaying golden earrings.
In the north, one should visualize within the womb-maṇḍala the goddess Gandhatārā, who holds a fragrant conch in her hand and resembles the color of blood.
(PDF 106, p.

185) These [deities] have one face and two arms, are adorned with all ornaments, and sit in the vajra-paryaṅka posture. These six goddesses have slightly terrifying faces and are poised in the *lalita-ākṣepa* stance. Having meditated upon all of these within the maṇḍala circle...

Having summoned the wisdom-wheel (*jñānacakra*) by means of rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, one should then meditate on Vajrāṅkuśī at the eastern gate—white in luster, enchanting, and possessing hands marked with the vajra-hook (*vajrāṅkuśa*). *jaḥ huṃ vaṃ hoḥ* (at the eastern gate). Then one should meditate on Vajrāṅkuśī, white in radiance, her form captivating, and her hands characterized by the vajra-hook as her primary emblem.
At the southern gate is Vajrapāśī, black in color and exceedingly dear to the Great Joy;
her body is adorned with divine ornaments, and she holds the excellent vajra-noose.
One should visualize Vajrasphoṭā, yellow in color and possessing a beautiful form, holding a vajra-chain as her hand-emblem,
at the western gate.
Adorned with various ornaments.
Then, at the northern gate, one should constantly behold the auspicious Vajraghaṇṭā, who has a divine form and is red in color, holding a vajra-bell as her weapon.
Then the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon Uṣṇīṣavijayā above, yellow in color and beautiful in form, who bestows the fruit of supreme sovereignty and holds a wheel.
Beneath that maṇḍala of her womb, one should visualize Sumbhā, who is black in color,
possessing a radiant and excellent form, and holding a snake-noose in her hand.
All these deities should be known as having two arms and one face, and being captivating to the mind.
These ten goddesses are manifested from ten syllables;
they are the pure ten perfections (pāramitās) for the accomplishment of all activities.
In that regard, there are ten syllables: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā*.
(pdf 107, p.
186) Likewise, the empowerment of mind, speech, and body, the consecrations, the drops (*bindu*), the subtle yoga, the recitation (*jāpa*), and so forth, are also to be meditated upon.
This supreme and most excellent mantra, honored by all the Buddhas, brings accomplishment through mere recitation; it is divine and was spoken within the Vajra-panjara.
Thus it is said.
Herein is the ritual procedure: having grasped the hem of the cloth with this mantra, having consecrated it seven times, and having tied a knot, even if one goes into the Vindhya forest—

By [this], one is protected from anything; tigers, thieves, crocodiles, lions, snakes, elephants, buffaloes, bears, gavayas, horses, and so forth, flee and dissolve away. Likewise, with this mantra, one should offer one hundred and eight lotuses (*utpala*): *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture amukīṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*. Whomever one desires, that person one brings under control. Likewise, with this...
Having recited the mantra thirty-two times over a crow’s wing-feather, one should hide it in the enemy’s house; within seven days, it causes [the enemy] to be driven away.
*Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture cala [ḍh: bala prabala] pracala śīghragāmini devadattamuccāṭaya hūṃ phaṭ*. This is the procedure for expulsion (*uccāṭana*).
Now, another application: Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture, may the father of the maiden named so-and-so give her to me in marriage, svāhā!
[One should use] madana, the fierce seed (caṇḍabīja), and the fruit of the unmadaka plant.
Likewise, one should offer five thousand oblations of Aśoka leaves and flowers.
An oblation of ghee, honey, and molasses is indeed recommended for the attainment of a maiden;
through this practice for seven days, one shall obtain the maiden desired by oneself.
Thus (ends the passage on) page 187 of PDF 107).
Now, another application: Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture, draw [the woman] named so-and-so from her own abode!
With this mantra, "jaḥ mamāntike," five thousand jujube thorns, smeared with the flowers of the *svayaṃmū* plant, should be offered as oblations. By this,
one attracts even the daughters of kings.

Furthermore, there is another practice: having drawn the Blessed Lady on a cloth stained with menstrual blood—two-armed, one-faced, and holding a goad, a noose, and a lotus in her hands—one should perform worship before her and, endowed with meditative visualization, recite the mantra beginning with "These flowers are auspicious and divine," etc., while chanting: *Oṃ tāre*.

*Tuttāre ture, [name], tell me my desired dream! Huṃ phaṭ!* With five thousand [recitations], she arrives. Having bound her throat with a noose and pierced her with a hook, having bound her feet with a blue lotus, one draws her in from all sides.
Having visualized the object of accomplishment at the soles of one's feet, one should enjoy them in the form of female slaves.
Now, another application: having consecrated the Tārādhāraṇī seven times, one should apply it as collyrium to both eyes.
When entering the presence of a royal court, the king will treat him with respect and so forth; he will become entirely submissive.
Now, another application: having recited the Tārādhāraṇī one hundred times, one should reduce a two-headed venomous serpent to ashes.
Then, having prepared a wick with the ghee of a red-colored cow or female buffalo and using *arka* cotton, one should light it and cause the collyrium to fall.
Taking that collyrium with the Sun and the Vajra—[or, according to manuscripts k, ḍh: with the Vajradharma; manuscript kh: ...]...

Having prepared [the ointment] with *vajrasūrya* and *vajradharma*, one should fumigate it with excellent incense. One should apply that ash as collyrium to the eyes. Whomever one sees with the *cakṣurvajra*, if she does not protect [one from] Padmanarteśvara, then I, Tārā, would not exist, and the Buddhas would have been slain by me.
"May they become Blessed Ones.
(pdf 108, p.
188) Now, another application: [one should hold] a belly-insect with a dhāraṇī.

Having consecrated it seven times with the mantra, one should unite it with Vajradharma and offer it with betel leaf. By this excellent practice, she consumes [it], releases [her inhibitions], and behaves like one’s own wife. Now, there is another practice: having taken a young girl who has not yet had sexual intercourse, [one should recite] the Tārā Dhāraṇī...
Having consecrated it seven times with mantras and combined it with *bhṛṅgarāja* and *gorocanā*, one should apply a tilaka-mark on the forehead;
whomever one looks upon, that person is brought under one's control.
Now, there is another practice: having anointed oneself with *mahātaila*, one should recite the *Tārādhāraṇī* ten thousand times.
While meditating, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should prepare a *śaṣkulikā* (a type of cake) from rice flour and *kuḍmala* (flower buds);
whoever is given this will not be released even upon death.

Now, there is another application as well: at the time of a lunar eclipse, while reciting the Tārādhāraṇī and performing service, one should consecrate conch powder with the Lokeśvara born from that [eclipse]. Whomever that [powder] is given to, she will remain until her death.
Another application: having recited the Tārā Dhāraṇī one hundred and eight times over a madana fruit, whomever one anoints with that fruit together with Hayagrīva becomes submissive.
There is yet another application: *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture, grant the release from bondage for [name], svāhā*. By means of this...
Having written the mantra interspersed with the name of the person to be accomplished on a leaf of the *arka* tree, one should conceal it in a hole dug in the earth;
thereby, liberation from bondage occurs.
Thus ends the Vajratārā-sādhana.
*Namo vajratārāyai*.
Having paid homage to Vajratārā, who has come down through the lineage of the gurus... (pdf 108, p. 189). [Note: This *sādhana* is found only in the Kh. manuscript; see folio 67a.]
Its means of accomplishment is clearly written by me for the sake of memory.

Seated in a comfortable posture in a place conducive to the mind, the yogi performs protection for the site, himself, and the yoga by reciting: *oṃ rakṣa rakṣa huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Then, having visualized the syllable *tāṃ* upon the moon at his heart, he draws forth the Blessed Lady Vajratārā together with her maṇḍala deities, possessing the arms and weapons to be described hereafter.
Having visualized [the field of merit] in space and honored it with flowers and other offerings:
"The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds;
I rejoice in the merit of the world; I direct my mind toward the enlightenment of a Buddha."

Having recited this, one should cultivate the meditations on loving-kindness and so forth. Thinking, "I must deliver all sentient beings from the suffering of saṃsāra and establish them in the state of Buddhahood, which is great bliss," one should meditate on emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
This very mind, being deluded, appears in various forms; just as in a dream, there is nothing to be grasped other than the mind itself.

Because there is no object to be grasped (*grāhya*), the mind also does not exist as a grasper (*grāhaka*); therefore, one should perceive this entire universe as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), pure by nature (*prakṛti-pariśuddha*), primordial, and unarisen. Thereafter, through the power of previous vows, that which has arisen in space is the nature of pure mundane consciousness (*śuddha-laukika-vijñāna*).

Having meditated on a solar disc arising from the syllable *ra*, and upon it, a white source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*) transformed from the black syllable *huṃ*— standing upright, triangular, hollow within,
and its center presided over by a universal lotus and a universal vajra— one [meditates] upon the universal vajra-altar.

One should meditate on the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). From the syllable *khaṃ* arises a yellow square earth mandala, marked at its corners with three-pronged vajras; above that, from the syllable *vaṃ*, arises a white water mandala.
Above that, one should visualize the fire-maṇḍala, which is circular and marked with the letter *ra*; it is triangular, with each corner marked by the letter *ra*.

Above that, one should visualize the wind-maṇḍala, transformed from the syllable *yaṃ*, shaped like a half-moon, marked at its two ends with fluttering banners, and smoke-colored. From the transformation of that [wind-maṇḍala], there arises the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*).
It consists of the five jewels, is square, has four doors, and is adorned with four archways;

it is decorated with necklaces, half-necklaces, ribbons, garlands, and strings of flowers; it is beautified by eight pillars, which are topped by circular bands and encircled by rows of vajras; and it contains five central chambers at the doors, as well as below and above.

The universal lotus. There, upon the central seat, by the transformation of the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, there is a moon mandala whose nature is mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); above that, by the thirty-four consonants beginning with *ka*, there is a sun mandala; the unification of these two is the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). Above that, upon the pericarp of a blue lotus arising from the syllable *tāṃ*:

The syllable *Aṃ* situated upon the moon is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). Upon the entry of all the Tathāgatas, who have been drawn in by the rays of light from its seed-syllable, there arises the wisdom of performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). Following that, the manifestation of the Blessed Lady is the wisdom of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*). Thus, these five aspects [of awakening] occur precisely through the sequence of complete enlightenment.

One should contemplate that Blessed Lady as having arisen simultaneously with the ten deities, who are produced through the transformation of the seed-syllable and emblem emerging from the syllable *TĀṂ*; she is yellow in color, has four faces— yellow, black, red, and white— and eight arms, with her right hands holding a vajra, a noose, a conch, an arrow, and displaying the gesture of granting boons.

One should meditate on her holding a vajra-aṅkuśa, an utpala lotus, a bow, and a tarjanī mudrā in her left hands; adorned with all ornaments, embellished with a red radiance, in the full bloom of youth, seated in the vajraparyaṅka posture upon a viśvapadma seat, and wearing a crown of the five Tathāgatas.
On the eastern petal is white Puṣpatārā, born from the syllable Oṃ, with two arms, holding a garland of flowers, adorned with all ornaments, and [seated] on the syllable Tā in the south.

One should meditate on Dhūpatārā, black in color and holding a branch of incense, with the syllable *re* in the west; Dīpatārā, yellow in color and holding a lamp-stand, with the syllable *tu* in the north; and Gandhatārā, red in color and holding a scent-conch, with the syllable *ta* within the inner mandala. Furthermore, one should meditate on Aṅkuśatārā, holding a hook in her hand, with the syllable *re* in the south.

To the west, by means of the syllable *tu*, [one visualizes] Pāśatārā, black in color, holding a vajra-noose in her hand; to the north, by means of the syllable *re*, Āveśatārā, red in color, holding a bell in her hand; below, by means of the syllable *svā*, Sumbhatārā, black in color, holding a snake-noose in her hand; and above, by means of the syllable *hā*, Uṣṇīṣavijayatārā, yellow in color.
One should meditate upon her as holding a wheel.

Thereafter, having visualized the syllable *tāṃ* within the moon at the heart of the Jñānasattva—which has arisen from the transformation of the seed-syllable and emblem situated upon the moon at one's own heart—one should summon the mandala of wisdom with its rays and worship it with the mantra: *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*.

One should perform the acts of summoning, entering, binding, and pleasing. Thereafter, the six deities beginning with Mohavajrā are to be visualized in the eyes and other sense organs; and Khecarī, Bhūcarī, and Nairātmā, transformed from the syllables Oṃ, Āḥ, and Hūṃ, are to be visualized in the body, speech, and mind. Following that, one should visualize the Tathāgatas summoned by the rays of light from the seed-syllable in the heart.
Having performed worship, one should pray for the consecration: "May all the Tathāgatas consecrate me.

One is then consecrated by those Tathāgatas with vases filled with the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*). As they are being consecrated, the Conquerors of the consecration (*abhiṣekajina*) arise upon their heads. Among them, Ratnasambhava [arises] for the Blessed Lady, and [the respective Buddhas arise] for Puṣpatārā and the others in due order.
Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi are [the lords] of Aṅkuśā, Tārā, and the others as well.
For the downward-facing deity and the upward-facing deity, one should worship Akṣobhya and Vairocana with flowers and other offerings emanating from the seed-syllables at their hearts,
praise them with the lute and other instruments, and having presented what has been offered by Rasavajrā and the others, [worship] each individually.

Having accomplished the welfare of the world through emanation that continues until exhaustion, one should contemplate the flowers and other offerings being established in sequence within the heart of the Bhagavatī. (Bhagavatyāḥ, p.

Furthermore, by means of the yoga of vibration (*sphuraṇa*), having perceived the entire universe as being like an illusion, like a dream, and dependent upon one's own thoughts, one should meditate on the establishment [of the deity] within the seed-syllable of one's own heart. Thereafter, having meditated on that seed-syllable—appearing as a mass of rays, gradually dissolved, in the form of a subtle drop (*bindu*), and consisting of great bliss—one should render even that non-perceptible. Immediately thereafter, one should cultivate the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras)—namely, those designated as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—according to the sequence to be described. In that regard, what is this loving-kindness?

It is characterized by the love one feels for an only son toward all sentient beings, or it takes the form of bringing about their welfare and happiness. Furthermore, what is compassion like? It is the desire to rescue [beings] from suffering and the causes of suffering—those creatures who have entered the iron house of saṃsāra, which is ablaze with the great fire of the three types of suffering—from that very place.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) is either the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) "I shall deliver [them]," or the desire to rescue from the ocean of *saṃsāra* those beings who are afflicted by the three types of suffering. Joy (*muditā*), however, is as follows: joy is gladness;
or rather, it is the thought, "May all wandering beings in *saṃsāra* [attain] such Buddhahood and its means, which are beyond compare."

The resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is that they should be established [in the Dharma]; it is *muditā* (sympathetic joy), or rather, it is the state of having a mind drawn toward all beings' roots of virtue as well as their enjoyments, sovereignty, and so forth. What is *upekṣā* (equanimity)?
It is the abandonment of the bonds of aversion and attachment toward sentient beings, whether they are harmful or beneficial.

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the practice of supreme benefit; or rather, it is the spontaneous flow of activity toward the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) that consists in the welfare of others, free from all attachment and latent tendencies; or else—

Through the cultivation of the true path, that [defilement] would be ceased. Therefore, all [phenomena] are pure by nature.
