Always staying at a solitary linga, in a cremation ground, or in an empty house,
the yogi should accomplish the vidyā that brings liberation from the three worlds.
Seated upon a soft *masūraka* cushion or resting on other tender seats, one should accomplish the supreme siddhi.
Having become well-composed through the yoga of instantaneous visualization, one should meditate upon the triple vajra in the three places and then radiate forth rays of light.
One should again bring forth those beings wandering in the three realms of existence who were previously illuminated;
then, during the withdrawal, one should meditate once more on the entire universe as empty in every respect.
Then one should recite the mantra of the Jina: *oṃ śūnyatādisvabhāvaka*.
Thereafter, one should meditate on the intermediate space and, from the syllable *āḥ*, a red lotus.
Furthermore, one should meditate above that upon the syllable *ṭāṃ*, from which arises a lotus vessel;
in the center of that, one should again meditate on the syllable *huṃ*, resembling the color blue.
Then one should visualize a curved knife (*kartṛkā*) born from the syllable *huṃ*, adorned with the seed-syllable.
One should meditate upon oneself as transformed by that curved knife, equal to Tāriṇī.
She stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, formidable, adorned with a long garland of severed heads;
she is short-statured with a pendulous belly, terrifying, and radiant with blue lotuses.
She has three eyes and one face, divine, radiant with a terrible loud laugh,
exceedingly joyful, mounted upon a corpse,
and adorned with eight serpents.
With round red eyes, her waist wrapped in a tiger skin,
endowed with fresh youth, and adorned with the five mudrās.
With a lolling tongue, exceedingly terrifying, and fearsome with prominent fangs;
holding a sword and a curved knife in her right hands, and bearing a blue lotus and a skull-cup in her left.
One should meditate upon her with a single tawny, fierce matted lock, adorned at the crown of her head by Akṣobhya;
through the perfection of this meditation on the immovable, the yogi becomes a great poet.
Even one who is dull-witted, if he is a fool yet devoted to the flavor of meditative cultivation,
shall obtain charming speech by reciting a hundred thousand mantras.
This three-syllabled great mantra, ending with the syllable *huṃ*, abides in the heart;
endowed with five rays of light, it is the burner of the fuel of ignorance.
I shall describe the procedure for its door according to the practice of the Yogācāras:
first,
having placed the letter following Ha (Ya), adorned with the fourth vowel (Ī).
One should then place the syllable *traṃ* (or *uṃ*), mounted upon the letter *repha*, throbbing and radiant, joined with the lunar drop (*bindu*), and adorned with the fourth vowel.
One should again join the syllable *haṃ* endowed with the long vowel *ā*;
then one should add the syllable *haṃ*, whereby the mantra is perfected in its entirety.
Having meditated upon the garland of rays devoid of the sun in the place of the sword,
the wise one should recite the supreme mantra by means of the vibrating process of withdrawal.
With a steady mind, the wise one should imagine himself as a great poet;
through the practice of constant cultivation, this certainly comes to pass—of this there is no doubt.
Whatever merit has been accumulated by me through composing this *sādhana* of Tārā,
may all living beings thereby become wise scholars within the teaching of the Jina.
This work, which accomplishes wisdom, is by Śāśvatavajra;
may the profound scholars and virtuous ones here deign to forgive it.
The *Mahācīnakramatārāsādhana* is completed.
Homage to Sitatārā!
Having meditated as before up to the point of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Seated in the center of a white lotus, she rests upon a lunar throne;
she is bound in the vajra-paryaṅka posture and holds the gesture of granting boons and a blue utpala lotus.
Having the form of an autumn moonbeam, seated upon a moon at her back,
fully adorned with all ornaments, and possessing the physical appearance of a sixteen-year-old.
Having meditated on Noble Tārā in one's heart, one should visualize her wheel, white in luster,
consisting of eight squares and completely filled with eight syllables.

With a one-pointed mind and firm resolve, one should meditate for six months upon the navel [of the deity], wherein the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*)— preceded by *oṃ* and *hāḥ*— is situated in the middle of the consonants.
One should recite this ten-syllable mantra with an undaunted mind.
In this regard, the mantra is: Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā.
One who meditates on the heart-cakra of Tārā shall not be stained by the defects of death;
and being devoted to that, within the limit of six months, one shall become a possessor of all siddhis.
The Sadhana of Tārā for Deceiving Death.
One who meditates on the heart-cakra of Tārā shall remain unstained by the defects of death (pdf 120, p. 213). [In some versions: unstained by the faults of mantras.]
And one who is devoted to that for the duration of six months shall obtain all siddhis.
By the command of Vāgīśvara, from the *Mṛtyuvañcana-saṃgraha*,
this meditation on Sitatārā, which destroys all fear, has been extracted.
Having seen her in the sky, radiant with the formless splendor of the four *gargas* and others,
seated upon a white lotus and the moon, one should recite the "Three Refuges" (*triśaraṇa*) once more.
For a moment, one should contemplate emptiness in order to eliminate the superimpositions of ordinary perception;
thereafter, by the power of that very nature, the bodhicitta becomes immutable.
Seated upon a moon-disc throne situated in the center of a white lotus,
she sits in the vajra-paryaṅka posture and holds a varada-mudrā and an utpala lotus.
Having the form of the autumnal moonbeams, seated upon the moon at her back,
fully adorned with all ornaments, and possessing the body of a sixteen-year-old.

Having meditated upon Noble Tārā in one's heart— the mother of all the perfectly awakened Buddhas and their sons, whose abode is desire-form (kāmarūpa)— one should visualize her wheel as having white radiance.
The eight-square grid is filled with eight syllables;
it has the syllable *oṃ* at the center, with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) placed between the vowels and consonants, starting from the navel.
With a one-pointed mind and firm resolve, one should meditate for six months;
with an undaunted heart, one should recite this ten-syllable mantra.
Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, one should subsequently employ *tāre*.
After *tuttāre* comes *ture*, ending with *svāhā*; this is the mantra for all purposes.
Even one whose hair-tips remain unbroken conquers death like a liberated soul, [empowered] by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Candra, Arka, Rudra, the Directions, Time, and Manmatha.
It brings about the destruction of wrinkles, grey hair, misfortune, disease, and poverty;
it is the destroyer of the mass of sufferings arising from the eight great fears, such as lions and other dangers.
The acquisition, without asking, of garments, drinks, food, celestial chariots, jewels, and so forth;
as well as the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as the sword, collyrium, foot-ointment, the auspicious jar (bhadra-kumbha), and others.
Poetic skill, eloquence, intelligence, and utterly pure wisdom,
as well as other desired accomplishments, arise from this wheel;
it is the practice of Sitatārā that destroys death and disease.
By whatever merit has been extracted from this, may she herself become the savior of the world.
The Sadhana of Sitatārā for Deceiving Death [Sitatārā]

As before, immediately after emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth, there is Mount Sumeru composed of various jewels, transformed from the syllable *suṃ*. One should meditate on her bestowing boons joined with a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇiratna*), fulfilling the hopes of all sentient beings, and holding a cluster of blue lotuses in her left hand. To her right side is Mārīcī, yellow in color, seated upon a moon, wearing blue garments, and having two arms; she holds a sprout of red *aśoka* in her left hand and [a jewel] in her right.

Having thus visualized [Tārā], who holds a white chowrie in her right hand and a white chowrie in her left, wearing a red bodice and ornaments; and on her left side Mahāmāyūrī, dark as a priyaṅgu flower, two-armed, holding a peacock feather in her left hand and a chowrie in her right—[one should recite]: *Oṃ bhagavati tāre*...
“O Tārā, enter my heart, svāhā!”—with this, one should empower oneself. Then, one should recite the mantra: Oṃ namas tāre manohare huṃ hare svāhā.
The Sadhana of White Tārā.

Likewise, immediately after the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one should visualize a sun disk transformed from the syllable *raṃ*, upon which stands the syllable *huṃ*; this transforms into a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), from which arise the vajra-fence and other protections. In the center of that—

Upon a lotus born from the syllable *paṃ* [according to *k*: a vajra-lotus], on a moon disc born from the syllable *a*, one should visualize a white *huṃ* syllable from which arises a blue utpala lotus with its seed-syllable. Following the radiation of light from that and so forth, one should visualize the Blessed Lady White Tārā, transformed from that [seed-syllable], having three faces and six arms, with her right and left faces yellow and blue respectively, and each face—

She has three eyes; her three right hands hold the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), a rosary (*akṣasūtra*), and an arrow; her three left hands hold a blue lotus (*utpala*), a red lotus (*padma*), and a bow; she sits in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*);
she rests on a moon-seat and possesses moon-like radiance; and Amitābha resides in her crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmukuṭa*).

Having visualized oneself as her, with a head adorned by five skulls and a crescent moon serving as a crest-ornament, wearing various ornaments, having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, and standing in the midst of the eight cremation grounds; and having visualized one's own seed-syllable situated upon the moon at the heart—one should recite the mantra: *oṃ acale animittavare huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. (One *phaṭ* is omitted).

*In kh] svāhā*. For one who recites this for one month at the four junctions of the day (*catuḥsandhyā*) preceded by worship through the *poṣadha* vow, pacification (*śāntika*) and other rites will be accomplished.
This concludes the *Ṣaḍbhujaśuklatārāsādhana* (The Sadhana of Six-Armed White Tārā).

217) Homage to Jāṅgulītārā!
Having bowed to the Blessed Lady Tārā, who assumes the form of Jāṅgulī...
For the sake of compassion toward sentient beings, its accomplishment is here written down.

First of all, the practitioner, being pure and having bathed, wearing white garlands and garments, seated on a comfortable seat in a secluded, well-smeared place sprinkled with fragrant white water and strewn with a scattering of white flowers, should cultivate loving-kindness and compassion toward the world and recite: *Oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ*.

One should recite: "All phenomena are pure by nature; I am [pure by nature]. Then, having brought emptiness before one's mind, one should contemplate a white hundred-petaled lotus born from the syllable *paṃ*, and upon it, a white moon disc born from the syllable *a*, and upon that, the white syllable *hrīḥ*, emitting a multitude of shimmering rays of light.

Therefore, one should meditate upon the Blessed Lady Jāṅgulī as white in color, four-armed, wearing a crown of matted hair, clad in white garments, adorned with white jewel ornaments, and decorated with white serpents; she sits in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, playing the lute with her two primary hands.
One should meditate on her holding a white serpent and the *abhaya* mudrā with her second left and right hands,
adorned with a garland of moonbeams; and one should visualize the syllables *āḥ*,
*hrīḥ*, and *huṃ* situated upon moon-maṇḍalas at the head, throat, between the breasts, and the navel.

One should perform the visualization until exhaustion. Thereafter, one should recite the mantra: *hrīḥ*. One should recite it seven hundred thousand times and offer seventy thousand oblations of white flowers while wearing white ornaments. Then, one becomes like Garuḍeśvara in power, a poet, and an expert in all treatises.
The *Āryajāṅgulītārāsādhana* is completed.
Homage to Noble Tārā!
Tārā is green, with one face, four arms, and two eyes; she is pleased by praise.
[The hymn to the two-eyed one, satisfied with praise]: In whose maṇḍala-circle there are twelve goddesses who possess two eyes.
I shall briefly proclaim the practice for the attainment of the Lord of Wealth (Dhanada), which is a most rare and distinguished mantra of the Blessed Noble Tārā.

In the morning, having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), the yogi—having performed the purification of the mouth and other rites—visualizes a green syllable *tāṃ* upon a moon disc at his own heart. Having recited, "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature;
I am pure by nature," he then recites, "Oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ."

Having dispelled the obstacles of the ten directions with various showers of nectar-sprays, one should visualize one's own seed-syllable situated upon a moon born from the syllable *A* atop a red lotus born from the syllable *Paṃ* in one’s own heart; then, one should [visualize] the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas residing in the sky, drawn forth by its rays.
Having performed worship, confessed one's misdeeds, and so forth, and having meditated upon and blessed emptiness,
one should visualize before oneself a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) arisen from a black syllable *hūṃ* situated upon a sun disc produced from a red syllable *repha*;
then, by means of the vajras of its rays, one should visualize a vajra-fence, a vajra-canopy, and a vajra-ground.

One should meditate as follows: Then, upon a pedestal of crossed vajras (*viśvavajra*), on a red lotus born from the syllable *paṃ*, and situated upon a moon disk born from the syllable *a*, one sees a white wheel transformed from the syllable *bhrūṃ* with the syllable *bhrūṃ* in its center.
Upon that lotus and moon, one visualizes [the deity] born from the transformation of the seed-syllable of the wheel, consisting of all jewels.

It is endowed with qualities such as being square and so forth, consisting of two enclosures, and adorned with nine moons within the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus situated in the inner enclosure; it is radiant with four suns located at the four gates.
One should visualize a gabled pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). Then, upon the central moon, one should visualize that very syllable *TĀṂ* (or *AṂ* according to manuscript *k*).

From that, there is the radiation and reabsorption [of light]. Then, from that seed-syllable, one should meditate upon oneself as the Blessed Lady Tārā, possessing the radiance of a moon-seat, gentle, and seated in the sattva-paryaṅka posture.

[Visualize her as] greenish-black, with one face, two eyes, and four arms, holding a rosary, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), a blue lotus, and a book, and adorned with variegated garments and ornaments. Then: *Oṃ* on the head;
*Tā* on the forehead; *Re* on the two eyes; *Tu* on the throat; *Ttā* on the two arms; *Re* on the heart.
One should place *re* at the navel, *svā* at the secret place, *hā* on the two knees, and [the remaining syllables] on the two feet.

Then, one should meditate on oneself as being consecrated by the goddesses Locanā and the others—impelled by the rays of light from one’s own seed-syllable situated upon a moon-disc within a lotus at the heart—and wearing a crown of Amoghasiddhi. Alternatively, having instantly visualized the goddesses Vajratārā and the rest upon the moons within the [five] cavities, afterwards...
One should visualize: in the east, Vajratārā, black, holding a vajra in her hand;

in the south, Ratnatārā, yellow, holding a jewel in her hand; in the west, Padmatārā, holding a red lotus in her hand; in the north, Buddhatārā, white, holding a wheel; and in the southeast corner, Puṣpatārā, white, holding a garland of flowers; in the southwest corner...
In the northwest corner is Dhūpatārā, black in color, holding an incense burner in her hand; in the northeast corner is Dīpatārā, yellow in color, holding a lamp-stand;

and [in the southeast] is Gandhatārā, red in color, holding a scent-conch. These eight [deities] possess the luster of the moon, sit upon living beings in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, and rest upon moons situated on the petals of a universal lotus.

Holding blue lotuses in their left hands, with smiling faces, and wearing various ornaments and garments; at the eastern gate is Vajrāṅkuśī, black, holding a vajra-hook in her hand; in the south is Vajrapāśī, yellow, holding a vajra-noose in her hand; in the west is Vajrasphoṭā, red, holding a vajra-chain; and in the north—
One should visualize a white vajra-bell with a vajra-bell in her hand;
these [deities] should be seen upon the suns at the four gates, possessing solar radiance. (pdf 124, p. 220)

[The goddesses] have tawny hair blazing upwards, stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, are adorned with serpents, have distorted faces, wear tiger-skin garments, and hold blue lotuses in their left hands. Then, having unified them with the *jñānasattva*, one should contemplate with an unwavering mind the extremely subtle seed-syllable of oneself situated within the lotus of one's own heart. Then, one should recite the mantra.

Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture, give me wealth, svāhā! Then, at the time of rising, having offered the bali with the mantra beginning "Oṃ, the letter A is the mouth... and so forth, using the utpala-mudrā, and having made the aspiration (praṇidhi), one should dissolve the circle of deities into one's own seed-syllable.
Incorporating the recitation (*japa*) and so forth, one should dwell at ease while maintaining the ego-identification (*ahaṅkāra*) with one’s own deity.

At the midday and evening junctions (*saṃdhyā*), however, one should instantly manifest the mandala of deities from the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in one’s own heart and perform meditation, recitation, and so forth as before. [At the evening and midday junctions...]
Furthermore, this is the specific distinction: having worshipped the gnosis-maṇḍala with flowers and other offerings, one should dismiss it with the mantra *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture muḥ*.
This concludes the *Sādhana* of Dhanadatārā.
Homage to the Three Jewels!
Homage to the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Great Compassionate One; homage to Tārā!

Namely: Oṃ tāre tāraya huṃ huṃ huṃ! O you who abide by the pledge (samayasthite), O bearer (bhara)! O you adorned with all ornaments! O lotus, O lotus, O you whose arms are like lotuses, O you who are seated upon the lotus throne! Laugh, laugh! O you who grant boons to the three worlds, O you worshipped by all gods and dānavas! Remember! (smarāhi)
In the presence of the Blessed Tathāgata, maintain the pledge: *dhara dhara mahāsattvāvalokite maṇikanakavicitrābharaṇe oṃ vilokaya bhagavati tāre hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
This is the root mantra; one should recite it one thousand and eight times at a reliquary containing relics (*sadhātuka-caitya*). Then, when that is complete—

One beholds the Blessed Noble Tārā and obtains whatever boon one desires. By reciting "Oṃ Maṇitāre Hūṃ" one hundred thousand times, the Noble Lady appears before one and grants everything that is wished for. Success is achieved through mere recitation alone, without the need for mandalas, ritual bathing, or fasting. All activities [are accomplished].
And thus he establishes that it must be performed.
The section on the ritual manual of the Blessed Noble Tārā, as found in the *Amitābhagarbha-tantra*, is completed.

This is a brief ritual procedure for the Blessed Lady Tārā, who wears a garland of flowers.
For the sake of destroying all ignorance, that which arises from it should always be practiced.

Having bathed with the application of mantra-water, one should remain in a clean, pleasant place provided with the requisites for worship, or even in a place merely visualized as such in their absence.
Facing east, the yogi, with a mind intent on the welfare of others,
should visualize the Goddess seated upon a white lotus and moon, endowed with a multitude of manifold virtues.
At the border, one should worship Bhakta Nāgasambhūta, whose bodily splendor is adorned with fresh youth and white as the light of the autumn moon,
and whose eyes are like the petals of a blue lotus.
Her slender body was resplendent with earrings, necklaces, and armlets, accompanied by girdles and the tinkling of anklets; her pair of breasts were beautiful with garlands of pearls.
Clad in decorated fine silk garments, with eyebrows as captivating as a bow adorned with blue lotuses for ears,
she removes the mental afflictions, verbal faults, and visual sins of all sentient beings through her contemplation, speech, and gaze.
Thus she is beautiful, bearing a charming mass of matted hair in the center of which is the Buddha Amitābha, her head adorned with a golden band thickened by a network of jewel-rays.

One should generate the sense of identity, thinking: "I am she who is the Blessed Lady; she who is the Blessed Lady is I. In all instances of the ritual procedure for worship, it should not be performed by means of noble action (*āryakarma*) alone, but through the application of the method of mantra (*mantranīti*), which is the empowerment of the mantra. And this [practice] should be performed at the three junctions of the day and at all times by one who is constantly bathed, who has taken up the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and who is intent upon changing his garments three times a day.
The practitioner, who avoids the ten unwholesome actions and strives with a mind intent upon the complete exhaustion of all unwholesome factors, should meditate continuously (p.
Until that Blessed Lady herself appears; and in this regard, the instruction must serve as the instrument for shattering the dense mass of the net of the darkness of the heart.
It is as follows: upon a circle marked by the deer-marked one (the moon) in the center of the *ali-gupta* [triangle], there is the seed-syllable of Māyā, bearing a stream of nectar.

One should meditate for a long time with a steady mind upon that [syllable], which resembles the pure sun, situated at the level of the wind-mandala below it, blazing intensely with a radiance equal to ten million suns of the seed-syllable of reality (*tattvabīja*), completely purifying the darkness of all delusion extending through the ten directions from its very root, and being bathed by streams of nectar flowing down from the seed-syllable at the crown of the head.

Then, being weary, the yogi should meditate on the seed-syllable according to the guru’s instruction within the red lotus-petal of the tongue; then, visualizing the garland of mantras emerging [from it],

drawing in the power of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs, as well as the nectar of the Tathāgata’s gnosis, and seeing it enter the pit of the stomach, pervade the lower parts, and rise up again, he should recite the mantra.

If he performs it in this manner, then he immediately experiences great results. Likewise, if he practices for seven days and nights with firm meditation, then he becomes highly wise, eloquent, clever, one whose speech flows in verse, a knower of numerical systems, and one who composes prose and verse continuously without interruption; he is able to speak Sanskrit effortlessly.

Now, the composition of the praise is described: there was a great scholar named the venerable Sarvajñamitra, whose mind was possessed by the feet of the Blessed Lady Tārā, and who was the preeminent ornament among the circle of wise men in Kaśmīra; by him [this was composed].

Even from my mouth, though fallen into distress, having propitiated that very Blessed Noble Tārā with a mind intent on the desire for death, with my gaze fixed upwards and my palms joined in reverent salutation,
O Mother, become a *sragdharā* garland for me, a poor man of feeble merit.

Having made the aspiration, "May I obtain the lotus feet of the Blessed Lady even in a future birth," he offered this [hymn] to the Blessed Lady; thus, the name *Sragdharā* became appropriate for her. Furthermore, because this hymn was composed in the *sragdharā* meter, the name *Sragdharā* was bestowed upon the Blessed Lady after that [meter].

In this regard, a practitioner who is a *vidyādhara* and desires to directly realize the *prajñāpāramitā* should, for half a month, perform the previously described ritual procedure three times daily;

observing all the previously mentioned vows and conducts with a single-minded focus, he should incessantly and uninterruptedly praise the Blessed Lady in a solitary place. Regarding that, the instruction is as follows:

At the time of recitation, having placed the seed-syllables of Tattva, Śakti, and Māyā respectively upon the Ātmarī, the Mūla, and the tips of the Avals, one should think: "I am indeed bathed by the rays of light flashing forth from the three times through the knowledge of the Blessed Lady."
By whatever merit has been gained from this composition of the *Sragdharā* hymn to Tārā, performed with great care and devotion,
may the entire world quickly become like the Saviouress herself.
The ritual procedure for the hymn of praise to Sragdharā is completed.
Having bowed with devotion to Tāriṇī, who increases all prosperity,
her sādhana is now written down in brief according to the tradition.

First of all, the yogin, having entered a delightful meditation chamber adorned with fragrant perfumes, flowers, and so forth, sits upon a comfortable seat in the full-lotus posture (paryaṅka) and visualizes a moon disc transformed from the syllable *a* within his own heart, with the yellow seed-syllable *tāṃ* upon it.
Having beheld the wheel of the Blessed Lady in the space before him, drawn by those rays,
one should emanate the goddesses of the flowers and other offerings from the seed-syllable in one's own heart and perform worship with the flowers and other articles.
...one should perform [the ritual]. Then, in front of that very wheel of the Bhagavatī, one should carry out the confession of sins and so forth:
"I confess all my own sins before all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Noble Ones, and ordinary beings."

I rejoice in all merit; and I dedicate all my own merit toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. From this moment until awakening, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost among two-legged beings; I go for refuge to the Dharma, the complete Mahāyāna.

I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the assembly of irreversible bodhisattvas. Oh, may I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake, benefit, and happiness of all sentient beings, until they reach the ultimate end in the realm of nirvāṇa.

And for the purpose of establishing them in the enlightenment of a Buddha, I take recourse in this path of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, namely, the Vajrayāna. Then, one should recite the verses on the three refuges. Thereafter, one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which has the aspect of bestowing happiness upon all sentient beings, and compassion (*karuṇā*), which has the aspect of removing all suffering.

One should cultivate sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which has the aspect of the certainty of non-separation from divine bliss; and equanimity (*upekṣā*), which has the aspect of bringing forth the path that serves as the antidote to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Then, having mentally apprehended all phenomena, one should investigate them: "This is merely the mind itself, deluded by various such aspects."

It appears as follows: just as in a dream there is no external mind apart from the mind itself—because of the absence of an external object to be grasped, the mind itself becomes the grasper—therefore all phenomena have the mind as their essence.
Having thus determined with absolute certainty that their ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the emptiness of subject and object, one [abandons] that which is superimposed by delusion.
Having abandoned the aspect of all phenomena, which is the mark of delusion, one perceives their nature alone,
characterized solely by non-dual representation.
One should perceive [it] as infinite, resembling pure crystal and like the cloudless midday sky.
This is called supramundane gnosis of emptiness (*lokottara-śūnyatājñāna*), free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
Then, one should consecrate it with the mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako 'ham*. She herself is the Blessed Lady.

That very perfection of wisdom is the supreme protection. Therefore, one should meditate upon the formal protection that is its natural outflow, which has the nature of pure mundane knowledge. Then, having visualized the sun in front by means of the syllable *repha*, one should visualize a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) arising from the syllable *huṃ* within that sun.
With that very same vajra, one should visualize a wall and a binding vajra-cage;
having radiated in all directions with the rays of the universal vajra— unbearable like the fire of cosmic destruction— and having become dense,
one constructs a blazing vajra-wall extending crosswise and square, a vajra-cage above, and a foundation made of vajra below.

One should visualize the ground fashioned down to the netherworld (pātāla). Then, having become rays of light through the sun and the universal vajra (*viśvavajra*), they radiate out into the ten directions;

becoming solidified, the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) is to be performed at the outer gate—this is the meaning of the verse. In the center of that is the so-called *dharmodayā*, which has the nature of the great element of space.
The nature of Mahāvajradhara is white as the autumnal moon, subtle at the bottom and broad at the top,

triangular in shape, and having the character of the internal space; in its center is a vast universal vajra situated upon the pericarp of a multi-petalled universal lotus, and upon its pedestal are the four great elements.

One should visualize the four mandalas, which have the nature of the four goddesses, one above the other. Therein, first, by means of the syllable *yaṃ*, there is the northwest mandala, bow-shaped, smoke-colored, with two ends marked by fluttering banners; then, by means of the syllable *raṃ*, the southeast mandala, triangular, with its corners red.
Then, with the syllable *vaṃ*, there is the circular Varuṇa-maṇḍala marked by a white water-jar; then, with the syllable *laṃ*, there is the square Mahendra-maṇḍala.
In the corners, there are yellow triple-pronged vajras; above them, the practitioner should now visualize a wheel born from the syllable *bhrūṃ*.

This is the supramundane gnosis itself, abiding as the all-pervading nature. From that arises a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) in the center of the pedestal, produced through the transformation of the four great elements.
The completely pure buddha-field, in its condensed form, is the great city of liberation, a gabled palace composed of various jewels, having the nature of Vairocana—
quadrangular, with four gates, and adorned with eight pillars.
[It was] surrounded by pillars, enclosed by the four Vedas, and adorned with four archways.
Adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, silk bands, garlands, canopies, mirrors, and yak-tail whisks;
with radiant vajra-threads and the shimmering light of the Buddhas' enlightenment; with the quarters of the sky made resonant by the bells at the tips of swaying, variegated banners;
and gladdening through the supreme offerings of the five objects of desire—this double-layered pavilion.

One should meditate on one [triangle] with its filaments, and the other is said to be a triangle; in the center of that is the moon transformed from the syllable *dviguṇāli*, above which is a vajra transformed from the syllable *tāṃ*, and within its hub is the syllable *tāṃ*. Beyond that as well—
The sun is transformed by doubling the syllables *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *da*, *dha*, and *ya*, and by doubling the syllable *kāli*.
The union of these two is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the supreme joy (*paramānanda*).
The moon possesses mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); it is that same extent, the forty-nine-fold.
Observation by means of the seed-syllables and the signs of one's own deity is taught;
the performance of the unity of all [deities] is the accomplishment, which is the state of pure reality (*śuddhadharmatā*).

Thus is awakening through the five aspects. Having drawn in sentient beings with the rays of light from its seed-syllable and likewise caused them to enter the maṇḍala of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), the yogin should visualize the goddess Tārā as the transformation of the sign and the seed-syllable (pdf 128, p.
She has eight arms and four faces, adorned with all ornaments;
she resembles the color of gold, is auspicious, and shines with the characteristics of a maiden.
She wears the great crown of four Buddhas, born from the Vajra-sūrya consecration;
she possesses the beauty of fresh youth, with swaying golden earrings.
Seated upon a universal lotus, adorned with a red radiance,
she holds a vajra-noose and a conch, while her right hand brandishes an arrow.
Holding a vajra-hook and an utpala lotus in his left hands, along with a bow and a threatening gesture,
the yogin who is the very essence of Vajratārā has reached the further shore of the welfare of all sentient beings.
One should accomplish the three worlds through the yoga of the vajra-paryaṅka posture;
to the east is Puṣpatārā, white in color and beautiful.
She is perfected from the wisdom of the syllable Oṃ, her hands are busy with a garland of flowers;
she has two arms, one face, and is adorned with all ornaments.
To the south, however, is Dhūpatārā, black in color and beautiful in form,
her hands busily occupied with a branch of incense, and adorned with all ornaments.
In the west, one should visualize Dīpatārā, her hands busily holding a lamp-stand,
yellow in color, adorned with magnificent ornaments, and wearing swaying golden earrings.
In the north,
one should visualize the goddess Gandhatārā within the womb-maṇḍala, resembling red in color and holding a scent-conch in her hand.
Then one should meditate upon the female gatekeepers, distinguished by [their attributes] such as the goad (Aṅkuśī) and so forth:
she who stands in the center of a solar disc, white in color and beautiful, holding a goad in her right hand and making a threatening gesture toward the wicked with her left.
Aṅkuśī (holds) a noose in her right hand, while with her left she makes the threatening gesture toward the wicked. (pdf 128, p. 229)
She stands in the center of a red maṇḍala, fair-complexioned and enchanting.

One should visualize Pāśinī— [Yoginī according to k and ḍh]— red in color, standing in the center of a vajra-maṇḍala, with her right hand making the *sphoṭa* gesture and her left hand holding a raised index finger (*tarjanī*).
Vajrasphoṭā,
with her left hand occupied in holding a vajra-bell and making the threatening gesture at the wicked,
stands in the midst of a circle of rays, resembling a red utpala lotus.
The vajra-bell; in the corner sections, there are four symbols according to the ritual application:
the Bodhicitta-vase, Mount Meru, the fire-pit, and the great banner.
And above is Uṣṇīṣavijayā, white in color and of beautiful form;
she holds a vajra (or wheel) in her right hand, and with her left hand she makes the threatening gesture against the wicked.
One should visualize Sumbhā below, black in color and most terrible, holding a serpent-noose in her right hand and making a threatening gesture with her left.
Then, having meditated, one should recite the mantra while vibrating it: *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā*.
By means of these ten syllables, the ten deities who are the basis of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) should be cultivated through practice for the sake of accomplishing all activities.
One should place Mohavajrā in the eyes, Dveṣavajrā in the ears,
Īrṣyāvajrā in the nose, and Rāgavajrī in the mouth.
In the case of touch, one should indeed [visualize] Sparśamātsaryavajrā, who removes the darkness of all afflictions.
She is to be known in the sense-bases as the heart-pleasing Yoginī of Selflessness.
Thus is the locus of the eyes and so forth.
And the women should have two arms and one face, yet possess various forms.
With their hands busily occupied by tridents and skull-bowls, they stand upright with their life-breaths departed.
Then follows the consecration of body, speech, and mind:
"Oṃ! This great vajra is the ornament of the vajra-body.
Huṃ! The vajra-mind, the vajra-delusion, abides in the state of Vajrasattva."
The syllable ĀḤ is considered the supreme reality, both external and the opener [of the path that obstructs speech].
One should place it, consisting of gnosis, in the heart of all the Mothers.
Through the application of the knowledge of the *sattva*, one shall attain the awakening of a Buddha;
the conceptualization of the insignia of the mudrā arises from the syllables of one's own mantra.
Having performed the emanation and reabsorption,
one should meditate on the mandala of gnosis arising from the midst of the space-element.
One should worship with all forms of worship and honor that which is strewn with the qualities of the five wisdoms and manifests in various forms on all sides; one should not neglect it.
By means of the application of the female gatekeeper, one should accomplish the ocean of gnosis;
having caused the intensely radiant wheel of gnosis to enter the wheel of commitment,
the yogi becomes equal to all Buddhas and non-dual in an instant.
Oṃ vajrāṅkuśī ākarṣaya jaḥ | Oṃ vajrapāśī praveśaya huṃ | Oṃ vajrasphoṭa bandhaya vaṃ | Oṃ vajrāveśe vaśīkuru hoḥ | (pdf 129, p. 231)
Having drawn in the Buddhas residing in the three realms with rays of light in the form of hooks issuing from the seed-syllable in one's own heart,
and having honored them with the eight Mothers, he supplicates them: "May all the Tathāgatas consecrate me!"
Just as the great festival was bestowed by Bodhivajra upon all the Buddhas, so too,
for the sake of my protection, O Khavajra, [bestow this] today.
Ḍha: O Khavajra, grant this to me!
Thus is the request for initiation:
"I bestow the great vajra initiation, which is venerated by the three realms and arises from the abode of the three secrets of all Buddhas."

Thus, one is consecrated by five vases held by Buddhas in the form of Heruka, who consist of the five Tathāgatas and contain the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). While being consecrated, a rain of flowers falls,
the sound of drums resounds, a rain of saffron occurs, and one is worshipped with vajra-songs by Rūpavajrā and the others.

While being consecrated by Locanā and the others, the Vajrasūrya arises upon the crown of the head. In the four directions of the crown are the Tathāgatas Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi; likewise, they appear respectively in the crowns of the four goddesses of the inner enclosure and also in those of the gatekeepers and of Uṣṇīṣā.
Ratneśa is on the crown of Sumbhā; Akṣobhya is [on the crown] of Kumbhā.
Homage to you, O Hatred-Vajrī; homage be to you, O Delusion-Vajrī.
O Avarice-Vajrī, protect me; O Passion-Vajrī, grant me [your grace].
O Great Minister, O Great Goddess, O All-Vajra, be gracious to me!
You are the Mistress of all Vajra Samayas and the accomplisher of all activities.
Praise: (pdf 130, p.
232) These flowers are auspicious, divine, pure, and born of purity.
Having accepted what has been offered by me with devotion, be gracious to me.
Flower:
This supreme incense, the essence of the forest tree, pleasing to the heart and rich in fragrance, has been offered by me with devotion; accepting it, be gracious unto me.
Incense— destructive of demons, purifying, dispeller of darkness, and auspicious to the mind—
I have offered this with devotion; accepting it, be gracious to me.
Lamp. These divine, auspicious, pure perfumes, born of purity, are offered by me with devotion; please accept them and be gracious to me.

Fragrance. Thereafter, upon a wind-maṇḍala marked with a bow and a banner, which has arisen from the transformation of the syllable *nīla-paṃ*, and above a triangular fire-maṇḍala produced from the seed-syllable *raṃ*— [red].

Having meditated upon the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*)— which are immeasurable and have the nature of the five Tathāgatas— and the five seeds known as *gokuṭa* and *dahana*, one should visualize, at a distance of one span above them,
a great white five-pronged vajra produced from the syllable *huṃ* situated upon a moon disk; below that...

Then, having visualized the syllable *oṃ*, one should see all that—impelled by the wind, by the fire of the *āgneya*-maṇḍala, and by the vajra-fire above—transformed. By the touch of its vapor, one should meditate on the *praṇava* melting into the vajra and becoming of one flavor (*samarasībhūta*) with that very nectar like butter (*navanīta*). Above that...
Having drawn in all the nectar existing within the belly of the three worlds by means of white-colored rays of light,
and having internalized it therein through the equality of the *dharmadhātu*, [one should contemplate].

Having drawn forth the nectar of gnosis residing in the hearts of all the Tathāgatas and having unified it with those very [deities], one should meditate on the three principles (tritattva) above that; having consecrated it with that same [mantra], one should meditate on the maṇḍala-circle within the heart of every member of the maṇḍala, and upon their tongues, [the syllable] *huṃ* born from a white [syllable].

Having meditated on a white vajra the size of a barley grain, one should satisfy the deities of the mandala and oneself with that five-nectar (pañcāmṛta). By this means, having performed the meditation at the three junctions of the day, one should remain once the mandala is accomplished. One should always abide in the form of the deity.
In this regard, the mantra for recitation is: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā*.
This supreme and most excellent mantra has been honored by all the Buddhas;
it brings swift accomplishment through mere recitation and was spoken within the Vajrapañjara.

Now, there is also another mantra of Dhāriṇī: Homage to the noble Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Great Compassionate One. It is as follows: Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture! For my sake, paralyze, immobilize, delude, and bind all the wicked and the extremely wicked! Huṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ! [The immobilizer of all the wicked.]

*Tāre svāhā*. The ritual procedure for the ten-syllable mantra: having consecrated the hem of a cloth seven times with this mantra and tied a knot, one cannot be overcome by anyone even while traveling in the Vindhya mountains.
Tigers, thieves, crocodiles, lions, snakes, elephants, buffaloes, bears, gavayas, and the like perish and dissolve by the mere recollection of the name.
With this mantra, one should offer one hundred and eight lotuses (*utpala*) into the fire. *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture [name]*.
"Bring [him] under my control, svāhā! Furthermore, having recited that same mantra thirty-two times over a crow’s wing feather, one should place it at the enemy's house.
If one conceals [the ritual], she will be expelled within seven days: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture cala pracala śīghrayāmini devadattam uccāṭaya hūṃ phaṭ*.
Now, there is another application as well: *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture amukābhidhānāṃ kumārīm*...
"May her father grant me through his speech, svāhā!
One should offer five thousand oblations of madana, caṇḍabīja, unmattaka, as well as aśoka leaves and flowers.
An oblation of ghee, honey, and molasses is praised for the attainment of a maiden;
then, within seven days, the yogi shall obtain the maiden of his desire.

Now, there is yet another application: *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture, summon [the one] named so-and-so from her own place into my presence! Jaḥ!* With this mantra, five thousand jujube thorns (*badarakaṇṭaka*) smeared with *svayambhū* flowers should be offered as oblations. By performing this, even kings [will be brought under one's power].
It attracts a maiden.

Furthermore, there is another practice: having drawn the Blessed Lady on a cloth stained with the menses—two-armed, one-faced, and holding a goad, a lotus, and a noose in her hands—and having performed worship before her...

One should worship with the words, "These flowers are auspicious and divine," and so forth. Afterwards, endowed with meditative visualization, one should recite the mantra: *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture, [Name] girl, tell me my desired dream in my ear! Hūṃ phaṭ!* She arrives after five thousand recitations. Having bound her by the throat with the noose (*pāśa*) and pierced her at the heart with the hook (*aṅkuśa*), [one summons her].
Having visualized the woman to be won over at the soles of one's feet, one should enjoy her in the form of a servant-girl.

Now, there is another practice as well: having consecrated the Tārādhāraṇī seven times, one should apply it as collyrium to one's two eyes. When entering the royal court, that king [will treat one] like a disciple.
Like a disciple, she shows respect; she does not speak what is contrary [to his will],
offers no negligence, speaks with endearing words, and submits to servitude— even when he is angry, she remains under his control.
Thus, the observed result will be truly effective.

Furthermore, there is another application: having recited the Tārā Dhāraṇī one hundred times, one should reduce a two-headed venomous serpent to ashes and prepare a wick with the ghee from a red-colored cow using a leaf of the Arka plant.

Having prepared and ignited [the lamp], one should let soot fall. That soot should be ground with Vajrasūrya and Vajradharma and fumigated with *paramānna*. One should apply it as collyrium to the eyes together with ashes. Whomever one sees with the eye of the Vajra—if she does not protect [him] from Padmanarteśvara, [he will] perish.
"Then I would not be Tārā, and the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, would have been slain by me.

Now, there is another application as well: having taken a young female bee that has not yet tasted [blood], one should empower it seven times with the Tārā Dhāraṇī; then, having combined the root of *bhṛṅgarāja* with *gorocanā*, [one should apply it] to the forehead.
Having applied a *tilaka* mark, one brings whoever one looks upon under one's control.

Furthermore, there is another application: having consecrated a "belly-worm" (*udarakīṭa*) seven times with the *Tārādhāraṇī*, one should give it to a maiden along with betel-leaf together with Vajradharma. Merely by its being consumed, [she is brought under control].
She does not leave her lord, the yogin; she finds no pleasure in another, she does not go to another, she desires no other man, and she abandons her own husband.
Furthermore, there is another practice: having anointed oneself with great oil, [one should recite] the Tārādhāraṇī...

One should recite the *dhārā*. One should recite it immeasurably and meditate upon it. At the conclusion of the recitation, having prepared a *śaṣkulikā* (a type of cake) from rice flour and *kuḍmala* (flower buds), whoever or whichever [being] it is given to—even if that person has already passed away—[the spell] shall not release them.
(PDF 132, p.

236) Furthermore, there is another practice: at the time of a lunar eclipse, while reciting the Tārādhāraṇī and performing the preliminary service (*sevā*), one should take the image of Lokeśvara that has appeared [therein] and meditate upon it with conch-shell powder.
Then, it should be given to the woman until she reaches death; she desires only him and no other.

Furthermore, there is another application: having recited the Tārādhāraṇī mantra one hundred and eight times over a madana fruit, with that madana fruit, together with Hayagrīva, whichever woman he impregnates— [k, g: ...]
Upon seeing her, she becomes submissive.

Furthermore, there is another application: with this mantra, *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture amukasya bandhanamuktiṃ kuru muḥ svāhā*, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished interspersed within the petals of an arka leaf and conceal it in a hole dug in the ground.
For him, there will certainly be liberation from bondage.
Whatever merit has been acquired by writing down this ritual manual (*sādhana*) of Vajratārā—
by that merit, may this world proceed to the state of the Sugata.
The Sādhana of Vajratārā is completed.
This work is the composition of the venerable Ratnākaraśānti.
Having worshipped the Goddess with *karavīra* flowers, one should recite the mantra eight hundred times at the three junctions of the day (cf. PDF 132, p. 237).
Noble Tārā will certainly grant within a single month whatever desired boon has been requested.

Oṃ jambhe mohe svāhā! Homage to Tārā; homage to the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Great Compassionate One; homage to the Blessed Noble Tārā. Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture, O Heroine, deliver us from difficulties! Hrīṃ hrīṃ, O Blessed One, deliverer from all suffering, savior from hardships, Great Mistress of Yoga!

*Hrīṃ! Homage be unto you, Svāhā!* One should repeatedly [visualize] this Blessed Lady Durgottāriṇī Tārā: dark-complexioned, four-armed, holding a noose in her left hand and an elephant-goad in her right;
comforting the devotee with her right [hand], bestowing boons with her [other] right [hand], wearing divine garlands and garments, and holding a blue lotus in her left hand.
One should meditate three times a day upon her whose body is clothed in white garments and who sits in the lotus posture;

she delivers one from all sufferings. She releases one from bondage. She delivers one who is entangled in chains, bound by a noose, or seized by a planetary spirit. This mantra should be recited by one held in captivity, either a thousand times or eight hundred times per day.

If one recites it during the day, he releases [the victim]. If he does not release him, then his head bursts open and he rolls upon the ground. When restored to health, he says, "Release so-and-so. If he still does not release him, then a headache occurs, a great fever arises, and a severe cholera-like affliction (*visūcikā*) ensues.
She grants a vision to the practitioner and will certainly liberate him on the seventh day. This is the Blessed One, the Deliverer from Difficulties (Durgottāriṇī), who has been described.
Having consecrated a flower seven times with the mantra *hrīṃ hrīṃ* [or *hūṃ hroṃ jaḥ*], it should be offered. (pdf 132, p. 133)
Worship: In the center, *khaṃ* and *tāṃ*; counter-clockwise, *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *jīṃ*, *huṃ* (*hrīṃ*);
counter-clockwise, *loṃ* (*lāṃ*), *māṃ*, *pāṃ*, *tāṃ*.
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of Durgottāriṇī.
Having risen at the morning twilight, seated upon a soft cushion on a beautiful spot of ground, he should [visualize] within his own heart the lunar disc.
The first [syllable] of the fifth [group], however, joined with the second vowel,
conjoined with the half-moon and the bindu, and adorned with white rays.
Having drawn Tārā into the sky by means of his white rays,
she who has two arms, a white body, and who holds a boon-granting gesture and a blue lotus;
Having worshipped with devotion by means of the five-fold offerings, one should thereafter perform the confession of sins, the rejoicing in merit,
the dedication of that merit, and likewise the taking of the three refuges.
One should recite: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness.
Thus, the yogi who knows the ritual procedure, having meditated upon both self and other as empty, [should visualize himself] upon a moon-disc seat situated in the center of a white lotus.
The goddess Tārā, beautiful and arisen from the previously mentioned seed-syllable,
is seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture and holds the gesture of granting boons and a blue lotus.
Having the form of the autumnal moonbeams, resting upon a moon at her back,
fully adorned with all ornaments, and possessing the body of a sixteen-year-old.
Having meditated upon Noble Tārā, the mother of all the Buddhas and their sons, who possesses a form at will, one should visualize her wheel of white radiance within the heart.
The eight-square grid is filled with eight syllables:
OṂ, with the name of the person to be accomplished placed in the middle of the oblation-syllable (HĀVYA), starting from the center.
With a one-pointed mind and firm resolve, one should meditate for six months;
with an undaunted heart, one should recite this ten-syllable mantra.
Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, one should subsequently employ *tāre*;
then there should be *tuttāre ture*, ending with *svāhā*—this is the mantra for all rites.
Even one whose hair-tips remain unbroken conquers death like a liberated soul, through Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, the Moon, the Sun, Rudra, the Directions, Time, and Kāmadeva.
It brings about the destruction of wrinkles, grey hair, misfortune, disease, and poverty;
it is the destroyer of the mass of sufferings arising from the eight great fears, such as lions and the like.
The attainment of food, drink, mansions, garments, and so forth without having asked for them;
as well as the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as the sword, collyrium, foot-ointment, and the auspicious jar.
Poetic skill, eloquence, intelligence, and utterly pure wisdom,
as well as other desired accomplishments, are produced from this wheel.
Thus ends the *Tārāsādhana*, the instruction for deceiving death.
(From *pdf* 134, p.
240) Homage to Viśvamātā!
Having meditated upon you in the midst of the moon and sun, together with the vowels (*ali*) and consonants (*kali*), [there is] a single water-seed-lotus (*toyabījābja*).

Having dispatched a goddess who has arisen as one-faced, whose two hands hold lotuses, who is moon-colored, mounted upon a white nāga, holding a white lotus in her hand and displaying the gesture of fearlessness, clad in white garments, adorned with white ornaments, and possessing a smiling countenance— to the dwelling of the one to be converted.

Therefore, having accepted the task to be accomplished, they entered once more into the maṇḍala of the Lord; and having received their husband’s command, Locanā and the others, filled with joy, [returned] with jars of nectar.
The ten excellent Śaktis bathe that Sādhya; Rūpā and the others worship him;
Prakaṭa, Daśabala, Āsyā, and the others nourish him; and [Kāmyā and the others] satisfy him.
The ten classes of spirits known as Bhūtas call out; the Krodhas protect;
the Nāginīs kiss; the twelve celestial maidens embrace;
and the Caṇḍas provide protection upon the entire surface of the earth. They depart.
For the very purpose of nourishment, the yogi should thus cultivate everything that is to be accomplished, which brings about supreme bliss.
The Sadhana of Viśvamātā is completed.
Homage to Tārā!
By means of the practice of the former sequence, [one should visualize] within the center of the bhaga, upon a lunar mandala.
The goddess Tārā, golden-hued, most formidable, and possessed of great supernatural power,
has three eyes, eight faces, and is adorned with sixteen arms.
Her hair is tawny and stands upright; she wears a necklace made of fifty fresh human heads;
she is endowed with the pratyālīḍha stance; she is the protector of the world and possesses great power.
Adorned with various garments and ornaments, she was laughing and in the bloom of youth.

The principal face is yellow; the second on the right is blue, the third is dark green, and the fourth is sky-blue; on the left, the first is like a kunda flower, the second is red, and the third is sky-blue;
the upward-facing face has the appearance of smoke-colored light.

and three eyes, holding a vajra and a bell, and established in meditation; from his heart, one should emit a black *huṃ* syllable that radiates various rays of light.

One should visualize that the Tathāgatas, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vidyā-deities, and the Wrathful Ones (krodha) and so forth, residing throughout the infinite reaches of the ten directions, are summoned; having returned, they enter into that very sun, and one should contemplate them as being none other than that Great Vajradhara.

One should visualize the Tathāgatas and the others as having become one with him, entering into the sun; blazing and radiant in form, pervading a thousand *yojanas*. Above that, one should see a black syllable *HŪṂ* joined with various rays of light, and from that *HŪṂ*, one should see rays of light streaming forth. Furthermore, right there...
Having entered (Praveśya, PDF 142, p.
257), that very syllable becomes the terrifying black Great Vajra situated upon a white skull-cup (kh; a: omits).
One should meditate on [the white one] shimmering with various rays of light.
One should contemplate it as being situated in the sun, like a reflection—the ornament of the expanse of the sky—consisting of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Krodhas, Vidyās, and Devīs.
Having ripened sentient beings through those Buddhas and others, one should see them returning and entering the vajra-form. That very thing...
The Vajrabimba has twelve faces, is of a great black complexion, possesses twenty-four arms,
and tramples upon the four Māras. She stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a white skull,
her radiance equal to the fire of the great dissolution, with her mouth wide open and uttering the sound "hā hā."
With a lolling tongue, full of wrath, and with eyes moving in circular motion from the edges of her distorted, terrifying, and knitted brows—
she who is fearsome even to fear itself; adorned on her head with a garland of skulls and decorated with serpents,
endowed with the six seals, her first face...
He is Mahākṛṣṇa; his five right faces are white, yellow, green, red, and smoke-colored;
his five left faces are red, white, yellow, green, and white-red; and his upper face is smoke-colored, distorted, and wrathful—all his faces being thus.
With faces terrifying with fangs, three eyes, and blazing, upright, tawny hair; wrathful, dwarfish, and with a protruding belly; possessing full and elevated breasts; clothed in a tiger skin;
and holding in her twelve right hands a sword, a vajra, a wheel, and a stream of jewels...
Holding a parasol, a goad, an arrow, a spear, a mallet, a club, and a curved knife,
she is exceedingly joyful, mounted upon a corpse, adorned with eight serpents,
endowed with fresh youth, and radiant with loud, boisterous laughter.
One should meditate upon her with a single tawny, fierce matted lock, adorned at the crown of her head by Akṣobhya.
(From PDF 143, p.
258) Oṃ āḥ hūṃ: one should perform the consecration of body, speech, and mind. Oṃ hrīḥ trīṃ hūṃ:
these are the seed-syllables within the mandalas of Vāyu, Varuṇa, Mahendra, and Agni. [ḍh: omits; k: has]

Just as instructed, the mantra-practitioner, being thus transformed into the nature of the Bhagavatī, should again draw forth the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra) from the hollow of the sky, manifest it before him, dissolve it, and cause it to enter his own wheel of commitment (samayacakra). Having caused it to enter, he should unify them.

Bearing the ego-identification with the deity, he is consecrated by the waters from vases filled with the five nectars, emanated from the mass of light rays issuing from his own body as Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, Vidyā-deities, Krodhas, and so forth.

One should worship with various special offerings and meditate upon oneself. For the *aṅganyāsa*: *huṃ* at the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), *oṃ* on the forehead, *āḥ* at the throat, *hrīḥ* at the heart, *trīṃ* at the navel, *huṃ* at the base of the navel, *trāṃ* at the secret place, and *aṃ aḥ phaṭ svāhā* at the feet. Having thus become a *samayin*, by this...
In accordance with the ritual procedure, whatever mantra-syllables are uttered— having emerged from the mouth of the deity as rays of light— one causes them to enter one’s own mouth,
issues them forth through the path of the vajra, and they enter the lotus of the goddess; then again, from the mouth of the goddess...
The goddess should recite the mantra continuously from her own mouth according to this sequence.

Having thus performed the recitation until exhaustion, she should then, within her own heart, cause it to gradually become unperceivable—like a mass of light rays or like the flame of a lamp. Then, having formed the lotus mudrā as described, [she should place it] upon her head.

Having placed [the seed-syllables] on one’s own head, forehead, throat, navel, the surface of the navel, the secret place, and the two feet, one should recite the mantra through the yoga of signlessness (*animittayoga*). In this regard, the mantra is as follows: *oṃ hrīḥ trīṃ huṃ phaṭ* is the root mantra;
*oṃ hrīḥ trīṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā* is the heart mantra; *oṃ hrīḥ trīṃ*.
Huṃ! This is the *upahṛdaya* mantra.
(pdf 143, p.
259) Having reflected thus and having made oneself firm, one should meditate; or else, one should meditate on the Blessed Lady as depicted upon a cloth painting.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times as the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*). One should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with a tenth part of that amount.

One should perform the *homa* using the fruit, flower, or leaf of the *śrīphala*, or the flower of the white *arkapuṣpa* or the white *karavīra* flower, together with cow’s ghee. Having had the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) executed according to the prescribed rite, one should perform worship, meditation, and recitation.

One should perform [the practice]. Even for one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), success is achieved through ten million recitations. Having realized that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), one should instantly visualize a lotus in the heart; upon the lotus, in the center of the sun and moon, is a red syllable *huṃ*, subtle in form, a thousandth part of the tip of a hair, in the form of a drop (*bindu*), and endowed with the syllable *huṃ*. [This is to be placed] at the vajra-flame of the nose.
One should meditate on Vajrayoginī, who arises from the syllable *Hūṃ*, red in color, with two arms, one face, and three eyes; she is naked with disheveled hair,
displays a graceful wrath, is endowed with the six mudrās, and resides within the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*).
One should meditate day and night upon her who stands with one foot on top of the other upon a corpse, holding a curved knife and a skull-cup, and full of wrath.
This concludes the *Sādhana* of Ekajaṭā named *Vidyujjvālākarālī*.
Homage to Ekajaṭā, the Tārā who causes terror to Māra, who is always worshipped by the best of gods. (pdf 145, p. 260) [k, g: ṅkarai] Suravaraiḥ sampūjitā sarvadā.
Victorious is she who acts for the welfare of the worlds, who protects like a mother;
endowed with compassion, she shines as the savior of various people terrified by cyclic existence, eternally destroying the fear of the worlds for those possessed of devotion.
The immediate accomplishment arising from Ekajaṭā shall come to pass;
by that knowledge, all ritual actions will now be successfully accomplished.
Having uttered the syllable *Āṃ*, emptiness is always established;
having uttered that very same syllable, one performs the meditation on the universal lotus.
In the center of the universal lotus, one should meditate on the syllable *ṭāṃ*;
a white skull-cup is visualized, and in its center is the syllable *hūṃ*.
And this is said to be blue,
endowed with blue rays,
through the process of transformation by means of the mind of the Self.
At that very moment, the goddess is meditated upon, possessing a luster like blue collyrium,
four arms, three eyes, and blood-red, formidable, beautiful eyes.
Clad in a tiger skin, radiant with ornaments of skulls, she shines,
adorned with a beautiful necklace of pearls.
The goddess has the appearance of one sixteen years of age, with full and elevated breasts;
she possesses a single matted lock of beautiful tawny hair and is exquisitely adorned by her protruding belly.
Her face is slightly terrifying with bared fangs, her tongue is lolling, and she is fearsome;
she is adorned with extremely dreadful blue serpents of intense radiance.
Adorned with armlets, anklets, and other ornaments, as well as with small bells,
she holds a skull-cup in her left hand and is beautified by a flaying knife in her right.
And in another hand, one should visualize an utpala lotus together with its bud and stalk;
furthermore, one should diligently visualize a sword in the right hand.
Through the yoga of transformation into a sword, a rosary is also seen;
and from the center of the skull, she appears in the ālīḍha stance, red with human blood.

He who, endowed with devotion to the Goddess, constantly performs meditation upon her— who possesses the brilliance of a mass of the fire of universal dissolution and is accompanied by flames of light rays— [attains the supreme state].
Indeed, whoever performs the recitation of these four and a half syllables,
the entire world shall come under his control, just as taught by the Buddha.
Furthermore, having diligently caused the object of accomplishment (sādhya) to enter into the middle of the skull,
one should press down upon the head and feet with the feet by means of that very posture.
Surely restraint is exercised if the mind consists of meditation,
and the mantra is correctly recited as that which awakens the Goddess.
The letter *ha* ending with the nasal *anta* (anusvāra), situated within the fire (*ra*), differentiated by the fourth vowel (*ī*),
joined at its head with the *bindu*, and further accompanied by the crescent moon (*khaṇḍendu*).
This is the seed-syllable, the great seed; now hear the second one.
It consists of the letter ending in *t* joined with fire (*r*), and then pierced by that very same [letter].
(From PDF 146, p.
262) The second [syllable] is stable when joined with *nāda* and *bindu*;
now I shall carefully explain the third seed-syllable.
The letter *ha* at the end, conjoined with the sixth vowel, and endowed with the *nāda* and *bindu*—
this is the most excellent of seed-syllables (*bīja*), the supreme one whose nature is to incinerate the three worlds.
And I shall relate the fourth, just as it was spoken by the Buddha—
peaceful, pure, rich in splendor, and the bestower of all accomplishments.

Listen to the half-syllable, which is the cause for the perfect accomplishment of the mantra; it is the letter ending in *ṭ* (ṭa), not deprived of its inherent vowel, and by its utterance, protection is achieved.
This king of mantras belonging to the goddess Ekajaṭā is of great power;
by merely hearing it, a person becomes free from obstacles.
Good fortune arises constantly, and enemies go to their destruction;
he shall always possess the mass of merit and become equal to a Buddha—of this there is no doubt.
This excellent *sādhana* of Ekajaṭā has thus been completed.
(From PDF 146, p. 263):
Homage to Ekajaṭā!
First of all, the practitioner of mantra, having meditated [as the manuscript *k* adds] upon a meditation-chamber suited to his mind...

Seated on a comfortable seat, having worshipped the Guru, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas with outer and inner offerings [outer worship], having performed the taking of the three refuges, the confession of misdeeds, and so forth, and having generated the firm thought of awakening (bodhicitta), one should utter the syllable *ĀM* and bring to manifestation the emptiness of all phenomena; then again—

Having uttered the syllable *āṃ*, one should visualize a universal lotus (*viśvapadma*) transformed from it; in its center, a lotus vessel born from the syllable *ṭāṃ* (or *dāṃ*), with a radiance equal to the moonstone,
in the midst of which infinite world-systems are illuminated by shimmering rays of light.
Having visualized the syllable *huṃ* with the luster of sapphire, one should contemplate her as its transformation:
possessing the radiance of a great sapphire jewel that pervades the three worlds, four-armed, most terrifying,
with three blood-red and fearsome eyes.
She wears a tiger-skin garment, is adorned with lotus-vessels,
and is decorated with a necklace of human heads; she has a fierce form, the appearance of sixteen years,
full and elevated breasts, a single matted lock of hair slightly reddish-brown, and is embellished with ornaments of cruel serpents.
Her face was made terrifying by matted locks and slightly bared fangs, with a lolling tongue;
she had a protruding belly, yet her mind was permeated with great loving-kindness and compassion.
Adorned with necklaces, anklets, armlets, tinkling bells, girdles, and other ornaments,
she had conquered the great army of Māra by means of the syllable *Huṃ*.
Holding a lotus vessel in her left hand,
she holds in her right hand a curved knife (kartī) together with a vajra that terrifies the hosts of Māras.
Furthermore, having seen an utpala lotus with its stalk and bud in the left hand,
and a sword in the right hand, through that transformation—

One should visualize a rosary, beautiful with a shimmering garland of stars, situated in the center of a skull-cup filled with blood, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture. (pdf 149, p. 264) [k: ...beautiful with a circle of stars...]
One should meditate upon the goddess Ekajaṭā, whose form dwells within the flames of rays like the fire of universal dissolution; thereafter, one should recite the vibrating mantra.
The mantra, possessing inconceivable power, consists of four and a half syllables;
through its penetration by the force of the world's agitation, it causes terror.
[With *kṛtyūrdhva*: This was spoken by the Buddha.

Having stepped upon the target with his two feet in the *ālīḍha* posture, and having visualized him thus within a lotus-vessel upon the two soles of his feet, the yogi, vibrating with the mantra, should recite it.

The perfected mantra, which correctly awakens the Goddess, is now declared: it begins with fire (ra), is mounted upon the letter following ra (la), ends with the final consonant (kṣa), and is differentiated by the vowel ī.
One should extract [the first syllable], its head adorned with a half-moon and a half-bindu;
the second is likewise, but one should differentiate it by means of the form of *tānta* (or *śānta*).
The third [syllable] is the letter *ha* itself, joined with the sixth vowel (*ū*),
adorned with the head as before; the fourth should end with *phaṭ*.
At the beginning,
the mantra practitioner should recite this mantra— *hrīḥ trīḥ krīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*— in this manner, without interruption.
The *Āryaikajaṭāsādhana* is completed.
(PDF 149, p.

265) Following the previously described procedure, immediately after the meditation on emptiness, one should visualize a *huṃ* syllable—[according to manuscript *k*: a blue *huṃ*]—in the center of a skull-cup (*kapāla*) transformed from the syllable *ṭāṃ*, situated upon a universal lotus (*viśvapadma*).

Preceded by the processes of emanation and reabsorption, through that transformation, one should visualize the Blessed Lady Ekajaṭā, whose entire body is black, who has four arms and one face, with three reddish eyes, clad in a tiger skin,
with a garland of skulls and tawny hair standing erect on her head, her fangs bared and her tongue lolling, and possessing a protruding belly.
Instantly visualizing oneself as [the goddess] whose ornaments are variegated with blue serpents, sixteen years of age, with full and elevated breasts,
all her white limbs adorned with necklaces, armlets, tinkling bells, and garlands of flowers, holding a sword and a flaying knife in her two right hands,
and an utpala lotus and a skull-cup in her two left hands.
Having performed the ritual service, one should recite the mantra: OṂ HRĪḤ TRĪḤ HŪṂ PHAṬ.
This concludes the *Ekajaṭā-sādhana*.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ oṃ vajrayoginī pratīcchemaṃ baliṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hahaha haṃ haḥ phaṭ mama śāntiṃ kuru svāhā | Oṃ āḥ aralli hoḥ— thus one should recite these and other such mantras.
[k, ḍh, g; pronounced with the *diṃ* sound] | Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sādhana of the two-armed Ekajaṭā:
the goddess Piṅgograikajaṭā, who holds a flaying knife (*kartṛ*) and a skull-cup (*karoṭa*).
Likewise, I shall describe the four-armed goddess as taught in the *Kalpa*:
she holds an arrow and a conch in her right hands, while her left hands hold a bow and a skull-cup.
Likewise, I shall describe the sequence for the eight-armed [form]:
in the right [hands], she holds a sword, an arrow, a vajra, and likewise a flaying knife.
In her left hands, she holds a bow, a blue lotus, and an axe, while carrying a skull-cup;
all are considered to be black in color and draped around their waists with tiger skins.
They have one face and three eyes, with tawny hair rising upward from their heads.
Dwarfish, with pendulous bellies and fierce, they stand in the pratyālīḍha posture.
With faces fierce with wrath, they are adorned with hanging garlands of severed heads.
Standing upon corpses, they are most terrifying; their heads are adorned with Akṣobhya, they are endowed with fresh youth, and they shine with a fierce, loud laughter.
Born from the seed-syllable ṬĀṂ, they produce immediate conviction;
they should be diligently visualized upon a sun disk above a universal lotus.
Having meditated on the *niraṃśumālikā* mantra— *hrīṃḥ trīṃ [trāṃ] hūṃ phaṭ*— the wise practitioner should visualize it in the place of the sword.
One should recite the supreme mantra, as previously described, in the proper sequence.
Upon the perfection of the power of cultivation, the yogi becomes a great poet;
by reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, he attains a melodious voice.
(From *pdf* 150, p.
267) Having performed the sādhana of Tārā, whatever merit has been acquired by me—
by that very [merit], may all living beings become [liberated].
Equal to Tāriṇī.
The Sādhana of Ekajaṭā is completed.
[This part of the colophon is not found in manuscripts K, G, Kh, or A. It was extracted from among the Tibetans by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna.
Homage to Śuklaikajaṭā!
She is white, born from the syllable *hūṃ* within an excellent lotus vessel resting upon a lotus; she stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, has heavy breasts, and her two eyes are deeply impassioned.

May the Goddess— who has a single matted lock of beautiful tawny hair, who is endowed with the partless [Brahman], who holds a rosary of beads in her right hand and a bud of a blue lotus in her left— protect you always.
Accompanied by eight fierce serpents, her tongue quivering with the power of compassion, her laughter terrifying,
her head adorned by the Lord of the Mind (Kāmadeva), and clothed in the skin of the deer-foe (the lion)— may Tārā destroy the darkness of existence.
Having bowed at the lotus feet of the glorious master Advayavajra,
the glorious Lalitagupta [or Guhya] sets forth this sādhana of Tārā.

First of all, the mantra-practitioner, having performed the purification of the mouth and other preliminary rites, seated upon a comfortable cushion in a place strewn with a profusion of fragrant flowers, should perform worship according to his means, [focusing] within his own heart.

One should visualize a white syllable *huṃ*. One should contemplate that from the syllable *huṃ*, five-colored rays of light issue forth through the pores of one's own body and through the openings of the mouth and so forth.
By those rays of light, world-systems as infinite and boundless as the sands of the river Gaṅgā are illuminated.

Then, the Blessed Lady residing in the Akaniṣṭha realm—possessing the color and other attributes to be described later—should be visualized as standing instantly before one after thinking: "Some being requests me; I shall empower him. Then, from that very syllable *Hūṃ*, various flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and so forth are emitted. From that...

One should also offer incense and other offerings with the mantra marked by the names of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), confession of misdeeds (*pāpadeśanā*), rejoicing in merit (*puṇyānumodanā*), dedication of merit (*puṇyapariṇāmanā*), and the three refuges (*triśaraṇagamanā*). Then, one should utter the syllable *ĀṂ*. Having said, "All phenomena are unoriginated from the beginning," one should contemplate the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all things. One should recite the mantra: *Oṃ*.
All phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
Then, through the power of the aspiration, there appears a white lotus transformed from the syllable Aṃ, in the center of which—

With the syllable *ṭāṃ*, one should visualize a skull-cup with the luster of a moonstone (*candrakāntimaṇi*), filled with blood; in its center, the syllable *hūṃ*, five-rayed, consisting of the five [elements], beautiful, and white. One should see a blue lotus bud transformed from that [syllable], presided over by the syllable *hūṃ*. Having transformed everything into one, [one should visualize] oneself...

One should meditate upon the form of the Bhagavatī as white, with two arms and one face; holding a rosary of rudrākṣa beads in her right hand and a blue lotus bud in her left; possessing a single matted lock of hair that is extremely tawny and pervades the entire expanse of the universe; adorned with ornaments of fierce serpents and a turban wrapped around her head.
*Karkoṭaka* is blue and serves as the neck ornament; *Takṣaka* is red and serves as the earrings for *Nanda* and *Upananda*, which are yellow;
*Ananta* is white and serves as the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*); *Vāsukī* is white and serves as the waistband; and *Kulika* is on the right arm as a bracelet.
The one on the left arm is the color of a pigeon; Śaṅkhapāla is white as a bracelet; Padma and Mahāpadma are red as anklets;

she is adorned with necklaces, anklets, armlets, small bells, girdles, and so forth; she stands upon a corpse in the *pratyālīḍha* posture; her form is exceedingly terrifying; she has slightly protruding fangs and a lolling tongue; and her crown is graced by the glorious Akṣobhya.

[One should visualize her] with a mind permeated by great love and compassion. Then, one should see a white syllable *Hūṃ* in one’s own heart, from which rays of light draw forth the wisdom-maṇḍala. Afterwards, having drawn it in, caused it to enter, bound it, and gratified it through the sequence of *Jaḥ Hūṃ Vaṃ Hoḥ*, the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) becomes of one flavor [with oneself], like water mixed with milk.
One should meditate.

Then, within the heart of the Bhaṭṭārikā, upon a lotus and a moon, one should visualize the syllable *hrīṃ*, resembling pure crystal, emitting hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light. When weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra.

Furthermore, the mantra-mandala of great power should be mentally inscribed neither too quickly, nor too slowly, nor indistinctly, nor lacking the proper measure. In this regard, the extraction of the mantra is as follows: the fourth letter of the seventh [vowel-series], conjoined with fire (*ra*), differentiated by the letter *ī*, and adorned with the half-moon and the bindu; thus one should recite it in the center of the navel.
