Upon that is an eight-petaled lotus, and above it, upon a moon disk, one should visualize a brilliantly shining syllable *hrīṃ*. Upon the tongue, one should see a moon mandala marked by the letter *a*, and above that, the syllable *hrīṃ*. One should also visualize the beads of the rosary as knots formed from the syllable *hrīṃ*; these emerge uninterruptedly from the mouth and enter through the path of the navel.
One should contemplate [the syllable] as emerging from one's own mouth. This single-syllable king of mantras is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*);
it destroys sins and diseases, and especially, one should recite this mantra spoken by the Buddha Akṣobhya.
With firm resolve, one should thus mutter the mantra. By a hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*), one becomes a great poet, a retainer of what has been heard, and eloquent.
He obtains the adamantine speech; possessing great wealth and long life, he becomes an expert in all treatises.
Like the Lord of Garuḍas, he renders the three worlds free from poison. He will swiftly awaken to enlightenment; there is no doubt of this.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: "Oṃ āḥ hrīṃ hūṃ haṃ haḥ—this king of mantras bestows Buddhahood; how much more so other accomplishments? Oṃ āḥ hrīṃ hūṃ ghātaya ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ phaṭ svāhā—one should offer this bali, which destroys all Māras."
The *Sādhana* of Śuklaikajaṭā is completed.
This is the work of the venerable Lalitagupta.

Homage to Cundā! Having bowed down correctly to all those Victors (Jinas), [this homage is absent in ḍh; k and b omit "namaḥ"; cundā is consistently spelled as cuṇḍā in kh and a]. I pay respect to all those Jinas.
I shall describe, in brief, the propitiation of the goddess Cundā, who possesses great supernatural power— a swift means of accomplishment.

First of all, the mantra-practitioner [should visualize] within the moon at his own heart the seed-syllable— the first of the third group of consonants, filled with the fifth letter of the first group, adorned with a half-moon and a bindu, garlanded with the rays of the autumn moon, divine, and empowered by all the Buddhas; then...

Having visualized the Blessed Lady produced from the rays [of light], as well as the Guru, the Buddhas, and so forth, one should worship them after saluting with this mantra: Oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ, Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ, Oṃ vajradīpe hūṃ, Oṃ vajragandhe hūṃ, Oṃ vajranaivedye hūṃ. Then—
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds; I rejoice in the merit of the world; I set my mind upon the enlightenment of a Buddha. (pdf 152, p. 271)

One should recite these and other verses. Then, preceded by that *praṇidhāna* (aspiration), one should meditate on the selflessness of all phenomena with this mantra: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. Then—[k, b: adds "having reflected"]—
One should contemplate the seed-syllable, which has the form of an illusion, as the entirety of the three realms without exception.
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. Then:

One should meditate on oneself in the form of the goddess Śrī Cundā, produced from the previously mentioned seed-syllable, possessing the luster of the autumnal moon, with four arms, and displaying the gesture of granting boons with the right hand.

One should visualize her holding a lotus marked with a book in her left hand, holding an alms-bowl with both hands, adorned with all ornaments, and seated upon a lotus and moon disc; thereafter, one should form the mudrā.
Having performed protection for the heart, the *ūrṇā*, the throat, and the head, one should perform the recitation (*japa*). In this regard, the mudrā is as follows:

Forming *añjali* with both hands, the two index fingers are joined in the shape of a coil between the two middle fingers, while the two thumbs are placed at the sides. This is the mudrā of Cundā, and her mantra is as follows: *oṃ cale cule*. (The word *cule* is omitted in some versions.)
k, b: [only] cunde svāhā | The *Sundāsādhana* is complete.
(From *pdf* 153, p.

272) Having first visualized the white seed-syllable *cuṃ* upon a moon disc in the heart, and having worshipped, prostrated to, and praised the Buddhas and others with its rays, one should recite the verse of the three refuges immediately after the sevenfold supreme worship beginning with the confession of misdeeds.
Having recited [the mantra], having asked for forgiveness, and having cultivated the four divine abodes (brahmavihāras), one should meditate on emptiness (śūnyatā). Then,
having again visualized one's own seed-syllable upon a moon disc on a multicolored lotus, through its transformation, one should visualize the noble Cundā,
with the luster of the autumnal moon, having one face and four arms.

Having instantaneously visualized oneself as [the deity], with the right hand granting boons, the left hand holding a lotus marked with a book, the remaining two hands holding an alms-bowl, adorned with various ornaments, wearing a crown of Vajrasattva, with a body radiating forth to accomplish the welfare of countless beings, and one's own seed-syllable in the heart;

Having visualized the mudrā, one should place it upon the three locations. Having formed the añjali with both hands, one should join the two thumbs in the shape of a coil between the two index fingers and position them on the sides.
The mantra is: oṃ cale cule cunde svāhā.
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of Cundā.
*Namaścundāyai*.
First, from the seed-syllable *cuṃ* situated in the center of the moon within the heart, rays of light of various colors emerge; by these, [the deities] are produced.

Having visualized the Guru, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas before him, he should perform worship and so forth with the mantras beginning with *oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ*. Then, he should recite the Verses on the Three Refuges. Immediately thereafter, having meditated upon emptiness, *oṃ*...

One should recite: "I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Then, one should visualize Cundā, arisen therefrom, with the luster of the autumn moon, four-armed, adorned with all ornaments, granting boons with her right hand, holding a book and a lotus in her left hands, and [holding other implements] with her remaining two arms.

One should visualize her holding a bowl, seated upon a living being on a moon-lotus in the *sattvaparyaṅka* posture. Then, having performed protection by touching the heart, navel, throat, and head with the mudrā, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ cale cule cunde svāhā*. In this regard, the mudrā is as follows:
Having formed the añjali with both hands, the two thumbs are joined in the shape of a ring between the two middle fingers and remain positioned on the sides.
Thus ends the *Cundāsādhana*.
(Namo mārīcyai |) Homage to Mārīcī.
According to the previously mentioned procedure, upon a moon disc atop a double lotus born from the syllable *paṃ*, [kh, a: by means of meditation].

One should instantly contemplate oneself as Mārīcī, born from a white syllable *Āṃ*, white in color, with five faces, ten arms, and four legs; therein, the principal face is white, the right is black,
the left is the red boar-face, the face behind is green, and the face above the head is yellow.
She wears a crown of matted hair adorned with a triple-pronged crest fashioned from various jewels; in her five right hands she holds a solar disc, a vajra, an arrow, a goad, and a needle;
and in her five left hands—[in the case of the *nīlavajra* version]—she holds...

One should visualize the maiden in the full bloom of youth, wearing various ornaments, clad in a white tunic and upper garment, and stationed within the interior of a *caitya*; she holds in her hands a moon-discus, a bow, an *aśoka* sprout, a noose, and a threatening-gesture thread (*tarjanīsūtra*), and is mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven boars, with her four feet treading upon Viṣṇu, Indra, Śaṅkara, and Brahmā.

Seated in the middle of that chariot, one Bhagavatī is black with a sow’s face, trampling upon a makara, and holding a vajra and a threatening gesture (tarjanī) in her right and left hands respectively; in the southern direction is another Bhagavatī,
red with a sow’s face and four arms, holding a goad and a needle in her two right hands.

In the left direction is another Bhaṭṭārikā, red in color, with a boar’s face, wearing divine ornaments, and holding in her two left hands a noose and a thread with a raised index finger; her remaining right and left hands hold a bow drawn to the ear,
an arrow, and a vajra-leaf of the Aśoka tree.
And she is adorned with various ornaments. Beneath the chariot-drawing boars, the nine planets beginning with the Sun (the word *ādi* is omitted in manuscript *k*) should be visualized;
they are crowded with various calamities and diseases, and having fallen below in human form, they should be contemplated. Then—

Having summoned the Tathāgatas with rays of light from the *māṃ* seed-syllable situated on the moon at the heart, she receives consecration and becomes sealed by Vairocana. Then, from the seed-syllable at the heart itself, the mantra syllables [issue forth] in the form of a rosary.
Having emanated [the mantra] from the mouth to the navel, from the navel to the mouth, and again from the mouth to the navel—by such a sequence of rotating the wheel—one should recite the mantra.
In this regard, the mantra is: OṂ MĀRĪCYAI MĀṂ HŪṂ.
*Huṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.

One should perform all activities, such as eating and so forth, while empowered by one's own seed-syllable (*svabīja*). Upon exhaustion, one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra and dwell at ease.
The Sādhana of the Ten-Armed White Mārīcī as Taught in the Kalpa [the title in Kh reads "White as Taught in the Kalpa"]
Homage to Mārīcī!

Now, immediately following the meditation on emptiness, upon a moon disk is a yellow *māṃ* syllable, which becomes a cluster of *aśoka* flowers; above that is another *māṃ*, which transforms into [Mārīcī], who is yellow, with two arms and one face, and wears a jeweled crown adorned by Vairocana.
She stands gracefully upon a moon disc atop a universal lotus on the back of a golden boar;

her left hand clings to a branch of an *aśoka* tree, while her right hand displays the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*). Her body is adorned with necklaces and other ornaments, and she possesses the loveliness of fresh youth. Having meditated upon her in this manner within the heart—
Having crushed the wicked with multitudes of boars empowered by rays radiating from the *māṃ* seed-syllable,
and having performed manifold benefit for sentient beings, one recites: *oṃ mārīcyai māṃ svāhā*.
One should recite the mantra.
Thus ends the sādhana of Aśokakāntāmārīcī.
(From PDF 155, p.
276) Homage to Mārīcī!
To the Gurus who have reached the further shore of wisdom through the limbs of unsurpassed bliss.
Having prostrated, the sādhana of Kalpamārīcī is now being written.

Therein, first of all, the yogin— possessing the resolute intention to uplift the entire world— should apply the "wrathful fist" (*krodhamuṣṭi*) to the heart, throat, *ūrṇā*, and the upper part of the head with the mantra *oṃ phaṭ*, and also with this: *oṃ mārīcyai vighnānutsāraya huṃ phaṭ*.

Having crushed the obstacles, one should meditate upon a yellow syllable *māṃ* within a sun disk transformed from the syllable *āṃ* at one’s own heart; then, having drawn the Blessed Lady into the sky by means of the mass of rays emerging from that [syllable], one should place Gaurī before oneself.
She is golden-yellow in color, with three faces, three eyes, and eight arms;

her right face is red, and her left is a blue, distorted boar’s face. Her four right hands hold a vajra, a goad, an arrow, and a needle, while her four left hands hold an *aśoka* sprout, a bow, a thread, and a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*). She wears a crown of Vairocana.
[The syllables] ḍha, ga, ka, ba, and kha: [she is] crowned, adorned with various ornaments, situated within the womb of a caitya,
wearing red garments, a bodice, and an upper robe, mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven boars,
standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a wind-maṇḍala arising from the syllable *yaṃ*.
In the center of a chariot presided over by the most fierce Rāhu, who seizes the moon and sun born from the syllable *haṃ*,
she is surrounded by a retinue of four goddesses; there, in the eastern direction,
is Vartālī (or Vetālī), red in color, with the face of a boar, and possessing four arms.
She holds a needle and a goad in her right hands and a noose and an *aśoka* branch in her left hands, and wears a red tunic;
likewise, to the right is Vadālī, who is yellow in color and holds an *aśoka* sprout and a needle in her left and right arms respectively.
(Holding a vajra and a noose in her right and left hands, she has the form of a young maiden, endowed with the ornaments of fresh youth;
likewise, in the west is Varālī, white in color, whose right arm holds a vajra-needle.)
Holding a noose and an *aśoka* branch in her left hands, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, and possessing a beautiful form— likewise, in the northern direction,
there is Varāhamukhī, red in color, with three eyes and four arms, holding a vajra and an arrow in her right hands.

Having meditated on her as having an exquisite divine form, holding an autumnal bow and an *aśoka* flower in her left hands, and being established in the practice of worship, prostration, praise, confession of sins, rejoicing in merit, dedication, supplication, the three refuges, and the four immeasurables; and having contemplated emptiness, one should recite: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.
One should take emptiness as the object of concentration (*śūnyatāsamādhi*).
Then, within a solar disc, one should visualize Vairocana, born from the syllable *Oṃ*, seated upon a lion throne, white in color, wearing a crown of matted hair,
and holding the mudrā of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅgī*).
The object of enlightenment is Śrī; [the seed-syllable] *k* is the male mudrā and *kh* is the female mudrā. He is peaceful and adorned with all ornaments.
In his heart, upon a moon disc, is the seed-syllable *āṃ*, perfected by its retinue of twenty-five syllables, from which arises an Ashoka sprout.

Above that, upon a moon disc, is the seed-syllable *māṃ*. Through the transformation of all these, there appears the form characterized by the colors, arms, and other features as previously described.

Having instantly meditated upon oneself in the form of Mārīcī, one should place Vartālī in the eastern direction with the mantra: *oṃ mārīcyai varttāli vadāli varāli varāhamukhi ākarṣaya jaḥ svāhā*. Likewise, [one should place her] with: *oṃ marīcyai yarttāli vadāli varāli varāhamukhi*.

With the mantra "Bind, bind the mouths of all the wicked and malicious ones! Hūṃ Svāhā," [one should place] the Vadālī [image] in the south. Likewise, with "Oṃ Mārīcyai Varttāli Vadāli Varāli Varāhamukhi... [one should place the image of Mārīcī].
"O Varāhamukhī, paralyze the mouths of all the wicked and malicious ones! VAṂ SVĀHĀ!"—thus for Varālī in the west. Likewise: OṂ...

"Oṃ mārīcyai varttāli vadāli varāli varāhamukhi sarvasattvān vaśamānaya hoḥ svāhā"—with this mantra, one should likewise worship Varāhamukhī in the north. Following the visualization, there is the recitation of the mantra: "Oṃ mārīcyai māṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. Thus.
One should dwell, presiding over the three junctions [of the day] by means of the yoga of the deity.
Thus ends the *Mārīcīsādhana* as taught in the *Kalpa*.
Homage to Mārīcī!

First, one should worship the Blessed Lady— who has been drawn forth by the rays of light from the white syllable *māṃ* in the moon at one's own heart— with various offerings, and perform the confession of sins and so forth.

One should cultivate the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*). Having recited "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness," one should instantly contemplate oneself as Mārīcī, born from a white syllable *māṃ* transformed upon a moon mandala atop a double lotus (*viśvapadma*) arising from the syllable *paṃ*; she is white like a jasmine flower or the moon, five-faced, ten-armed, and four-legged.

Therein, the principal face has the color of the body; the right face is black; the left face is boar-like and red; the rear face is green; and the face above the head is yellow. She wears a crown of matted hair with three crests variegated with various jewels, and in her five right hands:

In her five left hands, she holds a moon disc, a bow, an *aśoka* sprout, a noose, and a threatening-gesture thread (*tarjanīsūtra*), while in her [five] right hands she holds a sun disc, a blue vajra, an arrow, a hook, and a needle.

Her body adorned with earrings, armlets, a crest-jewel, small bells, and garments fashioned from various jewels; she is in the prime of youth, clad in a white bodice and upper garment, and situated within the interior of a *caitya*.

She is mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven boars, her four feet being stepped upon by Viṣṇu, Indra, Śaṅkara, and Brahmā. Standing in the middle of her chariot is another goddess, Kṛṣṇā, who has the face of a boar; she stands upon a lotus and holds a thunderbolt and a threatening gesture (tarjanī) in her right and left hands respectively.
In the southern direction is another Blessed Lady; she is red in color, has the face of a boar, and possesses four arms.
Her two right hands hold a goad and a needle, while her two left hands hold a noose and a rosary with the index finger extended.
She is adorned with divine ornaments. And in the western direction is another, the Bhaṭṭārikā.
She too is red in color and has the face of a sow;

her right and left hands hold a bow drawn to the ear, an arrow, a vajra, and an *aśoka* sprout; she is adorned with variegated garments and ornaments, and beneath the sows that draw the chariot are the nine planets, beginning with Āditya.

They exist fallen in human form, crowded with various deaths, calamities, and diseases. Having meditated upon the Bhagavatī in such a form, one should summon the Tathāgatas by means of rays of light emanating from the syllable *Māṃ* on the moon of the heart; having received the consecration, one should mark [the disciple] on the head with Vairocana. Then, from the seed-syllable in the heart, [one should project it] in the form of a rosary.

Having emanated the syllables of the mantra from the mouth, one should revolve the mantra by means of the sequence of rotating the wheel—starting from the navel to the mouth, from the navel back to the mouth, and so forth—while bringing to mind the suchness (*tathatā*) of the three spheres (*tri-koṭi*). In this regard, the mantra is: *oṃ mārīcyai*.

*Māṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. One should perform all activities, such as eating and so forth, while empowered by one’s own seed-syllable (*svabīja*). Upon exhaustion, having recited the hundred-syllable mantra, one should dwell at ease.
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of White Mārīcī according to the procedure taught in the *Kalpa*.
Homage to Mārīcī!
Oṃ āḥ hrīḥ svāhā. (PDF 157, p. 280)
Having visualized oneself at the crown of the head, the forehead, the throat, the heart, and the two knees, one should perform the ritual procedure starting from the syllable OṂ as before,
up to the recitation for purification; then, one should visualize Mārīcī Vajradhātvīśvarī, arisen from the syllable OṂ, possessing twelve arms, red in color, six-faced, and pot-bellied.
[She has] blazing, tawny hair standing erect,
wears a garland of skulls, has a girdle adorned with snakes,
and is clothed in a tiger-skin garment.

She stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture within the solar disc at the heart of the *caitya*, her multitude of various obstacles prostrated at her pair of feet; she is accompanied by Vairocana, and her chariot is being dragged by various boars;
she has five faces, beginning with the first, which are red, black, green, yellow, and white.

One should visualize her as red, green, and black, with a single black boar-face at the top; holding a sword, a club, and an arrow in her right hands, she has a gaping mouth and an exceedingly terrifying form. In the middle of the chariot, one should visualize the chariot-driver, who has two arms, holds a threatening gesture and an ashoka sprig in her hands, stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, and is fearsome.

One should meditate: preceded by the radiation of light and so forth, paralyzing, deluding, and slaying wicked beings—Oṃ Vajradhātvīśvarī, strike all wicked beings! Strike, strike! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Oṃ Mārīcyai Hūṃ!
One should recite the mantra: *oṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
The Sādhana of Vajradhātvīśvarī Mārīcī. [Variant readings: kh: Raktamārīcīsādhanaṃ; k: Mārīcāsādhanaṃ; k, b: Māhokṣasādhanaṃ]
First, the mantra-practitioner, seated on a comfortable seat, should touch the heart, the ūrṇā, the throat, and the head with the left fist using the mantra *oṃ phaṭ*. (pdf 157, p. 281)

Having touched the right fist in the wrathful gesture (*krodhamuṣṭi*) and raised it, one should contemplate [the practice] as being free from obstacles. Then, having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites,
and having sat down again, one should [visualize] the moon and sun produced from the syllables *a* and *ā*, according to the distinction between night and day, within one’s own heart.

Having visualized the sun within the body and contemplated a yellow syllable *oṃ* above it, one should see the Blessed Lady arisen from its rays in front of oneself; having worshipped her with whatever flowers and other offerings are available, and having performed the confession of sins and so forth before her, one should contemplate everything as empty. Then: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ*.

Having uttered "All phenomena are pure by nature; I am so," one transforms that [syllable] into an eight-spoked wheel, and having transformed the syllable *oṃ* situated in its center into oneself in the form of Vairocana— yellow in color, wearing a crown of matted hair, and clad in red garments— [one meditates].
One should meditate on him as wearing yellow robes, peaceful, seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon a lion throne in the center of a lotus,

adorned with all ornaments, and forming the mudrā of the branches of enlightenment (bodhyaṅgī). In his heart, there is an aśoka flower produced from the transformation of the syllable ĀṂ situated upon a moon disc.

Above that, one should visualize the syllable *māṃ*, emit its rays, and having accomplished the welfare of all sentient beings, draw them back into that very place and cause them to enter. Then, in front of oneself, upon a sun-maṇḍala transformed from the syllable *āḥ*, one should visualize the Blessed Lady born from the seed-syllable *māṃ*, possessing eight arms.
One should meditate on her as consisting of rays of light according to the instruction.
Immediately thereafter, while reciting the mantra "Oṃ Mām," one should visualize oneself as Mārīcī, situated within a caitya and mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven boars.
One should visualize: beneath the chariot, upon a wind mandala arising from the syllable *yaṃ*, is Rāhu, fashioned from the syllable *haṃ*. Therein is the Blessed Lady.

She wears a jewel crown, has eight arms, three eyes, and three faces; she is a brilliant yellow in color. Her primary face is yellow with lips like the bandhūka and javā flowers; the right face is red and round; the left is a boar’s face, wrathful, blue, with a lolling tongue and a distorted countenance.
Terrifying, with a face made formidable by a frown, she holds in her left hands a threatening gesture with a noose, a bow, an ashoka sprout, and a thread;
in her right hands, a needle, a goad, an arrow, and a vajra.
Adorned with all ornaments such as various bracelets and so forth, wearing a variegated red bodice and upper garment, she stands in the pratyālīḍha posture.
One should visualize her surrounded by four goddesses. To the east is Vartālī (or Vetālī),
standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, four-armed, with a single boar’s head, red in color, and holding [objects] in her right [hands].
She holds a needle and a goad in her [right hands], while in her left she holds a winnowing basket, a noose, and sprouts of barley.

She stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, has four arms, and a single face like that of a boar. She is yellow in color, and in her right hands she holds a flower, a sprout of the *aśoka* tree, and a needle with thread, while in her left...
In the west is Varālī, who holds a noose and a vajra;

she stands in the ālīḍha posture, has four arms, and is yellow in color. She has a single face like that of a boar; in her right hands she holds a vajra and a needle, and in her left hands she holds a noose and an *aśoka* sprout. Likewise, in the north is the boar-faced one, who is red in color.

Blazing with the color of the rising sun, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, four-armed, holding an arrow and a vajra in her right hands, and a bow and an *aśoka* sprout in her left hands; all of these reside within the spire of a *caitya*,
adorned with various ornaments, jeweled crowns, red bodices, and upper garments, and possessing three eyes.
The third [group of goddesses], adorned with various ornaments, should be visualized as white. Then, upon the entry of the Jñānasattva with *jaḥ* *huṃ* *vaṃ* *hoḥ*, one should bind the mudrā.
Having made both hands equal and joined in the form of an añjali,
one should make both tips open and raise both thumbs.
The two middle fingers are joined together, marked with the shape of a ring;
then, while seated in the paryanka posture, they are placed at the region of the navel.
One should place [them].

Then, preceded by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), one should recite the mantra: *oṃ mārīcyai svāhā*. One should complete any deficiency or excess in the ritual procedure with the hundred-syllable mantra beginning with *oṃ vajrasattva*, and so forth. At the time of dismissal (*visarjana*), however—
Oṃ mārīcyai mur iti, one should release one's own mudrā.
Thus ends the concise sādhana of eight-armed yellow Mārīcī.

This is the sādhana of Oḍiyāna Mārīcī. First of all, the practitioner visualizes within his own heart a sun disk transformed from the syllable ĀḤ; upon that is the thirteenth letter of the first group, adorned with a crescent moon and a bindu. Having likewise performed the confession of sins and so forth, by means of that very [syllable]—

The letter *māṃ* is fully manifested; from its total transformation arises Mārīcī, red in color, with six faces and twelve arms. Her first face is red, the second black, the third dark blue, the fourth yellow, and the fifth white.
Above that, situated on her head, is the black Vārāha with six faces; she is adorned by an Aśoka *caitya*,
has yellow Vairocana as her lord, possesses a protruding belly, is decorated with a garland of skulls, and has tawny hair standing erect.
Adorned with serpents, clothed in a tiger skin, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture,
treading upon a boar that crushes obstacles, with a terrifying face,
she holds in her right hands a sword, a vajra, a mace, an arrow, and a single-pointed vajra.
[The deity] holds in her left hands an axe, a noose with the index finger, a skull-cup, an ashoka sprout, the head of Brahmā, a bow, a trident,
and has three eyes; she is red and round, with a face terrifying with protruding fangs.
One should meditate upon another goddess, burnt [and] standing in the middle of the chariot, two-armed,

holding a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) together with a sprout-like noose (*pāśa-pallava*), [and— according to the Ḍh manuscript— holding a skull-cup (*kapāla*), an *aśoka* sprout, the head of Brahmā (*brahmaśiras*), and a bow together with a trident-sprout], thinking: "I myself am the Blessed Lady."
Then one should bind the mudrā:
having formed the vajra-añjali, by then slightly contracting the two middle fingers.
Her two big toes are joined in the paryanka posture, with their tips touching each other.
The mantra: Oṃ mārīcyai oṃ māṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.
The *Sādhana* of the twelve-armed, red-colored Oḍiyāna Mārīcī is completed.
(From *pdf* 159, p.

285) Having performed the confession of sins according to the previously mentioned procedure and having meditated upon emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one should visualize Oḍiyāna Mārīcī— red in color, arisen from the transformation of the red seed-syllable *māṃ* upon a multicolored lotus and sun disk.

She has six faces and twelve arms, with three eyes on each face; her five faces turn to the right, being red, black, white, green, and yellow, while the uppermost is a black sow's face; in her first six right hands, in successive order:
In her left hands she holds a sword, a discus, a mace, an arrow, an axe, a single-pointed vajra, a threatening gesture, a noose, a *khaṭvāṅga*,
and a skull-cup containing a *caitya* with the eight lordly nāgas at its base as ornaments for her body; her tawny hair stands upright.
[She is] with a face made terrifying by fangs, wearing a crown of five dried skulls,
with her neck draped with a garland of dripping heads,
mounted upon seven variegated boars beneath a chariot fashioned from many jewels.

[The seed-syllables are: *ra*, *tha*, *kho*, *rathābodhi*; *ḍha*: *citta*; *ka*, *ḍha*, *ka*: [one who has] mounted a red chariot, surrounded externally by eight cremation grounds, seated cross-legged in the middle of the chariot, holding a vajra, a needle, and a threatening gesture—thus is the red-colored Mārīcī.

Having meditated instantaneously upon her— clad in a yellow bodice, adorned with various jewel ornaments, decorated with a tiger-skin garment, possessing a red radiance, and with the five Tathāgatas flashing forth— from the sun at her heart,
Having received empowerment from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas summoned by hundreds of rays of light emanating from the *māṃ* seed-syllable,
one should visualize oneself wearing a crown of Vairocana. Then,
preceded by the service (*sevā*) of the samaya-substances obtained as available and consecrated by one’s own seed-syllable...
The mantra-practitioner, having emerged from that seed-syllable in the form of a rosary garland, issues forth from the heart (k: having issued forth).
One should recite the mantra— *oṃ mārīcyai māṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*— by means of the yoga of rotating the wheel from the navel to the heart again and again.
Having recited it at the conclusion of the subsequent meditative absorption (*samādhi*), [one should proceed].
[Omitting *jamā viharet*: By means of that very yoga, one should dwell at ease as one pleases.
The Sādhana of Oḍiyāna Mārīcī:
First, having summoned the Blessed Lady from the seat of the sun in the heart by means of the rays of the syllable *hūṃ*, and having worshipped her with manifold kinds of offerings—

Having performed the confession of misdeeds and so forth, and immediately after the meditation on emptiness, one should contemplate the mind in the form of a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*). Through its transformation, one should meditate upon the vajra-ground, the vajra-fence, and so on. In the center of that is the glorious seat of Oḍḍiyāna.

Kh: Oḍḍiyāna is a blood-red triangle; in its center is a five-pronged vajra resting upon the sun, its hub empowered by the syllable Oṃ. Through its transformation, she appears in the form of Bodhicitta, difficult to withstand like the sparks of the fire of the great dissolution, laughing with a loud, boisterous laugh (*aṭṭāṭṭahāsa*). [K: intoxicated with a loud, boisterous laugh.]
She tramples upon the four Māras, stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, possesses twelve arms and six faces.
She has three eyes and is red in color; in her first six right hands, she holds a sword, a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), a single-pointed vajra, an axe, an arrow, and a mace.
In her left hands she holds a threatening gesture, a noose, a trident, an ashoka sprout, a bow, a noose, and the head of Brahmā;
her entire body is beautified by a long garland of human heads hanging from all its limbs,
she is clothed in an upper garment of tiger skin, and her primary face is red.
Her two left faces are white and black, her two right faces are yellow and black,
and her upper face is that of a black boar with a protruding tongue;
she has upward-flaming hair and is crowned with Vairocana.

Adorned with ornaments of eight serpents, she destroys Māra in every direction with her own rays, surrounded by a terrifying halo of the shrieks and cries of "Hā! Hā! of the *ḍākinīs*, *bhūtas*, and *vetālas* fleeing in the ten directions.

Having instantly generated oneself as the glorious Mārīcī of Oḍḍiyāna— [the syllables *hat* for *kha*, *kāra* for *ga*]— one should contemplate the syllable *oṃ* at the head, *āḥ* at the throat, *huṃ* at the heart,
and the syllable *phaṭ* on all limbs. Then, above the navel, upon a universal lotus...

In the center of the union of the moon and sun, one should contemplate the syllable *huṃ*, which is the nature of a lotus fiber, multicolored, and imperishable. *Oṃ vajrasattveśvari sarvaduṣṭān hana hana daha*.

*daha paca paca oṃ mārīcyai māṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ* [kh, a: *phaṭ phaṭ*] *svāhā*—this is the heart mantra (*hṛdayamantra*). *oṃ āḥ huṃ*—this is the meditation mantra (*bhāvanāmantra*). *oṃ vajravetāli huṃ phaṭ*—this is the recitation mantra (*jāpamantra*). *oṃ*...

*Mārīcī*: Oṃ māṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the second recitation mantra (*jāpamantra*). Thereafter, at the four junctions of the day (*catuḥsandhyā*), the offering mantra (*balimantra*) is: Oṃ alalli [ācaṇḍiṇḍi, āralli, āralli]. (PDF 161, p. 288)

*G:* *Araṇḍi*. [The mantra given in *kh* is upheld here: *Hoḥ jah hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ oṃ vajraḍākini samayas tvaṃ dṛśya hoḥ kha kha khāhi khāhi sarvayakṣarākṣasabhūtapretapiśāconmādāpasmāraḍākaḍākinī-ādayaḥ*. [In *k*: *vyutpādaḥ*].
The word *ḍāka* is found only in manuscripts *kh* and *a*. "Accept this, this offering (*bali*);
drink it, smell it; do not transgress for the sake of the increase of my great bliss. (*Jighratha* is found only in *kh* and *a*; *pravṛ* is found in *k*, *ḍh*, *g*, *kh*, and *a*.)
"Be my companions, huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! One should partake of food and other such things after purifying them with the syllable *hrīḥ* or with *huṃ* and so forth.
The Sādhana of Mārīcī according to the Sequence of Oḍiyāna-Svādhiṣṭhāna, having twelve arms and red complexion.

Having placed a yellow syllable *māṃ* upon a moon disc within a universal lotus (*viśvapadma*) at one’s own heart, and having likewise contemplated oneself as nothing but a mere appearance (*pratibhāsamātra*), [one recites]: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ*.

One should recite: "I am pure by nature. Then, having transformed that [syllable] into an *aśoka* flower cluster via the syllable *MĀṂ*, and further transforming all of that into the Blessed Lady—who is yellow in color, two-armed, single-faced, with the crown of her head adorned by Vairocana, and wearing a jewel tiara—[one should meditate upon her].
Blazing with light, golden-hued, in the form of a sow, she stands playfully upon a moon on a universal lotus; exuberant in the bloom of youth, standing upright,
her left hand grasping a branch of an *aśoka* tree while her right displays the gesture of granting boons, her limbs adorned with necklaces and other ornaments.

One should visualize her clothed in white garments, residing in one's own heart, warding off the wicked by the radiating of many rays in the form of boars from the syllable *māṃ*. *Oṃ mārīcyai svāhā*. Then, having performed the dismissal (*visarjana*) in the proper manner, one should dwell at ease.

When traveling to another country, however, one should take hold of the corner of one’s own upper garment, recite this mantra seven times, take hold of the garments of one’s companion as well, and having tied them together with a proper knot, one should depart.
One will not be robbed by thieves and the like. Upon reaching the desired destination, [one should untie] the knot.

The instruction is that one should release [the victim]. Having properly tied a knot and consecrated the hem of the upper garment seven times, and having looked toward the ten directions while reflecting, "I am binding the mouths and eyes of the wicked," one should restrain the breath in the form of internal recitation (*antarjalpa*).
Reciting the mantra, one should tie a knot.
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of Aśokakāntāmārīcī.
Having prostrated correctly before Mārīcī, who is born from the family of Vairocana,
the sequence of her sādhana is now described according to the ritual procedure taught in the Kalpa.
In that regard, first, the mantra-practitioner, consecrated in the mandala of the arising of Śrī Mārīcī,
with a mind purified by the observance of his own samaya vows,
and with the intention of uplifting all sentient beings, should utter "Oṃ Phaṭ."

Having placed the *dhāraṇa-krodhamuṣṭi* mudrā upon the heart, the *ūrṇā*, and the crown of the head, and having performed the cleansing of the face and other rites, one should enter the temple, invoke the Blessed Lady from her form depicted on a cloth or other medium, and,
reciting the mantra for dispelling obstacles by Mārīcī over scented water, perform the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*) and so forth with this very same mantra.

[One should perform] the fivefold worship. In this regard, the mantra for dispelling obstacles is: *oṃ mārīcyai hūṃ sarvavighnānutsāraya hūṃ phaṭ*. Then, by means of the syllable at one’s own heart, [one should visualize] a moon-maṇḍala at night and a sun-maṇḍala during the day through the syllable *āḥ*.

Having meditated on the form of a mandala, one should visualize upon it the first of the thirteen seed-syllables, adorned with a crescent moon and a bindu, and possessing the luster of molten gold. Then, having emitted manifold rays of light and, by means of those rays, having perceived the Blessed Lady arisen,
as well as the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas above [her head], and having worshipped and prostrated to them, [one should proceed] with this mantra.

Oṃ mārīcyai puṣpaṃ pratīccha svāhā; Oṃ mārīcyai dhūpaṃ pratīccha svāhā; Oṃ mārīcyai svāhā—having thus consecrated the *argha* with these mantras, one offers it with "Oṃ mārīcyai arghaṃ pratīccha svāhā," or, in its absence, by means of meditation. Then:
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds; I rejoice in the merit of the world; and I direct my mind toward the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly.
For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others, I generate the mind set upon enlightenment.
I generate the supreme mind of enlightenment; I invite all sentient beings. I shall practice the desired conduct.
Having practiced the conduct of supreme enlightenment without fault, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of the world.

Having recited this three times, one should meditate on the selflessness of all phenomena preceded by a formal vow, while reciting this mantra: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Having thus recited—[the seed-syllable] having the form of an illusion, [representing] the three realms...
Having reflected especially upon the three realms,
it is seen and indeed touched everywhere, just like an illusion;
yet the stability of the entire world is not to be apprehended at all.
Having recited this and understood that there is merely an appearance, one should then remove the seed of false conceptualization which has no beginning, and resolve: "I am pure by nature.
Then, having uttered three times, "All phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature," thereafter—

From the seed-syllable previously mentioned, a moon disc arises; above that is the syllable Oṃ. All of this transforms into the glorious Lord Vairocana, seated upon a lion throne in the center of a lotus, sitting in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon a golden moon, absorbed in the samādhi of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga).
One should meditate on [Bodhyagrī], wearing a crown of matted locks, peaceful, and adorned with all ornaments. Then,
one should visualize a moon mandala in one's own heart, and upon it, the twenty-five syllables.

Having visualized the supreme heart-mantra of the first [syllable] joined with the second, adorned with a half-moon and a bindu, one should contemplate that it has become a cluster of *aśoka* flowers; above that, having meditated on the syllable *ĀṂ* situated upon a moon, one should visualize oneself as the complete transformation of all that, in the form of Mārīcī, thinking: "I myself am the Blessed Lady Mārīcī. She is intensely yellow.
Having the luster of Jāmbūnada gold, with a radiant body, situated within a *caitya*,
wearing red garments, a red bodice and upper robe,
adorned with all ornaments such as various bracelets, and resounding with the tinkling of anklets, girdles, waist-bands, and small bells.
She has eight arms, three faces, and three eyes; she is garlanded with blazing, flickering rays of light;
her lips resemble the color of a bandhūka flower in full bloom;
Vairocana forms her crown; and her head is adorned with a garland of *aśoka* flowers.

In her left hands she holds a rosary and an *aśoka* bow; in the right, she is fond of brandishing a vajra-needle, a goad, and an arrow. Her first face is gentle, with a blossoming countenance, brilliantly white like refined gold, and with wide-open eyes.
The left face of the Boar is colored with the dust of vermilion upon its lips, overflowing with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*), wrathful and distorted, formidable, fierce, and terrifying;
it has the luster and form of a sapphire, possesses a brilliance equal to twelve suns, and is made fearsome by its massive, furrowed brow.
The southern face, with its beautiful eyebrows and protruding tongue, is terrifying even to fear itself;
it is intensely red, divine, blazing, and radiant like a palace, strewn with garlands of flowers from the Aśoka tree that has risen from the mansion, and upon her head is the Lord Vairocana.
Endowed with the colors and mudrās previously described, she stands below upon a chariot drawn by seven boars, positioned in the *pratyālīḍha* stance; she is a maiden in the bloom of youth,
situated beneath the boars that pull the chariot.

In the wind mandala, the venerable one [visualizes] the planet Rāhu, transformed from the syllable *haṃ*, seizing with both hands the moon and the sun—the sun by day and the moon when it has gone to night.
One should meditate upon her as surrounded by a retinue of four goddesses.

There, in the east, with the mantra: *Oṃ mārīcyai varttāli vadāli varāli varāhamukhi siddhim ākarṣaya jaḥ svāhā*, one should likewise visualize the goddess who is red in color and has a single face like that of a boar (*varāha*).

One should meditate on [Varāhī], four-armed, wearing a red bodice and upper garment, holding a noose and an *aśoka* branch in her left hands and a vajra-hook and a needle in her right hands, adorned with all ornaments, attracting the desired accomplishment according to the procedure taught in the Kalpa.

Oṃ mārīcyai varttāli vadāli varāli varāhamukhi, bind the mouths, bind the mouths of all the wicked and extremely wicked ones! Huṃ svāhā! One should visualize the goddess Vadālī, possessing the same form, garments, and ornaments as previously described, yellow in color, holding a noose and a vajra in her left hands, and holding a sprig and a thread in her right hands, [and binding] the mouths and eyes of the wicked...
One should likewise visualize Varālī to the south, sewing;

[with the mantra]: *Oṃ mārīcyai vartālī vadāli varāli varāhamukhi sarvaduṣṭān stambhaya vaṃ svāhā*. Goddess Varālī is likewise [to be visualized], with garments, ornaments, and complexion [as described].
To the south, one should place [the goddess] holding a vajra-needle in her right hand and a noose and an *aśoka* flower in her left, paralyzing all malevolent beings;
[with the mantra]: *oṃ mārīcyai varttāli vadāli varāli varāhamukhi sarvasattvān me*.

With the mantra "vaśamānaya hoḥ svāhā," one should place the goddess Varāhamukhī in the northern direction— red in color, with garments and ornaments likewise red, holding a vajra and an arrow in her right hand, and an *aśoka* flower and a bow in her left, drawing all sentient beings toward herself with passion.
Then, one should perform the rites of summoning and so forth by means of the mudrās, such as Vajrāṅkuśī, and their respective mantras.
Having summoned, caused to enter, bound, and brought under control the Jñānasattva, one should accomplish the practice.

By forming the hook-gesture (*aṅkuśabandha*) with the index fingers and the little fingers, one becomes Mahāṅkuśī; and by pressing the joints of the arms and the tips of the elbows against the backs of the chains, one binds Mārīcī. Having summoned the Jñānasattva with the mantra "Oṃ Vajrāṅkuśi Jaḥ," one should offer the water for honor (*argha*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth before him. This is the sealing (*mudraṇa*) of Mārīcī.

Then, one should cause [the disciple] to enter with "Oṃ vajrapāśa hūṃ," bind [him] with "Oṃ vajrasphoṭa vaṃ," and satisfy [him] with "Oṃ vajrāveśa hoḥ. Thereafter, one should always effect non-duality with the Samaya deities. In this regard, the mudrā is as follows:
Having made both hands equal and joined in the form of an añjali,
one should make both tips open and bend both thumbs.
The two middle fingers, joined together and bound in the shape of a circle,
should then be placed at the region of the navel by one seated in the paryanka posture.
This mudrā is excellent and supreme; one should employ it in all rites.
Thereafter, one should receive empowerment by means of this great mudrā.
With the thumb as the essence of the being in the paryaṅka posture, its tip bent against the tip of the body;
with the middle and upper parts equal,
the remainder is like the radiance of the vajrāñjali.

Having thus placed [the deity] upon the head, one should meditate on Vairocana, who is golden-hued and established in the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), upon the head with the mantra: *oṃ bhūḥ khaṃ māṃ abhiṣiñca*. When weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra:
*oṃ mārīcyai svāhā*, visualizing the mantra shining intensely, situated upon a moon disk within one's own heart.
Having seen [this], one should recite [it],
preceded by meditation according to one's ability, while inspiring all the goddesses.

[Only in ḍh] Having visualized [k: subsequently], one should recite the mantra. Afterwards, one should fulfill any deficiency or excess in the ritual procedure with the hundred-syllable mantra. In this regard, the mantra is as follows: Oṃ vajrasattva samayamanupālaya.
Abide as Vajrasattva; be firm for me, be well-pleased with me, be devoted to me, be well-nourished by me,
grant me all accomplishments— do not harbor doubt.
And in all activities, make my mind auspicious:

*huṃ hahaha hoḥ! O Blessed One, Vajra of all Tathāgatas, do not abandon me; become the Vajra, the Great Samaya Being! Āḥ!* At the time of dismissal, however, having dedicated all this merit, one should pray for the desired accomplishment and [release] one's own mudrā.
One should release [the syllable] at the head with "Oṃ mārīcyai muḥ. Through union with one's own tutelary deity, one should perform all activities—eating, bathing, giving, sleeping, and so forth.
Having thus performed the protection of body, speech, and mind according to this sequence, one should dwell in ease.
By whatever merit has been acquired through composing this sādhana of Mārīcī,
may all sentient beings attain the state that is stainless with the primordial wisdom of Mārīcī.
Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi gṛhṇa gṛhṇa gṛhṇantu sārvabhautikā baliṃ mama śāntiṃ kurvantu svāhā. This is the mantra for the bali offering. The Sādhana of Mārīcī as taught in the Kalpa is complete.
This work is the composition of the scholar-teacher Garbhapāda.
Homage to Mārīcī!
First is a sun-maṇḍala; upon it is the first of the thirteen seed-syllables, adorned with a half-moon and a bindu.
From that, one should visualize Mārīcī, red in color, with six faces— the first red, the second black,

the third dark blue, the fourth yellow, the fifth white, and the sixth, the upper boar’s face, black— adorned with an Aśoka tree and a stūpa, pot-bellied, beautified by a garland of skulls, and with hair standing upright.
Adorned with serpents, clothed in a tiger skin, the destroyer of obstacles,

mounted upon a chariot drawn by boars of various colors, she holds in her right hands a sword, a vajra, a mace, an arrow, a single-pointed vajra, and an axe; in her left, she holds a noose with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).
[She holds] an Ashoka sprout, a Brahma-head, a bow, and a trident;
thus she has twelve arms, three eyes,
is red in color and circular in form, and has ornaments dangling from her mouth.

In the middle of the chariot, one should visualize a second [form] with two arms, holding a sprout-like threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) before her. Thinking, "I myself am the Blessed Lady Mārīcī," one should then form the mudrā. Having joined the hands in the vajra-añjali, then [the middle fingers...]
O Māra, because of the contraction [of the letters ḍ, dh, dh, k, ḍh, and g], [the reading] *samākulaṃ* [is found]; this provides no meaning.
This emendation is proposed on the basis of other similar stanzas.
Her two big toes are joined at their tips by her crossed legs in the paryaṅka posture.
Oṃ mārīcyai māṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā. The *Mārīcīsādhana* is completed.
In the teaching, for the sake of pacifying all calamities when [the teaching] has arisen for only a single eon.
The wise one should meditate upon Mārīcī in order to attain the form of omniscience.

Furthermore, having again worshipped according to the ritual the Guru who stands in the midst of all the Buddhas of the three times— beginning with praise— and so forth, one should perform the teaching and other rites from the moon at the heart.
[The forest deities] ||
I confess all my evil deeds; I rejoice in the merit of the world;
I go for refuge to the Three Jewels; and I set my mind upon perfect enlightenment.
Because of the non-existence of duality, it is empty, signless, and causeless;
for this reason, the world itself is the wishless, the threefold liberation.
In a shrine situated within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), containing relics upon the path of the Buddhas,
which is endowed with a square shape and so forth, pervading the sky with a radiating flood of Buddhas.
Outside and inside, within a four-cornered mandala of the moon marked by a three-pronged vajra,
it is established upon the king of mountains, whose base is trampled by wicked beings.
Therein, one should meditate upon the reality of Māmakī, born from a cluster of *aśoka* flowers,
possessing a luster like Jāmbūnada gold through the sentiments of love, heroism, and true joy.
Her central face is the color of sapphire,
while her other faces are crystal and moon-like; they possess the expressions of fear, disgust, and wrath, as well as compassion, wonder, and peace.
(From *pdf* 166, p.
298) With the three doors of liberation, she possesses the three eyes, and is the emanation of the enjoyment body of the Dharma.
She wears yellow eyes, ornaments, and fine garments, and dwells happily amidst rays of light.
She sews and binds his mouth and eyes with needles and thread;
she pierces his heart and throat with hooks and nooses, and with arrows and bows.
Having pierced the hearts of the wicked with the Vajra, and having rendered them unsatisfiable with the Aśoka,
one should cause those wicked ones to be destroyed by means of the eightfold eightfold [set] of liberations.
The practitioner should meditate upon Mārīcī, who has stepped upon the positions of wisdom and means, whose self-view and delight therein arise from the expansion and contraction of her feet.
Uttering "JAḤ HŪṂ VAṂ HOḤ," one should cause all the Buddhas— who manifest as the essence of all directions, times, and phenomena, and who perform the act of withdrawal— to enter into that [maṇḍala].

One should visualize the locus of the consecration of Śāśvata as an ocean of nectar in full jars, arising from the vidyās born of the limbs of the Buddha, and possessing a jeweled crown and a silken turban upon its form.

With those who hold the vajra and are occupied with all acts of worship, such as incense, flowers, and so forth, one should indeed perform worship and praise; by that means, one shall then behold this.
Stabilizing body, speech, and mind, one should recite the mantra over the cotton wick while addressing it with apprehension,
appending the name of all the wicked and malicious ones ending with the fourth case.
One should recite it eight hundred times at the four junctions of the day, or three times, or in the morning;
however, while contemplating that Great Vidyā for a great purpose, one should recite it one thousand times.
Having recited [the mantra], performed worship and praise, and having bowed down according to the auspicious purpose,
one should dissolve the perfectly awakened ones into oneself and, free from attachment, dismiss them.
The dismissal and the empowerment are known as the common three syllables,
employed in the tantra at the time of consecration for the accomplishment of body, speech, and mind.
Even during the intervals between the junctions of the day, one should recite this preceded by worship and other rites;
furthermore, at dawn, impelled by the Goddess’s assembly, one should do so again according to the previously mentioned rule.
Reciting this vidyā as well as others,
that excellent mantra-practitioner, being devoted to the tradition of the tantra, should accomplish [the goal] thoroughly.
By whatever merit has been acquired through this slight sketch of Picuvāleśa,
may the world be blessed in every respect, and may I myself become Mañjurāṭ.
The *Śrīmārīcīpicuvāsādhana* [variant: *pirucā*] is completed.
Having bowed to the goddess Mārīcī, the crusher of all malevolent beings,
I shall now describe her sādhana, which accomplishes all ritual actions.
Seated upon the sattva-paryaṅka, adorned with the syllable Oṃ within a moon-disc at her heart,
she is red in color, blazing with divinity, and filled with manifold rays of light.
By them were produced the perfectly awakened ones, the bodhisattvas, and those of great supernatural power (maharddhika).
Having prostrated, worshipped, and consecrated with mantras, one should present the food offering and other items.

With this mantra—*vajrapuṣpe*, *vajradhūpe*, *vajradīpe*, *vajragandhe*, *vajranaivedye*, *oṃ hūṃ*—[recited] in every instance. Then, taking refuge in the Three Jewels and generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should meditate on the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*) preceded by the aspiration, with this: *oṃ*.

"I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness. Then, having contemplated the nature of all things, both stable and moving, one should contemplate the seed-syllable; subsequently: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. From that seed-syllable arises a wheel, and upon its hub—
Above that is a solar disc, upon which is the fifth seed-syllable (the letter *ā*) adorned with the moon and the bindu;
when all that has been brought to completion, one should contemplate oneself in the form of Mārīcī,
red in color, with two faces and twice-four arms.
She is clothed in a gracefully draped tiger skin, with her matted hair tied upward, wearing a jeweled crown, possessing three faces,
both of which have the face of a boar; her first face is gentle and has a smiling countenance.
[He is] everywhere possessed of the grace of the erotic sentiment, three-eyed, with a red left face in the form of a boar,
saluted while holding a vajra-mallet; and with a right face in the form of a boar, the color of rock salt,
saluted by Purandara while holding a vajra-noose.

She stands in the *ālīḍha* posture within the womb of the *caitya*, trampling beneath her feet Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the rest— the Vasus and Lokapālas— all of whom remain terrified and trembling, offering salutations and commands to the Bhaṭṭārikā,
while she holds her bow drawn back to her ear.
One should visualize her piercing the heart of the one to be accomplished with an arrow resembling an *aśoka* bud (as stated on p. 167, p. 301).
She wears a red bodice and upper garment, is adorned with all ornaments, and has a crown bound with *aśoka* flowers;
she holds an *aśoka* blossom and a *vasu* flower in her left hand, while her [left index finger] is placed at her heart in the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*);
in her right hands, she holds a vajra-noose, a great skull-cup, a thread, and a *bhadraghaṭa* vessel upon her head.

Holding in her hands a needle, a goad, a *bhiṇḍipāla* javelin, a sword, a knife, a vajra, and a staff, she wears a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmukuṭa*) with a royal whorl; she is peaceful, her eyes opened by wisdom, and purified by knowledge.

Having visualized [the deity] adorned upon the head as the essence of gnosis, one should commence all ritual actions. According to the oral instruction, having summoned, caused to enter, bound, and brought under control the Gnosis-being (jñānasattva), one should accomplish the rite. This is the consecration.

Having performed the worship and praise of the binding of the armor-band, one should thereafter commence the recitation (*jāpa*). Just as a lamp burns in a house when it is not moved by the wind, even so does the Dharma blaze within the body of one who delights in recitation with a one-pointed mind. Then...
One should form the mudrā:
with the thumbs in the posture of a sattva-paryaṅka, the tips of the fingers slightly curved,
the middle and index fingers held straight, and the remaining fingers possessing the luster of the vajrāñjali.

Having placed [the seed-syllables] on the heart, the *ūrṇā* (between the eyebrows), the throat, and the head with this: *oṃ mārīcyai huṃ sarvaduṣṭān mardaya huṃ phaṭ*. The third of the third and fourth [syllables] of the eighth [group], filled by the fourth of the seventh—thus completed—and those two adorned by the first and second, are white.
The mantra for peace (*śāntimantra*) of Indrānana was revealed during the middle watch of the evening:
*oṃ mārīcyai devadattasya śāntiṃ kuru svāhā*. This is the thirteenth [syllable] of the first [group].

The seed-syllable, adorned with a half-moon and a drop (*bindu*), is yellowed by the middle finger at dawn; facing north, this mantra is proclaimed for rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*): *Oṃ mārīcyai devadattasya puṣṭiṃ kuru oṃ*. Furthermore, the fourth letter of the eighth group and the first...

The thirteenth [letter] joined with the sixteenth, or else at midnight, [the mantra] is distinguished by the color red and the ring finger. *Oṃ mārīcyai devadattasya vaśam ānaya hoḥ*. This is the supreme method for summoning all things when properly joined: *Oṃ mārīcyai, summon the success of [Name], jaḥ!* One who has been consecrated into the mandala of Mārīcī, who is devoted to the guru, and who speaks the truth, attains accomplishment; there is no doubt for one whose vidyā-mantra has been recited before the deity. One should perform the confession of misdeeds and so forth. Then, having contemplated all phenomena, oneself, and the seed-syllable as mere appearances in the form of an illusion, one should recite the mantra for natural purity (*svabhāvaśuddhi*). Then, that seed-syllable transforms into an *aśoka* flower cluster, upon which is the letter *Āṃ* situated on a moon disc; all of this—
Having transformed oneself, one should visualize oneself in the form of Mārīcī:
yellow in color, with three faces, three eyes, and eight arms; wearing red garments and a red bodice and upper robe, adorned with all ornaments, and having Vairocana as her crest-jewel.
She is surrounded by a mass of shimmering garlands of rays, her lower lip resembling the *bandhūka* and *javā* flowers;

in her left hand she holds a goad, a noose, a bow, and an *aśoka* sprout with a thread, and in her right she holds a vajra, an arrow, a hook, and a needle; she resides within the interior of a *caitya*, mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven boars.

She is a maiden standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, in the full bloom of youth, with wide-open eyes. Her primary face is gentle and imbued with the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*); her left face is black, wrathful, and boar-like, terrifying with its frowning brow.

The southern face has a protruding tongue, is deep red, restless, and clever; it resembles a ruby (*padmarāga*). Below, it is strewn with flowers from an *aśoka* tree situated on a palace; beneath that is a circle of wind, and within it, Rāhu—emanating from the syllable *haṃ*—is swallowing the moon and sun, surrounded by four goddesses.
One should meditate upon the Bhagavatī.
Therein, to the east, is the goddess Vartālī, red in color and four-armed, holding a noose and an *aśoka* flower in her two left hands,

To the right is the goddess Vadālī, yellow in color, with four arms;
in her two left hands she holds a noose and a vajra, and in the right [she holds a sword]. (pdf 169, p. 304)
To the west is the goddess Varālī, who bears a goad and a single thread;
she assumes that same form and holds a noose and an *aśoka* flower in her two left hands, and a vajra-needle in her two right hands.
To the north is the red-colored goddess Varāhamukhī, who has four arms and holds an *aśoka* flower and a bow in her two left hands.

One should meditate on her holding an arrow and a vajra in her two right hands. Then, by means of the mudrās of Vajrāṅkuśī and the others along with their respective mantras, one should perform the summoning and other rites of the Jñānasattva.

One should perform the *kṣā* mantra with "jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ. Having thus attracted, caused to enter, bound, and subdued the Jñānasattva, one should satisfy him. Then, by means of the Mārīcī mudrā, one should effect non-duality. Preceded by meditation, one should perform the recitation: *oṃ mārīcyai svāhā*. Having dedicated all merit, one should dismiss [the deity] with: *oṃ mārīcyai mur*.
The Concise Sadhana of Mārīcī is completed.

I pay homage to her who has the Buddhas as her crest-jewel, with a crown adorned by blazing jewels,

To Mārīcī, the bestower of fearlessness.

One should perform the offering of oneself with clouds of divine worship— consisting of flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, food offerings, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the counselor-treasure— as well as with all the goddesses and the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),

Then, the verse "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature" should be recited. Then, seeing oneself alone, situated in the intermediate space, stainless like a mass of shimmering nectar, like the full moon complete with the entire assembly of its digits—

Having emitted those rays, one should summon the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas and cause them to appear before oneself.

Then, one should worship them with mental offerings consisting of vajra-flowers and so forth, accompanied by their respective mantras. Thereafter, one should perform the confession of misdeeds and the other preliminary practices.

Then, one should recite seven times: "Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature. Then, one should contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena with the thought: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness. Thereafter...
One should visualize a red lotus seven cubits in height in front of oneself. Above that is a slightly red moon disc arising from the syllable *Aṃ*.
Above that is a lotus arising from the syllable *Doḥ*, and again, upon the lotus—

Above that is a moon disc, and upon it, the syllable *doḥ*. Then, having projected a cloud of light rays and established all sentient beings comprised within the six realms of existence in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, one should cause them to enter the syllable *doḥ* in the form of Vajrasarasvatī. Thereafter, one should enter it oneself.
(As stated in *pdf* 187, p. 339:

Immediately upon entering oneself, one transforms everything into the Goddess who has three faces and six arms, adorned with various ornaments, with tawny hair standing erect, and standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon a red moon disc.
One should visualize her: her first face is red, the right is white, and the left is black;

in the first right hand she holds a lotus marked with a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā, in the second a sword, and in the third a flaying knife; in the first left hand an eight-spoked white wheel, in the second a nine-faceted jewel, and in the third—

The Brahma-skull. Just as the seed-syllable for the manifestation of the deity follows immediately after the samādhi of emptiness, so too should one visualize it again in the heart of the Blessed Lady. Then, having emitted rays from that seed-syllable, one should summon the Jñānasattva, worship him, and cause him to enter. Thereafter, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra.

With a well-concentrated mind, having recited [the mantra] two hundred thousand times, one then begins the ritual action. In this regard, the mantra is as follows: *oṃ picu picu prajñāvardhani jvala jvala medhāvardhani dhiri dhiri buddhivardhani svāhā*.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should practice the refined recitation (*saṃskṛta*) while gazing at the moon until it sets, continuing until the full moon. On the full moon day, one should sleep during the day and contemplate the practice for as long as the ritual lasts.
Then, even those scriptures never heard before will become manifest; one shall retain a thousand verses day by day.
The crusher of all opponents, beloved by gods and humans. The *Vajrasarasvatī-sādhana*, extracted from the *Kṛṣṇayamāri-tantra*, is completed.
(Namo vajratarasatyai |) Homage to Vajratarasatya!
The sādhana is written according to the sequence of the four Brahmās. As before, having meditated on the syllable AṂ upon the moon at the heart...

From the syllable *aṃ* upon a white lotus and moon disc born from the syllable *paṃ*, she arises through the radiation and reabsorption of light, extending from the confession of misdeeds up to the realization of emptiness and enlightenment;
she is white in color, enchanting, holding a red lotus in her right hand and a volume of the *Prajñāpāramitā* in her left, and is marked by the *Vajrasamāja-mudrā*. Oṃ.
Having first performed the entry of the Jñānasattva with *vajrasamāja jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ*,

one should visualize Prajñāpāramitā seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture. Having meditated on the syllable *Aṃ* situated upon a moon at her heart, one should recite the mantra— *oṃ picu picu*— through the sequence of radiating and reabsorbing light.

*Prajñāvardhani jvala jvala medhāvardhani dhiri [kh, a: ciri ciri] dhiri buddhivardhani svāhā*. One should visualize this mantra as blazing like a row of lamps, emerging from the mouth and entering the navel-cakra; in this same manner, it should be visualized for others as well. And so it has been said:
First is the realization of emptiness; second, the union with the seed-syllable;
third, the accomplishment of the image; and fourth, the placement of the immutable syllable.
Thus ends the *Sādhana* of Vajrasarasvatī.

341) According to the previously described procedure, one should visualize [the goddess] produced from the yellow syllable *Bhṛṃ* (or *Huṃ*), having four arms and one face, yellow in color, with three eyes, in the bloom of youth, and holding a boon-granting gesture (*varada*) and a rosary (*akṣasūtra*) in her right hands.

Having meditated upon the Blessed Lady— who holds a water-pot (*karaka*) in her right hand and a triple staff (*tridaṇḍī*) and a water-vessel (*kamaṇḍalu*) in her left hands, who is sealed by Amitābha, and who is seated upon a lotus and moon—
she should form the mudrā with the two thumbs of her outstretched hands.
Having covered the two nails of the little fingers, one should then recite the mantra: *oṃ bhṛṃ svāhā*.
The Sadhana of Bhṛkuṭī.
Homage to Bhṛkuṭī.

According to the previously mentioned procedure, one should place the seed-syllable— the fourth of the sixth [vowel], joined with the first of the eighth [consonant]— in the center of the moon within one’s own heart.
It is filled by the deity Śūnya, stepped upon by an *ardhacandra*, and adorned on the head by that very same [deity].
From this, one should visualize Bhṛkuṭī, yellow in color, with four arms, wearing a crown of matted hair, peaceful,
granting boons with her right hand and holding a rosary, while with her left she holds a triple-staff (*tridaṇḍī*) and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).

One should visualize her seated upon a lotus and moon throne; then one should form the mudrā. As before, having covered the nails of the little fingers with the two extended thumbs, the remaining fingers are individually marked with the vajra-sign; this is [the Bhṛkuṭī-mudrā].
The Bhṛkuṭī Mudrā. Thereafter, one should recite the mantra: Oṃ Bhṛḥ Svāhā.
This is the *Sādhana* of Bhṛkuṭī.
